Owens has laid out a sophisticated picture of how the deontic features of our life might be grounded in interests. In this way, he develops the tradition of Hume in a form that modern nonconsequentialist philosophers can find satisfying and compelling.Were the appeal to normative and deontic interests only in service of answering these deep metaethical questions about the grounds for our social obligations, the project would be philosophically important. But it has a whole other dimension as well. It potentially informs first-order questions. According to Owens, “With rights and wrongings, form follows function” (35). The idea is that the interests that explain why a norm is binding also shape the rights and wrongings that the norm generates. Where the interests belong to a particular person, then the obligations are owed to them and breaches generate wrongings directly. Where the underlying interests are collective, the obligations have a different form and potential wrongings are only derivative. Importantly, there is a spectrum; many social obligations are a kind of hybrid. Norms of neighborliness arguably serve both individuals (e.g., me and the woman next door) and a community to which they apply (e.g., small-town Maine). The woman next door stands to be wronged directly if I am particularly brusque and antisocial as I head out for a run. I owe it to her to do better, which is a function of the fact that her interests are part of what ground the obligation. If someone else up the road must do extra caretaking because I drop the ball with my neighbor, that person too might be wronged, but only indirectly, as my obligation of neighborliness is not owed to them individually.In this vein, the second half of Bound by Convention is devoted to exploring how the modest conventionalism developed in part 1 can explain the contours of certain seemingly conventional obligations—rules of competition, the family, private property, truthfulness, and privacy. The book will be important reading for anyone interested in any of these topics. Each chapter is independently thought-provoking.Consider private property. Owens begins his discussion of private property by arguing that people have interests in certain things counting as theirs, interests that involve identification and control. Our interests in our bodies and our possessions cannot be fully explained in instrumental terms, as that cannot explain our concerns when another’s use wouldn’t interfere with our own—for example, being photographed while asleep, a harmless 3 a.m. trespass. Nor is our interest in control only about actual use, which can be impaired by natural phenomena. As Owens puts it, “The difficulty of reducing our interest in exclusion to our interest in use suggests that we are dealing with an essentially social interest, one that necessarily concerns my relations with others, relations that involve their being allowed differential access to myself and to what I own” (183). What we need to ground the relevant rights and duties is a normative interest, an interest in having normative authority.” Owens contends that property rights in certain personal things, like one’s home, exist at least in part to serve this authority interest. That’s why you owe it to me not to trespass in my home, and why you would wrong me if you did.But the social institution of private property extends far beyond private residences. Property rights are held by corporations, investors, and many others who in no way identify with the property. Here, Owens regards private property as an impersonal convention, existing to serve collective interests much as political offices do. Accordingly, rights and wrongings will follow that function. “Since individuals are not given the right to control such things as Trump Tower (as opposed to their own homes) in order to serve either their control or authority interests, there is no basis for Trump’s feeling personally wronged by harmless violations” (195). There is something intuitively plausible here, and it shows the power of Owens’s approach to understanding the shape of our interpersonal obligations by way of the normative interests that undergird them.As plausible as I find these claims, I am curious about the shift in focus to normative interests, away from the deontic interests that figured so prominently in part 1 but fade somewhat in part 2. Perhaps my ownership of my house serves to protect my control and authority interests. But if one is persuaded by Owens that it can be meaningful and good to be bound, one might wonder about other explanations. What if private property is less about empowering and more about binding? Notice that my owning my house is intertwined with my being a neighbor. What if the function of private property were to make us neighbors and stewards—to bind us to responsibilities that bring meaning to our lives? Indeed, perhaps what is noteworthy about the investor-owner is less that they don’t stand to be wronged by harmless trespass and more that they occlude others from the meaningfulness that ownership can convey.That’s admittedly a radical and underdeveloped suggestion. I mention it to flag the power of the conceptual tools that Owens develops. A potential complaint of some readers might be that Bound by Convention feels small-c conservative, a defense of existing social structures. But that’s not correct. It is a defense of the fact that our social structures shape our rights and obligations in profound ways. That is something that anyone thinking about normative relations of any kind should take seriously.

articles.t: Definition and Dispute: A Defence of Temporal Externalism
articles.ab: Metasemantic externalism holds that facts external to speakers or thinkers—say, the fact that the watery substance in their environment is H2O—can partly determine the meanings of their expressions, and the contents of their thoughts. Temporal externalism (TE) posits that “facts about what happens at later times can play a role in determining the meaning of our words (and the contents of our mental states) at earlier times” (3). This intelligent and rich monograph offers the first book-length defense of TE, which makes it mandatory reading for anyone interested in metasemantics. The book does quite a lot besides defending TE. Among other things, it rebuts the aspiration of conceptual engineers to provide a novel methodology distinct from theorizing (chap. 3), it argues that paradoxes like the liar are hard for the same reasons of scale and dearth of resources that makes scientific challenges hard (chap. 4), and it offers a pragmatics on which the conversational parameters determining who counts as ‘tall’ or what counts as ‘funny’ are retroactively set by the judgments the participants arrive at in the end (chaps. 8 and 9). However, I will exclusively consider the case for TE. Just like the author, I focus on TE as a metasemantics for language rather than for thought.Much of the discussion in the book concerns what the author calls ‘definitional disputes’ (2). These are those common “disputes that seem (in some sense) to turn on matters of definition” (2) we engage in whenever we discuss issues such as: Is same-sex marriage possible? Is Pluto a planet? Is free will compatible with determinism? Are atoms mereological simples? Must art be intended to be beautiful? Definitional disputes are ostensibly driven by reasons and argument. Suppose you surmise, “But art has to be beautiful!” I might bring you to change your mind by pointing out that artists may well intend their works to be disturbing rather than beautiful—just think of Marcel Duchamp and his urinal. Now ‘art’ is a vexing term, and debates about art are hard to interpret by anyone’s standard. Still, the author uses ‘art’ and something like our little dispute as his default examples throughout the book.Definitional disputes play a dual role in the author’s view. First of all, their outcomes are seen as metasemantically relevant. TE holds that future facts can determine the present meanings of terms such as ‘art’. Which facts are these? The author sees TE as particularly committed to the idea that future discursive facts can play this role: “The conclusion we reach at the end of the debate can act as a stipulation that determines what we meant all along” (101). Suppose that our dispute about art eventually leads to a number of claims we accept. On TE, these future claims can provide a meaning-determining implicit definition for ‘art’ that “fixes what all parties to the dispute meant all along, regardless of what they believed at earlier times” (101). Whose future claims are relevant? Yours and mine? Those of our distant discursive descendants? The author doesn’t commit. He defends TE as a generic view for ‘art’, ‘atom’, and their ilk. This allows him to defer all issues of theoretical detail to the last chapter and discuss them as matters of mere choice.So—why should we agree that TE has to be right? It is here where definitional disputes come in again. The author believes that TE has to be right because this metasemantics offers the best explanation of how definitional disputes work. More specifically, he thinks that TE proves right once we establish the following claim:Meaning Sameness is a contentions idea. It runs counter to the view that definitional disputes are metalinguistic negotiations. It also doesn’t square with the Ramsey–Carnap–Lewis metasemantics the author himself enlists in his argument against conceptual engineering. For if our meaning of ‘art’ is fixed Ramey–Carnap–Lewis-style by our collection of platitudes about art, and if my observation about Duchamp’s urinal and its disturbing qualities—which concerns art rather than ‘art’ and so isn’t metalinguistic—brings us to drop the platitude “Art has to be beautiful,” then our theory of art and the meaning of ‘art’ will both change.Although the dialectic is somewhat intricate, it seems fair to say that the author’s extensive case for TE very much pivots on Meaning Sameness. On the most natural reading, his first two signature arguments are meant to support Meaning Sameness, while the third argues from Meaning Sameness via generic externalism to TE. First, the Wrong Kind of Reasons Argument (chap. 3.2) aims to rebut the competing view of definitional disputes as exercises in metalinguistic negotiation that effect changes in meaning: If definitional disputes are metalinguistic and thus “about how to use words,” practical “reasons to speak a certain way” in the forms of threats or bribes should settle these disputes (27). Since they don’t—they are the wrong kinds of reasons for this—definitional disputes are not about how to use words. The limits of this argument become apparent once we recognize that our metalinguistic negotiation does not concern the unqualified question “How should we use ‘art’?” It rather concerns the more specific question “How should we use ‘art’ in order to sensibly classify things?” Bribes or threats don’t settle this matter, even though it explicitly concerns language use.Second, the Argument from Charity (chap. 6.4) aims to show that charity compels us to take retrospective reports of error such as the following at face value:There is much to be said here. Our situation is arguably more complex: We initially introduced atoms as those indivisible objects that play a specific explanatory role in chemistry-cum-physics but later found that being indivisible and playing that role came apart. According to the Ramsey–Carnap–Lewis view, we had a choice between concluding that there are no atoms after all and implicitly redefining their characteristic properties by adapting our platitudes, and we opted for the latter. Still, the most important thing to note is that for all their apparent naturalness, condensed and decontextualized (self-)reports make for equivocal evidence at best. This becomes apparent once we see that reports which explicitly say that meaning has changed may feel just as natural. Consider: “I used to say ‘Atoms are indivisible’, because I thought that atoms are indivisible. But then modern physics changed the meaning of ‘atom’, and I saw that I had been wrong. It turns out that atoms are divisible after all.”These arguments convince the author that we should accept Meaning Sameness. (Here I go with his summary on page 97.) He understands Meaning Sameness to establish some form of externalism, since this metasemantics best explains how ‘art’ and ‘atom’ can have stable meanings even though our beliefs about art and atoms differ a lot. But which variety of externalism should we accept? The Argument from Spurious Evidence (chap. 5.3.2) is meant to rule out externalist rivals to TE. The idea is this: Kripke-inspired views see meanings as fixed by initial introductions. But then “considerations about the historical origin of the practice of using a word” (84) should settle definitional disputes. Since they don’t—historical facts just aren’t relevant—these externalist alternatives to TE fail.This argument against causal-historic externalism hardly makes a strong case for TE. First, let’s agree: Evidence about past usage does not settle definitional disputes. But why should evidence about future usage fare any better? (Pointing to present paradigms such as Duchamp’s urinal does fare better, which supports the views mentioned below.) Second, Kripke (1980: 138–39) himself hints at a dynamic picture when he allows that “the ‘original sample’ gets augmented by the discovery of new items.” Third, externalist metasemantics such as Sally Haslanger’s (2012: 374) ‘objective type externalism’ or my own ‘paradigm term semantics’ (e.g., Nimtz 2017, 2021) see meanings as externally determined by the paradigms we presently accept (and, on my account, a suitable equivalence relation that does rather a lot of explanatory work). The author discusses no such views. True, neither approach considers ‘art’. But we are comparing generic theories, and we haven’t yet seen a detailed TE for ‘art’ either. The author is also right to emphasize that there may be no suitable unique objective type for ‘art’ (169). But this just means that ‘art’ may be indeterminate, polysemous, or context dependent. Given that we have no assurance that the future discourse on ‘art’ will converge rather than fragment, this hardly speaks in favor of TE. In actual fact, it may simply underscore once again that ‘art’ is a rather vexing term to begin with. So there is no easy argument for TE even if we accept Meaning Sameness for the likes of ‘art’ or ‘atom’—which, for the record, I don’t think we should.Beyond arguing for TE, the book provides a broad discussion of issues pertinent to this metasemantics, such as the metaphysics and epistemology of properties that things have at times in virtue of what happens at later times, such as being good on a consequentialist view that has goodness depend on the actual outcome (chap. 7), or the meta-metasemantic underpinnings of TE (chap. 10.4). Incidentally, I feel that the latter reveals much about the general perspective the author takes throughout the book. In virtue of what does TE hold true? Noting that the standard idea—that this is due to the dispositions speakers have (Cohnitz and Haukioja 2013)—doesn’t quite fit his case for TE, the author gives a fundamentally different answer: Future facts play a role in determining meanings “because [this] is the best way of interpreting us so that our definitional disputes and inquiries are reasonable and make sense” (177). This idea is highly instructive. For once we read TE as an interpretationalist metasemantics, it appears a far more enticing and, given the robustly realist moorings of standard externalism, a far more radical view indeed.

articles.t: Wittgenstein and the Possibility of Meaning: “To Follow a Rule Blindly.”
articles.ab: Alexander Miller’s book is a valuable contribution to the debates initiated by Saul Kripke’s reading of Wittgenstein’s rule-following considerations. It offers an excellent presentation of the problems, an appealing account of the historical development of some of the main attempts to deal with these problems, and a lucid proposal for how to address some of the difficulties faced by these strategies. The book is organized in five chapters and an epilogue.Chapter 1 sets out some basic parameters for the problems to be discussed. It presents Paul Boghossian’s ACER account of rule-following, summarized thus by Miller: “An agent following a rule can be said to have accepted [A] the rule in such a way that his actions are partitioned into those that are correct [C] and those that fail to be correct relative to his acceptance of the rule, and, moreover, explained [E] and rationalised [R] by that state of acceptance” (4; letters in brackets added). Miller’s book assumes that the ACER model is correct and treats its satisfaction as an admissibility condition for a candidate account of rule-following. He argues that his own proposal comes sufficiently close to meeting this demand. He also maintains that candidate accounts of linguistic meaning and mental content have to satisfy suitably adapted versions of the ACER model. He defends this view against the claim, which some find in Wittgenstein’s Philosophical Investigations, that language should not be seen as a rule-guided activity.Chapter 2 provides an excellent presentation of Kripke’s Wittgenstein-inspired argument for the conclusion that there can’t be facts about what a speaker means by a linguistic expression. On Miller’s presentation, the conclusion is derived from the impossibility of satisfying the ACER model. He pays particular attention to dispositionalist and nonreductionist accounts of meaning facts. Defending a version of the latter is Miller’s ultimate goal. The chapter also offers insightful accounts of the obstacles faced by error-theoretic and nonfactualist responses to Kripke’s reasoning.Miller takes the arguments presented in chapter 2 as successfully establishing that rule-following, linguistic meaning and mental content cannot receive satisfactory reductionist accounts—accounts that specify in nonsemantic terms, necessary and sufficient conditions for someone to follow a particular rule, attach a particular meaning to a linguistic expression, or have a propositional attitude with a particular content. It follows that a nonreductionist approach offers our only hope of providing a satisfactory account of semantic facts. Miller is well aware that nonreductionism is itself plagued by problems, including some that Kripke himself had raised, but he proposes to assume provisionally and for the sake of the argument that these problems can be overcome and that a nonreductionist account can survive Kripke’s arguments against the possibility of facts about rule-following, meaning, and content.Chapter 3 takes this assumption as its starting point in order to concentrate on arguments that have been claimed to threaten the possibility of semantic facts even if nonreductionism survives Kripke’s challenge. The arguments, versions of which have been developed by Paul Boghossian and Crispin Wright, relate to the notion of blind rule-following. They purport to show that any account of semantic facts, reductionist or nonreductionist, will be incapable of satisfying the rationalization component of the ACER model—on any account, a subject’s acceptance of the relevant correctness conditions won’t rationalize her responses. The conclusion is meant to apply even to accounts that have survived Kripke’s challenge. Chapter 3 is devoted to a detailed presentation of these arguments.We can present the general idea of the blind rule-following problem, along the lines of Boghossian’s version, by considering the circumstances under which my doing A could count as following a rule of the form “If C, then do A!” This would seem to require that I have an intention with this rule as its content and the belief that C now obtains. It would also seem to require that my action results from an action-guiding state with the content “Do A!” and that this state is produced by an inference from my intention and my belief. But performing this inference would require following a different rule: If you have the intention “If C, then do A!” and the belief “C,” then conclude “Do A!”And if concluding “Do A!” is to count as following this rule, then an action-guiding state with the content “Conclude ‘Do A!’” will have to be produced by an inference, which will require following a different rule, or a different application of the same rule. A regress looms.Chapter 4 presents Miller’s proposal for dealing with the blind rule-following problem. It is based on the Wittgenstein-inspired idea that there is a way of grasping a rule that is not an interpretation. Grasp of a rule can also arise, Miller contends, from “training in a custom, practice or institution” (6), and this alternative, noninterpretive form of rule grasp can still guide the rule follower in her application of the rule. Miller argues that the possibility of noninterpretive rule grasp blocks the regress that gives rise to the blind rule-following problem. If my acceptance of the rule “If C, then do A!” is noninterpretive, then I can count as applying the rule by doing A without being guided by the inferential rule that starts the regress.In chapter 5, Miller discharges the assumption introduced in chapter 3 that a nonreductionist account can survive Kripke’s arguments. He argues that the kind of noninterpretive rule-following that his position contemplates has the resources for blocking Kripke’s arguments against nonreductionism, including, prominently, worries about the ability of a nonreductionist account to explain the first-person authority of self-knowledge of meaning and intention.The epilogue briefly discusses two outstanding issues for the brand of nonreductionism that the book advocates: the extent to which the position should treat rule-following as involving an essentially social element and its ability to ascribe genuine causal efficacy to content properties.This is a nuanced, tightly argued book, demanding deeper engagement that would be possible in this review. In the remainder, I’m going to restrict myself to flagging two issues. I want to focus first on the role that training in a custom, practice, or institution is supposed to play in the account. I think the issue can be seen in the following way. Suppose S has the intention to do A if C and the belief that C now obtains. Now S forms an action-guiding state with the content Do A! and proceeds to do A. What conditions would have to be satisfied in order for S’s doing A to count as acting on her intention to do A if C? Miller assumes, plausibly, that some condition will have to be imposed—that having the relevant intention, belief, and action-guiding state is not sufficient for doing A to count as acting on the intention. One condition we could impose is that the production of the action-guiding state involves an inference from the intention and the belief, but imposing this condition, Miller maintains, renders the regress unstoppable. An alternative condition that we might want to impose is that the action-guiding state needs to be caused by the intention and the belief. Miller takes this to be a necessary but insufficient condition for doing A to count as acting on the intention. The reason why it’s insufficient is the possibility of deviant causal chains (105)—there are causal routes from the intention and the belief to the action-guiding state that wouldn’t make doing A count as acting on the intention. Ruling out deviant causal chains is Miller’s reason for the bracketed qualification in the formulation of the condition he proposes: “Following a rule R is a matter of being caused (in the right kind of way) to act in a manner that conforms to R in virtue (inter alia) of having an intentional state with the rule R as its content” (98–99).The point I want to highlight is that in this formulation of the condition there is no mention of customs, practices or institutions, and my question is what role these are supposed to be playing in the proposal. Here’s Miller’s answer to my question: An intention to uphold a rule combining with a suitable belief to cause an action “in the right kind of way” is a matter of the relevant agent’s having been suitably trained or brought up in an appropriate custom or practice. So the exclusion of deviant causal chains via the inclusion of “in the right kind of way” in our account meshes well with an account of rule-following in which interpretation is superseded by training, custom, and practice, etc. (107)One way of understanding this is as presupposing an independently intelligible notion of deviant causal chain and making a substantive claim to the effect that when an agent has been suitably trained or brought up the relevant causal chains are never deviant. If this is the right reading of the passage, Miller’s claim would need more support than is offered. Wouldn’t deviant causal chains still be possible when the right training is in place? In Miller’s own example of a deviant causal chain (105), there is no reason to think that the agent hasn’t undergone the right training.Alternatively, we could read the passage as providing a definition of when a causal chain from an intention and a belief to an action-guiding state counts as nondeviant—namely, when the agent has received the right training. If the passage is read in this way, then the qualification “in the right kind of way” in Miller’s formulation above should be understood as “when the subject has been suitably trained.” But if we read it in this way, Miller’s proposal for when doing A counts as acting on the intention to do A if C is much more vulnerable, as it is far from obvious that suitable training will rule out all causal chains of the kind that intuitively would not count as making the agent act on her intention, even if Miller’s definition classifies them as nondeviant.The second point I want to highlight, more briefly, is the role that Miller assigns to abilities in his account of rule-following. He writes, “Let’s say that accepting a rule consists in having an ability to suit one’s practice to its dictates and intending to do so” (119). Does accepting a rule really require the ability to suit one’s practice to its dictates? Miller points out, correctly “that it is possible to have an ability yet be prevented from exercising it” (120). This observation neutralizes some potential counterexamples to Miller’s claim, but he maintains that in cases in which the ability is really not present, “the agent in question has not after all managed to accept the rule” (121). I don’t think this is in line with our intuitions about when someone has accepted a rule. Suppose a novice sailor is given the following rule for upwind helming: If a gust comes, head up. It is perfectly natural to say that he can accept the rule even if he is too incompetent to suit his practice to its dictates—he can’t reliably recognize the arrival of a gust or he often bears away when he intends to head up. However, Miller can’t easily abandon the claim that accepting a rule requires having the ability to suit one’s practice to its dictates, as it is needed in his explanation of the noninferential nature of first-person knowledge of rule-following: “If S possesses the ability, S can have non-inferential knowledge of the identity of the rule she is following” (126).Miller has written an excellent book, certainly compulsory reading for anyone interested in the rule-following debates. His proposal will be of interest, in particular, to those of us who are convinced that reductionist accounts of semantic notions are not to be had, but are worried about the obstacles faced by nonreductionist views.

articles.t: On Gaslighting
articles.ab: “Gaslighting” has become a household word in a relatively short time. Yet it is deployed in various ways, suggesting a multifaceted referent, thus enticing philosophers to provide analyses and interpretations of the phenomenon. Kate Abramson’s contribution to this philosophical project is careful, insightful, nuanced, and eminently readable.She anchors her account to the dynamic between Paula and Gregory in the 1944 film Gaslight, from which gaslighting got its name. Here is the plot: Gregory is trying to drive his wife Paula insane so he can institutionalize her once he locates some jewels that are hidden somewhere in the attic of their London home, which Paula inherited from her aunt. His strategy is to routinely question, and to induce Paula to question, her accurate perceptions and memories. The title of the film refers to Gregory’s insistence to Paula that she is imagining things when she reports the gaslights dimming, when all the while he knows they are dimming each time he turns up the attic gaslights to search for the jewels.Abramson cleaves her analysis to the film because there is, she says, a real and distinctive interpersonal phenomenon exhibited there. Her objective is to capture what we are saying when we say that Gregory is trying to drive Paula “crazy.” Her method, to this end, is to offer an initial account of gaslighting and then refine it by specifying the typical contexts in which gaslighting occurs, the characteristic aims of gaslighters, and their paradigmatic tools. Next, she shows why gaslighting cannot be a structural phenomenon, as some have proposed. Finally, she outlines the multitude of wrongs and harms suffered by targets of gaslighting, elaborating extensively upon the harm gaslighters cause by exploiting targets’ trust.This is the core of Abramson’s account: “Gaslighting is a form of emotional manipulation in which the gaslighter tries (consciously or not) to induce in another not only the sense that her reactions, perceptions, memories and/or beliefs are so utterly without grounds as to qualify as ‘crazy,’ but also the sense that she isn’t capable of forming apt beliefs, perceptions, reactions and so on” (13). Gaslighters are both trying to make their targets think that they are crazy and trying to make them crazy. Abramson invokes here the colloquial notion of “crazy” with its pejorative valence and its association with incapacity: One who tries to drive another crazy aims to incapacitate that person, and one who wonders if one is crazy doubts one’s capacity to properly grasp reality.Gaslighting, she observes, is more common in certain contexts, including intimate and hierarchical relationships. Furthermore, gaslighting takes place diachronically. However, single incidents are identifiable as the sorts of incidents typically included in the pattern that constitutes gaslighting, and Abramson provides numerous vignettes to orient her discussion. Here are two: (1) A woman academic is slapped on the rear by a colleague at work and is told by the colleagues to whom she reports the event that it isn’t a big deal, and that she’s being oversensitive.(2) An employee’s new boss spreads false rumors about her and neglects to include her in important meetings. When she confronts him, he tells her she is being paranoid and suggests that she take some time off to “de-stress.”These vignettes, Abramson says, reveal a puzzle: gaslighters clearly want to dismiss their targets. Yet if dismissal is the objective, why don’t the individuals who are told of their colleague’s sexual harassment simply shrug and say, “Tough luck”? Why do they instead insist that the complainant is out of touch with of reality? This puzzle dissolves, Abramson claims, once we understand gaslighters’ motives: They aim not merely to dismiss their targets but to undermine them as deliberators and moral agents. Gaslighters are so threatened by challenges (from certain people) to how they see things that they must not only destroy the challenge but must destroy the challenger, and they do this by making her into a “crazy person.”The tools commonly used by gaslighters to position their targets as crazy, Abramson explains, allow us to distinguish gaslighting from adjacent phenomena such as guilt-tripping. More importantly, though, they explain how persons can be manipulated into doing something so profoundly undermining as doubting their standing as independent moral agents and deliberators. Those tools include exploiting targets’ trust, relying on their reasonable belief that they might be wrong, isolating them, taking advantage of their love for the gaslighter or their empathy for others, relying on the high cost of resistance, leveraging institutional authority, and exploiting cultural stereotypes. Gaslighting is especially insidious, Abramson adds, because in exploiting the target’s love, trust, empathy, and so on, the gaslighter turns the target’s basic human dispositions and capacities against her.Abramson concedes that living within unjust and harmful social structures is often “maddening.” Nevertheless, she maintains that we should not extend the notion of gaslighting to include some of our experiences with such structures. Such an extension would cause us to lose sight of what is distinctive about the phenomenon of gaslighting and what is distinctive about the structural phenomena we wish to assimilate through the extension. To be sure, the presence of pernicious social structures facilitates gaslighting: A boss’s claim that his female employee needs to take time off to “de-stress” is likely funded by the assumption that women tend to be overly emotional. In the end, though, gaslighting is something only persons do to other persons, Abramson claims, and individual gaslighters are morally responsible for their conduct.Abramson is insistently pluralist about the wrongs and harms of gaslighting, and her analysis of these is highly insightful. Some of the wrongs of gaslighting are wrongs of manipulation, others are epistemic wrongs, others relate to gaslighters’ tools, others have to do with the way targets are made complicit in their own undoing, and yet others are connected to gaslighting’s propensity to silence its targets. The harms of gaslighting include causing targets to be depressed and making a “devastated mess” of their ability to trust. Some of the specific wrongs identified by Abramson include diminishing targets’ self-respect, undercutting their deliberative abilities, and damaging their capacity for personal autonomy.Abramson’s analysis of how gaslighting harms targets in the domain of trust is most original. To make her case, Abramson identifies three features of interpersonal trust that have not been theorized: its normative framing feature, shape sensitivity, and demand for particularity. The first has to do with the fact that trusting someone enables that person to wrong one in ways that would not be wrongdoings if one did not trust them. The second has to do with the fact that what we can trust others with may shift over time. (One might come to trust one’s friend with one’s plants but not one’s pets.) The third relates to the fact that we trust people with respect to specific things and not broad roles. (One does not trust another simply “as a friend” but rather trusts that person with one’s plants as a friend.) Abramson’s argument is that gaslighters exploit these features of trust thus causing their targets to be in limbo, neither quite trusting nor distrusting them.One way a gaslighter may take advantage of the normative framing dimension of trust is to frame some aspect of his relationship with the target as a matter of his trust in her and then set her up to appear untrustworthy. An example from the film occurs when Gregory gives Paula a brooch which he claims belonged to his grandmother, explicitly stating that he is trusting her not to lose it and suggesting that she put it in her purse for safekeeping. Later he removes it when she is not looking and accuses her of losing it and thus betraying his trust. Gaslighters may exploit the shape sensitivity of trust by showing themselves trustworthy about something for a period and then abruptly betraying the target. A boss, for instance, might provide good mentoring advice to his employee and then suddenly undermine her by giving her a terrible piece of advice that hurts her career. Gaslighters may exploit trust’s demand for particularity by stressing to the target that the two of them are in a trusting relationship—as, say, spouses—but then betraying that trust regularly, causing the target to cast about for something particular she can trust the gaslighter with.I am generally sympathetic to Abramsons’s account, yet I believe her method of building upon the dynamic depicted in the film generates two problems, one methodological and one substantive. The methodological worry is this. Gregory’s conduct in the film is intentional, planned, and conscious. He has a specific goal of which he is aware, a malicious motive, and a well-honed strategy, and, importantly, he cares not at all for Paula. Abramson countenances a certain amount of slack between her characterization of gaslighting and the phenomenon depicted in in the film, granting that most gaslighters are not as self-aware, malevolent, and/or tactical as Gregory is. She also maintains that gaslighters are, unlike Gregory, often emotionally invested in the opinions of their targets. So, typical gaslighters, we learn, are not so much fiendish and calculating as much as they are beset with anxiety and afraid of disagreement.At the same time, though, Abramson opposes views of gaslighting that deviate in other ways from the film’s depiction. She rejects, for instance, the idea that someone can gaslight another without aiming to destabilize her, as some have proposed. She maintains further that gaslighting cannot be merely a matter losing confidence in one’s basic epistemic capabilities in a certain domain, as others have proposed. Yet we are hard pressed to discern in her approach a principle for determining which deviations from the classic case are conceptually permitted, as it were, beyond the observation that too broad an account will render the notion vacuous or cause us to overlook a distinctive practice. It seems that the many phenomena associated with gaslighting (dissembling, dismissing, doubting, deceiving, denouncing, etc.) might cluster together to form a morally significant and distinctive phenomenon reasonably denoted “gaslighting” that differs from Abramson’s conception. It is not clear how we determine which of these is the real thing.Considerations in favor of alternative views might include the following. First, a person may be as badly damaged by clueless individuals devoid of ill will telling them that they do not understand their own experiences as they are by those with malevolent intentions. Why insist, then, that gaslighters as such aim to undermine their targets? Second, if gaslighting succeeds only when a target questions her standing as a deliberator and moral agent, gaslighting might not often succeed. Some individuals who face the kind of treatment Abramson describes might remain generally confident in their standing as deliberators but suffer from debilitating bouts of self-doubt about specific matters—for instance, the motives behind, or the justifiability of, their boss’s conduct toward them. We might want to claim that someone who is suffering in this way has been successfully gaslit to avoid the implication that gaslighting is rarely successful.My substantive worry concerns Abramson’s claim that gaslighting is strictly an interpersonal dynamic as it is shown to be in the film. While it may be that structures themselves do not gaslight, as Abramson avers, it is hard to deny the existence of collective gaslighting, and Abramson’s view appears to make little room for this practice. Plausibly, a collectivity might try to manipulate someone into thinking that her reactions are utterly groundless, as when a person receives ongoing institutional reinforcement for his accusations of oversensitivity leveled at a victim of sexual harassment. Likewise, an individual—say, a political actor—might try to manipulate a group—say, the citizenry—into thinking its perceptions are not tracking reality. Indeed, these deeply troubling practices appear to be common at this time in the United States, and there seems little justification for treating them as something other than gaslighting, given their similarities with the interpersonal case.

articles.t: Of Rule and Office: Plato’s Ideas of the Political
articles.ab: Plato can easily appear to be a theorist untouched by anything like an “ideal of limited constitutional government” (5), one interested not in the institutional limitation of those in political power but simply in whether those in political power have the appropriate political expertise. Melissa Lane’s book Of Rule and Office shows just how deeply this appearance risks distorting our perspective: Lane’s Plato is deeply concerned with what she calls “the Juvenal conundrum” (6)—that is, how to ensure that roles of rule are appropriately delimited, filled, and controlled so as to foster the good of the ruled—and while Plato’s preferred solution to this conundrum does indeed involve entrusting the city to unaccountable expert rulers (what Lane calls “safeguarding rulers” [218]), he nonetheless recognizes the need for and importance of legally regulated accountable offices, not only in the second-best, nonideal city (of the Laws) but even in the ideal city (of the Republic); moreover, in Lane’s view, even the safeguarding rulers, while not accountable, still occupy legally delimited roles designed to help keep them trained on the good of the ruled. Plato, in short, is much more of an institutionalist than one might have thought.Lane builds up this picture in four parts.The first part is introductory, initiating us into the project (chap. 1) and providing the required conceptual, linguistic, cultural, and methodological background (chap. 2). It is here that Lane introduces and develops two distinctions that figure extensively in her study. First, she takes archē (and cognates) to be systematically ambiguous between a generic sense (“rule”) and a specific sense (“office”): while any epitactic or order-giving role counts as rule, only such roles as are rendered (sufficiently) accountable through a set of appropriate limits or parameters (paradigmatically in the form of procedural audits) count as offices. Second, Lane distinguishes between what she calls the taxis and telos of rule: the telos is the end toward which ruling is oriented—ultimately, on Plato’s view, the good of the ruled—while the taxis is the way rule is organized so as to contribute to this telos.The second part traces Plato’s constructive treatment of rule and office—the telos and taxis of rule and office as they should be exemplified—in the political theory of the Laws (chap. 3), Statesman (chap. 4), and Republic (chaps. 5–7). The Laws turns out to be quite traditional in its configuration of offices, more notable for the seriousness with which Plato takes the goal of the cultivation of virtue than for its relatively minor institutional innovations (90). Perhaps most surprising in Lane’s account is that the members of her Nocturnal Council are neither officeholders nor (mere) rulers: lacking any epitactic powers, they act merely as “guardians of the spirit of the laws” (111), a kind of collective constitutional conscience. The thesis is highly intriguing, though it does force some strained readings (e.g., of 968a1–4 and 968a7 [113]).By contrast to the council of the Laws, Lane takes the eponymous figure of the Statesman to exercise a kind of constitutional guardianship that, while not an office, is a genuine role of rule. The most original feature of her discussion is likely the (confessedly speculative) suggestion that the statesman leaves mechanisms such as election for the selection of officeholders intact, playing only an indirect role in selection by “set[ting] up background conditions for the activity of others” (135).Lane sees the basic pattern drawn in the Statesman—of a safeguarding, nonofficeholding ruler who maintains the orientation of the system of offices toward the good of the ruled—realized in detail in the Republic: the philosopher kings and queens of the Republic are nonofficeholding rulers whose function does not displace that of officeholders but is primarily focused on maintaining the educational system and the selection of who will be promoted to offices and to their own ranks. According to Lane, the Republic recognizes roles subordinate to that of the philosopher kings and queens as offices, since they are subject to parameters such as a definite process of selection, eligibility requirements, and limited powers (215). These are the roles held by the cohort of guardians aged thirty-five to fifty (217). More provocatively, Lane also suggests that the philosopher kings and queens are ultimately not so different from these officeholding subordinates: “While not officeholders,” she says, they “are nevertheless distinguished by limits that serve some of the same functions as those typically found in Greek offices” (222).The third part of the book describes Plato’s theory of what happens when rule and office fail to be appropriately configured, as we find it in the twin and parallel narratives of the degeneration of city (chap. 8) and soul (chap. 9) in the Republic. Perhaps the most significant thesis to emerge from her treatment of these narratives is that the two principles that drive the degeneration of the city, what she calls the Predominance principle and the Disunity principle, concern specifically offices and officeholders, rather than rulers generally. Lane takes the text introducing the Disunity principle to explicitly make this restriction—notwithstanding that it creates difficulties for herself, since she thinks the rulers in Kallipolis are not officeholders (271–72). In Lane’s view, this surprising restriction is at least partially explained by the fact that in the degenerate regimes, all rulers are mere officeholders at best (270). This claim, however, is somewhat surprising, as it seems to ignore what Aristotle calls “indefinite office,” the sort of position held by the democratic assemblyman (Pol. 3.1, 1275a26–33). This problem is obscured by Lane’s concession that Plato means to include those eligible for office, as well as those currently holding office, in the Disunity principle, since in Plato’s democracy (unlike the real Athens) everyone is eligible for office (270). This gets the right answer extensionally, but remains unsatisfying: surely disunity in the assembly as such—that is, not merely qua collection of potential officeholders—is relevant to explaining degeneration, yet the role of rule exercised by assemblymen as such is passed over by Lane’s Disunity principle. One worries that Lane here is clinging more tenaciously to her rule of thumb that archai (in the plural) means “offices” (43) than the text will bear.The book’s fourth and final part defends two general theses about rule and office. One of these concerns the source of the important social goods of civic freedom and friendship for Plato: according to Lane, these rest on a general willingness to obey rulers, in turn grounded in a general cooperativeness, that is often (but not necessarily) the result of a constitutional order of law and office (chap. 10). The other concerns Plato’s attitude toward anarchy as a political ideal: Lane’s Plato views external or political rule as necessary and good precisely to the extent that souls are unable to rule themselves, so that, while he holds out as an ideal the philosopher who does not need to be politically ruled, he embraces the necessity and goodness of political rule in a world in which not all are philosophers (chap. 11). Unfortunately, Lane only really defends half of this very interesting thesis: While she makes clear why a lack of self-rule creates a need for external rule, she does not make clear why there is no need for external rule for the well-ordered soul. (One would have thought that even a city of philosophers would need to solve coordination problems.)As this highly compressed and selective conspectus indicates, Lane’s study covers an impressive amount of ground. This scope is often a strength—but it is also sometimes a weakness. For example, Lane follows the degeneration of both city and soul in exceedingly close detail, following Plato’s narrative minutely and in order (or reverse order, in the case of the soul), rather than allowing her original theses to organize and constrain her treatment. The result is a certain lack of focus, as issues peripheral to Lane’s own main concerns and contentions crowd in and receive lengthier treatment than they perhaps deserve. The effects of this somewhat unfocused approach are exacerbated by a general lack of tightness in Lane’s prose that sometimes makes her discussion unnecessarily drawn out and difficult to follow.A more substantive issue is that the analytical machinery Lane deploys is in some respects underdeveloped. For example, it can be difficult to pin down exactly what Lane means by taxis, notwithstanding its status as her own term of art (27). Most usually, it refers to the order of a constitutional system as a whole: Lane introduces it as “an ordered set of roles and relationships … through which the telos might be achieved” (18). But immediately before this description, it appears to describe the order belonging to a given particular role of ruling: Rule, she says, is “a relationship between a ruler and one or more persons ruled, which can be characterized in terms of two dimensions: a telos … and a taxis” (17–18). This makes it seem as though any given relationship of rule is partially defined by the taxis of that relationship. Again, while typically used with reference to the institutional design of roles of rule, it sometimes seems to describe any sort of order in ruling, even if entirely self-imposed (123–24, 243). And, while usually the order that defines particular roles (or systems of roles), it is sometimes the order that belongs to rule as such (123–24). Finally, Lane sometimes uses taxis to describe not the order that delimits the ruler’s role but the order that the ruler imposes (44, 49, 52, 170). Such instability threatens to undermine the purpose of introducing terms of art in the first place.Similarly, there seems to have been a missed opportunity to develop a vocabulary that would have allowed for a more precise categorization and understanding of the different kinds of limits on rule. For example, one thing that emerges gradually from Lane’s discussion is that, although (at least in some moods) she is willing to countenance any sort of constitutional limitation on rule as conferring (some) accountability (5, 14), limits enforceable by an independent agent carry a special weight, since it turns out to be the lack of such enforceability that explains why safeguarding rulers are not officeholders (222, 231). But while we get considerable piecemeal discussion of various limits on rule, there is little discussion about what is distinctive of enforceable limits and the different ways and degrees in which a limit might be enforceable. Developing such a finer-grained analysis would have helped clarify the force and significance of the contrast between office and (mere) rule.Notwithstanding these shortcomings, Lane’s book remains a major contribution to our understanding of Plato’s political thought, whose fresh perspective has the potential to give new and exciting directions to Platonic scholarship for years to come.

articles.t: The Afterlife of Race
articles.ab: What should we do with the idea of race? This question animates Lionel McPherson’s far-reaching and thought-provoking new monograph. Its title tips his hand: McPherson is ready to move on.McPherson is a “deflationary pluralist” when it comes to ‘race’. The pluralist instinct is understandable: We have attached multiple meanings to that word. To this relatively uncontroversial position, McPherson adds two assessments. The first is that given the plurality of its meanings, ‘race’ is neither stable nor informative, to the point that racial discourse is semantically “unruly” (3). If it cannot be managed, then trying to make it work is wasteful and even counterproductive. The second is that the idea of race was created, distributed, and normalized to facilitate Europeans exploiting non-European peoples and lands: it is “more an effect than a cause of subjugation, exploitation, and nonrepair” (77).Given the fruitlessness and ugly etiology of ‘race’, McPherson arrives at deflationism: It’s time to give up the term in favor of alternative terms that carry less semantic and ethical freight. His favored replacement term is ‘geoancestry’. ‘Geoancestry’ marks the geographic origins of our progenitors and by stipulation acknowledges the varied social and political inheritances of organizing our world around those lineages. As McPherson carefully documents, deploying ‘geoancestry’ can accommodate a range of phenomena from mixed and blurred ancestry to social significance to injustice to color labels.The etiology is difficult to contest. McPherson’s survey of the ideological landscape pushes hard to the conclusion that the function of racial thinking has more or less always and pervasively been one of unjustly empowering and enriching one group of people at the expense of wronging and harming others, in a way that sculpted the idea of race we inherited and continue to reshape today.The unruliness charge and the conclusion that it is time to deflate ‘race’ appear more contestable. McPherson thinks that philosophers who have tried to identify the definition or at least one very common definition for ‘race’ have reached an unbreakable “stalemate,” where no one analysis is winning the philosophical battle. So, he concludes, the battle is no longer worth it. For those engaged in that branch of race theory, this inference may be too quick. The stalemate argument pivots on the premise that philosophical disagreement about ‘race’ persists. One wonders if we must also give up ‘free will’ or ‘mind’. Moreover, even acknowledging that various meanings have been attached to ‘race’, it seems that a whole nation, like the United States, can talk about race without the speakers babbling past one another, referring to different things. Sometimes dialogue about race is even international. If we are not just engaging in stark miscommunication, then some common meaning to ‘race’ must anchor those conversations. Even if that meaning is opaque to most or all communicators, and even if it is an elusive target for theorists, it seems too early to just give up on the project of identifying it.Surprisingly, McPherson himself offers an analysis of ‘a race’: “one of a few discrete human groups that formed when geographic collections of people became biologically distinct, with each group forming on separate landmasses” (14). We are also told that “we have no core understanding of race—except in the narrow sense that human beings descended in full or part from respective continents tend to look different in characteristic ways” (15; see also 79). This compounds the curiousness: Why go deflationist when we could adopt McPherson’s “narrow” analysis? And why is this analysis better than the rival candidate analyses put forth by other race theorists?McPherson does indicate one reason why race is not just about continental ancestry: there is supposed to be some additional “X factor” (13) that connects the body and mind in a way that explains all the awful conjectures about how culture, ability, character, and even bare humanity might tie to different geoancestral origins. But why attribute this baggage to the very core of the concept, rather than it being a belief that is contingently attached to and therefore removeable from conversations involving race, an appendage that is integrated but not inseparable? Is the very concept so rotten that we must entomb it in the Hall of Failed Meaning and Reference?An optimist might dream that one day we could see race talk without racist talk. McPherson argues that such optimism does not realistically track the history of how the idea of race has been used (e.g., 30, 55–59). So perhaps the point is more psychosocial than conceptual: If the race idea is not conceptually racist, it is inevitably deployed in racist ways. Then again, the fact that people float ideas—even widely contested, false, and immoral ideas—about a subject matter does not mean that there is no good definition of that subject matter. People persistently float ugly and inaccurate proposals about differences between the biological sexes, but this is not reason to avoid a narrow definition of biological sex (contested as that concept also may be).More questions arise regarding McPherson’s fascinating proposal to replace ‘race’ with ‘geoancestry’ “in order to avoid verbal conflict and mass confusion” (82). Is it more realistic to think that the ugly claims that have been made about race will not reemerge with ‘geoancestry’? Consider the alternative proposal of abandoning ‘race’ for the neologism ‘racialization’, which refers to the social fact of being treated as racially different. McPherson thinks this substitution attempt is hopeless (77). What, then, makes ‘geoancestry’ more worthy of hope? If it is unrealistic to say that ‘race’ can be severed from toxic associations, how is it more realistic to hope that those poisons won’t be adapted to whatever terms we invent in the vicinity of race?Given these outstanding questions, it seems that we still need an all-things-considered evaluation to guide conceptual engineering: How should we choose between keeping our term ‘race’ as is; replacing it with nearby alternates like ‘geoancestry’ or ‘racialized group’; and redefining ‘race’ to be both accurate and ethical? The pluralism-based deflationary argument is: Let us avoid the “metaphysical drama” (22) of philosophical debates about race and just note that people with ancestors from different parts of the world tend to look different. Fair enough. But while people ignore the metaphysicians, still they need to know why they should not keep using the term ‘race’ for that idea that people with ancestries from different parts of the world tend to look different.McPherson points out that we can examine how racial ideology has shaped our social world (40) or how racism works (44) without solving metaphysical questions about what race is or whether it exists. Moreover, the metaphysical questions philosophers of race often grapple with today are not “the [original] contested issue” on which the historical source of our grappling, W. E. B. Du Bois, was mainly focused (67). Both points are true. At the same time, it is also true that the social history of race ideology might not tell us much about what race is or whether it exists. It seems worth our trouble to conduct both investigations concurrently.These are just some of the questions raised by part 1 of the book. Readers will find further engaging explorations in the two further parts.Part 2 investigates the ethics and coherence of multiracial identity. McPherson elegantly rearticulates the pressing need for some people of multiple backgrounds to explicitly recognize their whole identity, noting both that such persons have often been alienated from their communities of origin—and in some important sense from their own selves—and that identifying as multiracial need not represent a betrayal of one’s more oppressed lineages. McPherson wants us to continue to facilitate recognition of individuals’ complex color-conscious self-identifications, so long as they respect the “conceptual constraint” that this self-identification reflects at least some part of one’s actual ancestry (117). (Another question: How does this conceptual constraint fit with deflationary pluralism?)At the same time, McPherson is doubtful that much sense can be made of the distinction between monoracial and multiracial identities. Descendants of American slavery, for example, have been counted as Black, but they are largely a population of substantially mixed African and European ancestry. What, then, does it mean to identify as multiracial if monoracial identity already includes multiplicity? For McPherson, the family relations that matter are more about social connection and only secondarily about ancestry (132).The problems he identifies get even more complicated. Does singling out multiracial identity imply that there is some important distinction between different fractions of the same ancestral line? Valorizing mixed racial ancestry also, he thinks, reentrenches the mythical and oppressive belief in natural races. Then there is the worry that multiracial identity is another mechanism for advancing colorism, the destructive privileging of lighter skin tones over darker skin tones regardless of (supposed) race, in its own way doubling down on a colorized social hierarchy.Part 3 covers the question of whether Black Americans carry special obligations of solidarity to end anti-Black social inequality, beyond the obligations all people have on that front. Insisting that Black Americans form a specific sociopolitical entity apart from any global Black race, McPherson again finds more utility in other conceptual categories besides race. He does believe that Black American political solidarity can be an effective tool in moving closer to equality, but also that it would place an unjustifiable “double burden” on Black Americans to require that, in addition to their group suffering under centuries of brutal white supremacism, they have a distinctive moral responsibility to shoulder the load of correcting that injustice.Instead, on McPherson’s account, all Americans have a morally urgent duty to rectify American injustices, and any special burden of repair falls on those who have been and continue to be complicit in America’s entrenched social hierarchy. Joining this movement is for Black Americans a commendable choice rather than a duty; as he puts it, those who join the solidarity movement must be “volunteers, not hostages” (169). Finally, McPherson argues that participating in the Black solidarity movement does not require being “racially” Black in any sense. Instead, everyone has good reason to support Black political solidarity: It is solidarity for Black American social equality, not necessarily solidarity by that group (171). In fact, the potential success of this morally urgent goal demands inclusivity.The Afterlife of Race is wide-ranging, interesting, and sure to provoke reflection and conversation about timely and central issues surrounding race. (It also includes a bonus chapter arguing that apology for oppression without material reparation is hollow, and forgiveness is beside the point of reconciliation.) If you read it, perhaps you will find yourself, as I have, exploring new avenues for thinking about the future of, or after, race.Thanks to Lionel McPherson for rewarding conversation that informed this review.

articles.t: Why Didn’t Nietzsche Get His Act Together?
articles.ab: Although Elijah Millgram identifies analytic philosophers as his “tribe,” he doesn’t have much use for the analytically competent work that has sparked the widely recognized improvement of Nietzsche scholarship over the last several decades. Such work, he complains, tends not to recognize that Nietzsche “writes funny” (2). It reads him “straight,” reconstructing his books on the “deeply misguided” assumption that he actually had views or beliefs. Actually, almost all important Nietzsche scholars of recent vintage recognize that Nietzsche doesn’t write like the typical philosopher, giving straightforward arguments for clearly marked positions. And they usually offer an explanation. Millgram’s explanation is certainly new: Nietzsche doesn’t write in the standard way because he couldn’t, for the same reason that he couldn’t get his act together. He is a decadent, a disunified agent “coming apart at the seams,” whose apparent beliefs do not count as such because they are not the expressions of an integrated person. Yet what emerged from his disintegration was the brilliant way of writing philosophy exhibited in his later books. The way to read them, Millgram claims, extending Alexander Nehamas’s reading of Beyond Good and Evil (hereafter BGE), is to ask “who their authors are” (39). He finds a different author for each book, a different voice or perspective, each exhibiting a different side of the agent that Nietzsche could not pull together: the genealogist or intellectual in Genealogy (hereafter GM), the good European in BGE, the convalescent in The Gay Science (hereafter GS), the psychologist in Twilight of the Idols (hereafter TI), and so on. This sounds interesting, even exciting, and it might have been if Millgram had made much of a case for his way of reading Nietzsche.It is hardly news that Nietzsche did fall apart, collapsing in early 1890 and spending the last ten years of his life insane. It would not be surprising if books finished shortly before his collapse showed signs of the impending disaster. And they do, it seems to us. The works of 1888, including TI, present their ideas more straightforwardly and even crudely compared to BGE (1886) and GM (1887), which exhibit a tremendous power to organize complex ideas in artistic and subtle ways. And it’s possible that we may find in the 1888 books what Millgram calls “blurts,” words that are not under Nietzsche’s control but are simply blurted out. The question is whether these are unfortunate effects of Nietzsche’s degeneration, as we are inclined to think, or essential aspects of the philosophy he was doing in his later books, as Millgram claims. The evidence he presents for his view is that the same kind of blurts are found in GM and BGE. This is the crucial claim on which the plausibility of his whole interpretation rests.Millgram takes three elements from BGE—its theory of the soul as a collection of drives that may or may not be united into a fully integrated agent, its claim that Europeans are not fully integrated, and the occurrence of extended blurts in the text—from which he infers that BGE is presenting its author, “the good European,” as “a field of unregimented, quasi-independent drives successively seizing control of him for the duration of one or another ranting diatribe.” These rants express “misogynistic, antisemitic, and nationalistic excesses” that the good European goes on to disavow “on the elaborately theorized grounds that this personality was unable to anchor the full-fledged attribution of opinions, choices, and attitudes generally” (256–57). This is nonsense. First, the so-called diatribes do not read like rants. With the exception of the remarks on women, there is no vitriol in them, and they seem very much under Nietzsche’s control. But it does take some work to read them. The nationalistic “diatribe” begins with an over-the-top ode to Wagner’s overture to Meistersinger, but then changes tone, saying of Wagner’s overture, “no beauty, nothing of the south or of the southerly brightness of sky, nothing of gracefulness, no dance, hardly any will to logic” (Nietzsche [1886] 2003: 240). For anyone who knows Nietzsche’s views on music, this is clearly in Nietzsche’s own voice. It tells us what he wants from music and what Wagner’s music lacks. Contrary to Millgram’s reading, Nietzsche is referring not to this statement when he goes on to say “I have just given an example” of the “hearty fatherlandishness” that good Europeans may sometimes “permit themselves” for short periods, but only to the ode. Second, Nietzsche ([1886] 2003: 241) explicitly presents the ode’s nationalism as a “lapse into old loves and narrowness” and identifies overcoming “such atavistic attacks” as a “return to reason, that is to say, to good Europeanism.” So good Europeans may permit themselves patriotic feelings for a short period of time (think of cheering for one’s country at the Olympic Games), but only the overcoming of such narrow and outmoded feelings makes them good Europeans. Third, issues regarding unity and attributability (Millgram’s obsession, not Nietzsche’s) have nothing to do with Nietzsche’s disavowal of fatherlandishness. Rather, he is showing us what must be overcome to be a good European. In a good European patriotism is not an “unregimented” drive but rather a feeling that is “permitted” occasionally but has been put in its place. And it is perhaps a necessary feeling. If you don’t love your country, how are you going to learn to love less narrow communities?The so-called anti-Semitic tirade is even harder to read because instead of offering its perspectives consecutively, it goes back and forth between the one Nietzsche disavows and his own, making it impossible to discern which is which without carefully examining the content. Millgram doesn’t bother, finding the content “uninteresting” and “almost” what “you could have heard in pretty much any pub in Germany or Austro-Hungary” at the time. This is almost dishonest. Only in a footnote does Millgram explain the “almost,” acknowledging the suggestion at the end of Nietzsche “diatribe” that “it would perhaps be a good idea to eject the antisemitic ranters from the country” (251). That should certainly have led him to examine the content carefully to sort out the perspectives and see if it is really either anti-Semitic or a diatribe.BGE’s alleged misogynistic remarks are the only ones that even sound like a rant. One of us has written about this issue, arguing that these remarks are directed against “woman,” the social construction of womanhood (which a passage in GS [Nietzsche [1882/1887] 1974: 68] blames on men), and not against individual women who may not exemplify it (Clark 1994, 2015). Millgram lauds Clark’s article and accepts its view that the way Nietzsche frames his remarks suggest that they do not represent his beliefs about women but only his sentiments (302). But he disagrees with Clark’s view that Nietzsche is showing us how he overcame misogynist beliefs, even if some of the corresponding sentiments may remain. However, he does not acknowledge Clark’s argument (which is based on the wider framing of the relevant remarks, their presence in a chapter titled “Our Virtues,” and that chapter’s contents), much less provide any reason against it. He merely reiterates his account of Nietzsche’s alleged nationalistic and anti-Semitic rants. This might have some force if he had made plausible his account of these “rants,” but we have shown that he does not. In fact it is striking how unlike these “rants” his misogynistic comments are in tone and how difficult it is to see that Nietzsche’s own perspective differs from the one he disavows. It is as if Nietzsche is letting us know that he is still dealing with these feelings, unlike the nationalism and anti-Semitism he is way beyond.There is still hope for Millgram’s interpretation in his account of the author of GM as “prone to emotional outbursts that induced sudden swerves in his train of thought, and which made him unable to remain consistent over even short stretches of text” (256). That account provides the most detailed textual support for Millgram’s overall interpretation, and he appeals to it repeatedly to bolster weak interpretations of other books and to brush off any suggestion that Nietzsche’s “blurts” might be merely unfortunate effects of his impending collapse. If this account is plausible, we might grant that he needs weaker evidence for his account of the BGE “diatribes.” But it is not. Millgram’s claim is that Nietzsche obviously contradicts himself in GM; he is “standing up, waving a large, brightly colored flag, and practically shouting to the skies, ‘I am contradicting myself’” (17). The contradiction is supposed to be this: Nietzsche criticizes a theory on the grounds that forgetting is a lot harder than the theory supposes. Later, however, he claims that forgetting is the normal state for humans, so that severe punishment was required to “create a memory” in them. He even argues that forgetting is so easy that those who invented hell forgot that they invented it! And then “he rubs it in by later referring back to the discussion of his predecessors: ‘To say it again—or haven’t I said it yet? [i.e., I’ve already forgotten]—they are worthless’ (5:297/GM 2.4). And why worthless? Because they’ve forgotten the history of morality” (16). This is a terrible reading of the text.Nietzsche’s initial point about the difficulty of forgetting is directed against the “English psychologists,” those whose philosophical psychology is rooted in British empiricism. He sees them as trying to explain how human beings came to the idea that human qualities can be good in themselves, as opposed to simply useful or good for oneself. Kant’s account of the good will and the categorical imperative provides an answer, but he is no English psychologist; he is not attempting to fit morality into naturalistic picture of the world. Hume is trying to do so and therefore has a different answer, roughly that empathy moves us from an egoistic to a common perspective. Nietzsche does not accept either answer, but does not offer his objections when considering the answer of his naturalistic predecessors. This is because, apparently unbeknownst to Millgram, the predecessor he is most interested in is his own earlier self. He is criticizing and correcting his own theory from nine years earlier: that “one begins by calling actions good or bad … solely on account of their useful or harmful consequences” for oneself or those one cares about. “Soon, however, one forgets the origins of these designations and believes that the quality ‘good’ or ‘bad’ is inherent in the objects themselves” ([1878] 1996: 39). He criticizes his earlier view on multiple grounds, including the “psychological absurdity” of supposing that people come to consider a quality or resulting action good in itself (a virtue or virtuous action) simply by forgetting that they value it because of its usefulness to them, a “usefulness [that] has been the everyday experience in all ages, something therefore that was continually underscored anew; accordingly … could not help but impress itself upon consciousness with ever greater clarity” ([1887] 1998: I: 3). It is like explaining people’s pursuit of money as if it were good in itself by saying that they simply forget that they value it for what it can buy.Nietzsche’s criticism of his earlier and simplistic account in no way commits him to holding that forgetting is in general or always hard. It therefore in no way contradicts the claim that humans are naturally forgetful, by which he means that many of our mental processes are kept out of consciousness and that this is required for health. Nietzsche alleges forgetfulness made punishment necessary in order to keep five or six “I will nots” in consciousness. The problem was never that humans forgot what it was in their own interest to remember (and that may not even have required consciousness) but that they had a hard time remembering—or caring about—what was in the community interest. That’s why it was necessary to create a memory in them. Millgram rightly points out, as if it is a problem, that this “creation of a memory” presupposes the existence of memory. If you are not already able to remember the pain it causes, punishment can’t teach you to remember anything. But Nietzsche is talking about a specific kind of memory here, what he calls “a memory of the will,” a memory of promises one has made. That one must already have the kind of memory animals have in order to develop a memory of commitments in no way contradicts GM’s original claim regarding the psychological absurdity of arriving at the idea of something being good in itself by forgetting that one calls things “good” to indicate that they serve one’s own interests.Consider now Millgram’s claim that Nietzsche uses the ease of forgetting to make it seem plausible that slaves invented the idea of hell to get revenge against the nobles who were oppressing them. “But if the slaves have invented their revenge,” Millgram objects, “why don’t they know it’s imaginary? And if they do, how can they find it satisfying? The account only makes sense if the slaves have forgotten.” But Nietzsche never says that the slaves invent hell for the purpose of getting revenge against the masters. Millgram seems to picture the slaves sitting around wondering how to get revenge on the nobles until someone says, “I know, why don’t we invent the idea of hell and its everlasting torments?” To the extent that Nietzsche thinks the slave invented the idea of hell, the point is that their ressentiment against the nobles attracted them to believing in a place after death, the idea of which had been in place for some time and which was developed into a place of punishment by resentful priests. There is no reason to take Nietzsche to hold that the priests, much less the slaves, were ever aware of why they believed in hell, and so no reason to think they forgot. So none of this shows anything like an obvious contradiction. Perhaps Millgram’s best argument for his claim about Nietzsche’s forgetfulness concerns Nietzsche’s evidently throwaway line: “to say it again, or haven’t I said it yet?” Millgram may be right that Nietzsche is indicating that he is being forgetful, but that is completely consistent with his theory. Further, he may be alerting us to a distinction between forgetting what you said and forgetting what you think. Nietzsche knows what he thought, but wonders if he said it. Is that really the sign of a personality falling apart, or a prompt to figure out the different kinds of forgetting Nietzsche is talking about?Millgram has one final card, which is his attack on the Principle of Charity (POC). He would undoubtedly charge that our “smoothing out” of the contradictions in GM is made possible only by our acceptance of the POC, which “requires you not to impute contradictions to a text whenever that is at all avoidable” (24). Although “philosophers are trained to apply and invoke the Principle,” Millgram claims that they don’t know why; “if you ask almost any professional philosopher for a justification, you’ll get reiterated insistence, but not an argument.” And so he chastises his analytic colleagues: “We shouldn’t apply the methods we were taught in graduate school merely by reflex.” When Millgram courageously breaks from his tribe to ask, “Why be charitable?” he discovers that charity was “originally … warranted by a feature of the text [the Bible] that made it appropriate, namely, its divine authorship.” Likewise, his reading of Nietzsche’s texts is warranted by a feature of these texts, that they are constructed “to exhibit the tendency of a personality type to inconsistency.” But since such texts “should be expected to exhibit inconsistencies,” this makes objecting to an interpretation on the basis of Charity “a mistake.” In the case of Nietzsche’s texts, “bracketing the Principle is no more than respect for the text in front of us” (25). We are of course applying a modified version of the POC in our interpretation of GM. As with any interpretation, one must aim to make the most sense of what the author is claiming, and that cannot be done if one leaves simply leaves apparent contradictions in place without considering how they might be resolved.
