Millgram’s own interpretation of GM is based on the same modified version of the POC that we apply, in its implication that it makes no sense for Nietzsche to say the things he does unless he is trying to show us that he is contradicting himself. Are we supposed to simply take his word for this, or are we allowed to consider whether it actually makes the most sense of what Nietzsche says in GM? We have argued that it doesn’t even come close.We end on a note of agreement with Millgram’s evaluation of Nietzsche as “an impressive figure, a deep and powerful philosopher, and someone that you have to take completely seriously, even when you’re not about to sign onto one or another view or program. You owe it to yourself, as a philosopher, to think his ideas through, and more often than not, my own experience has it, doing so will change your mind about something you had thought was a settled matter” (263). We just wish his book had provided much evidence for this evaluation.

articles.t: Dogwhistles and Figleaves: How Manipulative Language Spreads Racism and Falsehood
articles.ab: It’s easy to feel lost when trying to understand how language works in the contemporary political landscape. Social and political philosophers of language have made significant strides in providing tools for thinking about the relationship between language and politics—offering theories of slurs, silencing, hate speech, propaganda, generics, and a range of other power-laden uses of language. But understanding how these uses of language operate in the messy, complicated, ever-changing world of contemporary politics still presents a serious challenge. The ground seems to constantly shift beneath our feet.Jennifer Saul’s Dogwhistles and Figleaves embraces this challenge wholeheartedly, offering a model for future work in the social and political philosophy of language. Saul’s central aim is to provide a theory of two communicative maneuvers—dogwhistles and figleaves—and demonstrate the crucial role they play in propagating racism, misinformation, and polarization. Of particular interest to Saul is accounting for the rise of explicit racism and blatant falsehoods in political speech during the first Trump presidency and the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic.The book is divided into two parts: Part I introduces the core theoretical machinery of the book—the White Folk Theory of Racism, racial dogwhistles, and racial figleaves. Part II then draws on these theoretical tools to explain the proliferation of blatant falsehoods and conspiracy theories in political speech.Saul’s basic picture in part I is as follows: There is a norm—Don’t be racist—that prohibits the expression of explicit racism (20). Some language users actively support this norm (those committed to some form of anti-racism), some reject the norm (those who openly advocate racist ideas), and others accept a thin version of the norm but can be convinced to “look the other way” if the speaker can claim plausible deniability for racist speech (10). In this environment, dogwhistles and figleaves serve a particular function—they allow speakers to disseminate racist ideas while maintaining the appearance of abiding by the prohibition against expressions of racism. In the case of dogwhistles, this result is achieved via covert, coded speech. Saul divides dogwhistles into two main kinds: (1) “overt code” dogwhistles, which involve a “secret code” that is decoded by one group in the speaker’s audience while remaining unrecognized by another (42); and (2) “covert effect” dogwhistles, which prime the racist resentments of audience members without their awareness (48). For instance, speakers might refer to “States’ rights” or “inner city” Americans (43, 49). Figleaves, by contrast, are “additional bits of speech” that offer “cover” to speech that would otherwise be (correctly) understood as racist (10). For instance, a speaker might add “I’m not a racist, but …” at the beginning of an utterance or “… and some of my best friends are Black” to the end of an utterance (75–76). Successful figleaves and dogwhistles provide a form of deniability to speakers—dogwhistlers can always appeal to the code word’s ordinary (“innocent”) meaning, while the use of figleaves raises doubt about whether the speaker is really racist (57). In both cases, the speaker evades responsibility for racist speech, norm rejecters are emboldened, norm accepters are pacified, and norm supporters who point out the racism may be accused of oversensitivity (“wokeness”).The return to explicit racism presents a potential puzzle for Saul’s influential earlier work on dogwhistles: If there is a norm against explicit expressions of racism, why is it that explicit expressions of racism appear to be staging a comeback, with only limited negative political consequences? Saul’s initial theory of dogwhistles might seem to suggest the opposite trajectory—that speakers’ expressions of racism would become increasingly covert as they seek to avoid violating the prohibition against explicit racism. Yet now it seems that “saying the quiet part out loud” is increasingly accepted and even celebrated (as “owning the libs”) (2).Saul addresses this puzzle by providing an account of how figleaves can offer cover for even blatantly racist speech. Key to Saul’s argument is her discussion of the White Folk Theory of Racism. Saul argues that the theory of racism embedded in the norm—Don’t be racist—builds in a set of overly restrictive assumptions about what it means to be racist. For instance, Saul suggests it is often assumed that racism must involve a conscious belief in the biological inferiority of a racial group, that only individuals can be racists (not speech or institutions), that an individual must be racist “in their heart,” and that racists must be monstrous (24). With this tightly constrained definition of racism operating in the background, it is relatively easy for speakers to generate a figleaf for almost any expression of racism. All a speaker has to do is raise “just enough” doubt to “block the inference to the claim that the speaker is racist” (74). Speakers can raise doubt in various ways: by presenting their utterance as humorous (“It’s a joke!”), by deferring responsibility to others (“People are saying that …”), or by turning the accusation of racism on others (“I’m not racist, [my opponent] is the real racist”) (75–84). As long as these strategies cast some doubt on whether the speaker counts as racist according to the White Folk Theory of Racism, the figleaf will achieve its purpose. Members of the norm accepting group will be more likely to become convinced that even brazen expressions of racism are “not really racist” (98).A key innovation in part II of Dogwhistles and Figleaves is Saul’s theorization of the ways dogwhistles and figleaves contribute to the spread of conspiracy theories and misinformation. Alongside the norm against racist speech (Don’t be racist), Saul suggests we also accept a norm in favor of truth-telling: “Be truthful” (136). As with the norm against racist speech, dogwhistles and figleaves serve as ideal tools for speakers who wish to violate the norm of truth-telling while maintaining the appearance of abiding by it. Dogwhistles can be used for coded communication about conspiracy theories. For instance, seemingly innocuous phrases like “Nothing can stop what’s coming” and “Save the children” can signal a social media user’s support for QAnon (156–58). Figleaves can be leveraged to raise doubt about whether speakers have violated the norm of truthfulness. As with racial figleaves, speakers can claim that they are “just asking questions,” present themselves as merely reporting what “a lot of people are saying,” or qualify their confidence by saying, “I don’t know if this is true or not, but …” (144–48). Saul is careful not to overstate the case here—lies, bullshit, and conspiracy theories are not a new phenomenon in political speech, she reminds us. What has changed, Saul suggests, is that politicians have become more comfortable appealing to blatant falsehoods (with little fear of backlash) and conspiracy theories are increasingly “playing a larger role in our political discourse” (131). Dogwhistles and figleaves, Saul argues, have played a key part in enabling this new status quo by stretching the boundaries of what is understood as consistent with the directive to “be truthful.”One challenge for Saul’s project in Dogwhistles and Figleaves is the astonishing variety of different uses of language she aims to account for. Dogwhistles range from more familiar forms of coded speech to uses of language that prime racist attitudes below the level of conscious awareness. Figleaves are even more heterogenous. Figleaves may be bits of speech added just before or after an utterance (synchronic) or speech that is added much later on (diachronic) (74). Figleaves can appeal to humor, friendship, ignorance, political correctness, or any number of other potential qualifications or evasions. The same string of words may be a figleaf when used by one speaker and an innocent caveat when used by another. Saul even suggests that individuals can serve as “human figleaves” when members of a targeted racial group are strategically used to publicly defend racist policies (96). Finally, both figleaves and dogwhistles can come in intentional and unintentional forms.A natural objection to raise here is: Do dogwhistles and figleaves really pick out particular, distinct varieties of speech? Extending Saul’s account of dogwhistles and figleaves to deal with blatant falsehoods broadens the scope of her framework, but one might worry that it ends up too broad—and risks losing sight of the core linguistic phenomena that Saul’s account seeks to illuminate.This objection, though, misses what is distinctive about Saul’s approach in Dogwhistles and Figleaves. Throughout the book, Saul repeatedly draws our attention to the fact that speakers who use dogwhistles and figleaves must navigate and manage multiple audiences: those who reject norms against explicitly racist or obviously false speech, those who merely accept these norms, and those who actively support these norms. A key social function of dogwhistles and figleaves, Saul suggests, is to generate conflict and division between these groups. When a speaker uses a dogwhistle or figleaf, a specific dynamic tends to emerge: some members of the audience (norm supporters) point out the racism or falsehood, other members of the audience (norm rejecters or accepters) defend the speaker by appealing to the figleaf or innocent, surface-level meaning of the dogwhistle. A dispute ensues. Because the speaker is able to claim deniability for the racist message or the obvious falsehoods, criticisms of the speaker come across as judgmental and oversensitive. In this context, it is easy for norm accepters to be persuaded that the speaker is not really racist or not really a liar. The combination of doubt, deniability, and the high bar set by the White Folk Theory of Racism give the speaker near-immunity from challenge. The end product is rising polarization.Saul’s project is thus best understood as an account of the social function dogwhistles and figleaves play in these group-level dynamics of conflict over racist and false speech. What unites figleaves and dogwhistles is not anything about these utterances at the level of semantic content or even their specific pragmatic features. Rather, these uses of language are distinguished by the function they play in generating a particular kind of conflict and division between groups. This means that the array of speech included as instances of dogwhistles and figleaves will necessarily be broad and varied—any utterances that fulfill the social function will count. In my view, this is not a deficit of Saul’s approach. Rather, Saul’s attention to group-level dynamics offers a much-needed corrective to our typical focus only on interpersonal contexts of language use.Saul’s Dogwhistles and Figleaves is essential reading for anyone interested in understanding the politics of our time, the relationship between language and power, and foundational questions about the social infrastructure of language and communication. It is timely, accessible, and packed with richly detailed examples. It is attuned both to specific features of uses of language and the broader political context they occur in. Most importantly, readers will come away feeling a little less lost—and with some tools to help us address these pressing problems.

articles.t: Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons
articles.ab: Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons is as apt as a title can get. In the initial chapters, Robert Brandom gives us reasons for why one would develop a logic. These reasons are that logic studies and explicates reason relations, the foundational notion in a conception of language as a game of giving and asking for reasons. Ulf Hlobil, in the following chapters, gives us such logic(s) for reasons. In a jointly authored conclusion, Hlobil and Brandom ensure that the pieces fit together. The logic(s) for reasons indeed satisfy the reasons for logic. Hlobil adds an optional epilogue in which he presents a speculative metaphysics, derived from taking as Firsts the most general description of what is postulated by the logic(s) for reasons.Brandom’s chapters are, by themselves, a reason for the philosophical pursuit of rigorous logic as well. Writing against the background of the worked-out logics of the latter chapters visibly aids Brandom’s presentation, highlighting the use of logic to achieve clarity. One finds here the most lucid view yet of Brandomian neopragmatism. Some prior (if passing) familiarity is, however, still needed. The neopragmatist moves are made here with renewed perspicuity but not discussed in the same depth as elsewhere. Readers find a clear picture of what it is to rest a philosophy of language on reason relations but must look elsewhere for objections and responses, for the virtues and vices of this strategy compared to other approaches, or for its intellectual history. Such further discussion would, however, be misplaced in this work. The achievement here is to make the view and its upshots as clear as possible, both in its exposition and in its formalization.These initial chapters elaborate familiar Brandomia that are newly suffused with bilateralia, insights derived and elaborated from the expanding literature on bilateral logic. Reasons can occur as reasons for and as reasons against, so there are reason relations of entailment and of incompatibility. Bilateral logic promises an avenue to spell out such bifurcations and the latter chapters make good on the prospect. Overall, then, this is a happy marriage. It is only in the margins that the Brandomia occasionally rub against the bilateralia. For one, Brandom remains committed to the claim that “the fundamental speech act is that of … asserting” (3), but bilateralists require distinct “fundamental acts” of both “affirmation and denial” (30). This has downstream consequences.The book’s running theme is that logical vocabulary is explicative of more fundamental reason relations. To begin, suppose A is a reason for B. This can be expressed in a formal metavocabulary as A⊢B. However, it may not be possible to express in the object-language that A is a reason for B. Only after expanding the language with a symbol ‘>’ for the conditional, one can express that A⊢B with the object-language sentence ‘A>B’. Thus, having the conditional allows one to accept or reject that A is a reason for B, whereas without it one could only use A as a reason for B. Conversely, A may also be a reason against B, which may be expressed in the metavocabulary as A#B. Brandom’s primacy of asserting is thus about the relata of reason relations in the object-language: potential assertions stand in relations of entailment or incompatibility. Bilateralism provides a bifurcated metalinguistic description of the reason relations themselves.More precisely, Hlobil and Brandom define A⊢B to mean that commitment to accepting A precludes entitlement to reject B, and A#B to mean that commitment to accepting A precludes entitlement to accept B. It is clearest here how new bilateralist talk of acceptance and rejection refines old Brandomian talk of commitment and entitlement. But, oddly, the left-hand side of either definition mentions only acceptances while on the right-hand sides there is once acceptance and once rejection. It seems, however, that commitments to rejections can preclude entitlements just as much as commitments to acceptances. One’s commitment to reject ‘Socrates is speaking’ may preclude entitlement to also reject ‘Socrates is mute’ and preclude entitlement to accept ‘Socrates is orating’. Such relations may well be part of the game of giving and asking for reasons—now understood as involving commitments and entitlements to acceptances and rejections, no longer commitments and entitlements tout court—but cannot be expressed in the proposed metalanguage, at least not literally. That rejecting A precludes also rejecting B is equivalent to ‘⊢A,B’ and that rejecting A precludes accepting B is equivalent to ‘B⊢A’. But these expressions, strictly speaking, describe other rules of the game.Reason relations obtain between sentences but the relations themselves are described in terms of commitments and entitlements to acceptances and rejections. The role of commitments to rejections is absent. So the bilateralism of acceptance and rejection does not seem to map perfectly onto the bifurcation of entailment and incompatibility. Here is another reason to think so. As the conditional makes explicit the turnstile, negation is supposed to make explicit the pound sign. But negation alone is insufficient to express A#B in the object-language, as negation is unary and incompatibility is binary. One requires additional expressive power, conjunction, to say ‘not (A&B)’. So although negation can make explicit (unary) rejection, it cannot by itself make explicit (binary) incompatibility.My even being able to raise such fine-grained complaints is a testament to the clarity and rigor of the presentation here. That they even are complaints is a testament to the ambition of the project. The goal is to be able to make explicit any and all possible reason relations. This ambition is fulfilled to a remarkable degree. The matter of rejective commitments can be tentatively set to the side, as equivalent reason relations are covered.In chapter 3, Hlobil introduces the Non-Monotonic, Multi-Succedent (NMMS) logic. It has the property that for any set of atoms that stand in any configuration of entailment/incompatibility relations (given minimal constraints), each such relation can be expressed by an NMMS sentence. The logic is starkly substructural, so as to avoid making any undue demands on the foundational reason relations. Using a suite of charming examples, it is demonstrated that both entailment and incompatibility could be nonmonotonic and nontransitive. Then, since logical vocabulary is what allows one to explicate a reason relation, logical validity can be construed as whatever is valid regardless of the underlying reason relations. Hlobil demonstrates that these logical validities include the classical validities (consequence is, of course, still substructural). The examples and the results are so compelling that one could easily miss how sophisticated NMMS really is.For one, some operational rules are nonstandard. The usual right-rule for conjunction is to conclude Γ⊢A&B from Γ⊢A and Γ⊢B, but Hlobil adds a third premise, Γ⊢A,B. As before, Γ⊢Δ means that accepting all members of Γ precludes rejecting all members of Δ. Thus, a situation in which the two standard premises hold, but not the added third one, is one in which accepting Γ precludes rejecting A and rejecting B but does not preclude rejecting both. It is initially puzzling how this could be and, so, what work the third premise does. Earlier, Hlobil explains that Γ⊢A is merely a necessary condition for it being proper to accept A based on Γ. Thus, one can extrapolate, it can be that Γ⊢A without it being proper to accept A based on Γ. Then, the desired situation is one in which necessary conditions for the proper acceptance of A and B obtain (Γ⊢A and Γ⊢B), but it is still improper to do so since a necessary condition for accepting either does not obtain (not Γ⊢A,B).Similarly, the left-rule for disjunction lets one infer Γ,A∨B⊢Δ from Γ,A⊢Δ and Γ,B⊢Δ and Γ,A,B⊢Δ. The first two say that, given Γ, accepting A precludes rejecting Δ and accepting B precludes rejecting Δ. One may be inclined to shorten this to say that accepting A or B precludes rejecting Δ, so the third premise may seem superfluous. But, again, two necessary conditions for accepting Δ may obtain (namely, that accepting A precludes rejecting Δ and that accepting B precludes rejecting Δ), but a third necessary condition fails (namely, that accepting both A and B precludes rejecting Δ). For instance, Γ might have consequences not blocked by A and not blocked by B, that are yet blocked by A and B together. Thus, Hlobil logic has a three-legged disjunctive syllogism.These may be counterintuitive readings of the bilateral language. Readers are regularly reminded of the technical definitions, but some examples for the new rules would have helped. It seems that the Nixon Diamond will do for conjunction. That Quakers are pacifists is a necessary condition for properly accepting “Nixon is a dove” based on his religious affiliation; and that Republicans are interventionists is a necessary condition for properly accepting “Nixon is a hawk” based on his party affiliation. Yet it would not be proper to accept either conclusion, since either one is a reason against the other and, so, a necessary condition for accepting either fails. Hlobil’s third premise is therefore not met here and, thus, works to block the bad conclusion that Nixon is both a hawk and a dove. The initial puzzlement is resolved by reading the normative terms themselves as nonmonotonic: it could be precluded to reject A but still proper to reject A and also reject something else.Apprehending this reading is rewarded with a better understanding of how Hlobil and Brandom conceive of reason relations. Based on this understanding, however, some pragmatists may now say that the reason relations are once-removed from language use. There could be reason relations that never show up in the game of giving and asking for reasons since these relations express merely necessary conditions for something whose sufficient conditions are never (and perhaps cannot ever be) fulfilled. Then again, one may also take this to mean that the reason relations are the underlying subject matter of semantics beyond surface use, roughly akin to how representationalists study truth conditions that may never be met. Hlobil and Brandom go some way navigating this dialectic in the remaining chapters.The bilateral normative-pragmatic metavocabulary is merely used for the first formulation of NMMS. Chapter 4 explores the semantic-representational metavocabulary, in which entailment and incompatibility are alethic relations of inclusion and impossibility. This leads to a development of a truth-maker semantics for reason relations—and a natural definition of truth-maker consequence that is isomorphic to NMMS. Hlobil and Brandom note that both the normative-pragmatic and the semantic-representational viewpoints involve conceptual resources that go beyond the mere idea of reason relations. This makes them extrinsic metavocabularies.Thus, although both metavocabularies are about entailment and incompatibility, they do not share a notion of content. Chapter 5, then, presents a third route to NMMS, implication-space models, whose metavocabulary only involves conceptual resources derived from the reason relations themselves (making it intrinsic). This yields a definition of contents as inferential roles that requires nothing more than that the bearers of such contents stand in reason relations. This is a remarkable achievement and a significant contribution to the study of (propositional) contents. To compare: one might think of content as what is truth-apt. But to spell this out, one typically requires a host of additional notions (such as properties or truth-makers). Hlobil and Brandom present a notion of content free from such additions.The formal work is, therefore, deep and significant. Hlobil and Brandom make a conciliatory move in the debate between inferentialists and representationalists. Both approaches, they maintain, are just two ways of talking about one subject matter. Representationalists study reason relations in alethic terms; inferentialists study them in normative terms. This is a striking intervention. Both inferentialists and representationalists can speak of the same contents by using the intrinsic metavocabulary. Previously, given some suitable completeness result, they could at most agree on equivalent consequence relations among very different contents. Hlobil and Brandom thus open an avenue for conciliation also on the metaphysics of meaning.Naturally, this can only go so far. Not all representationalists (nor all inferentialists, for that matter) will agree that their object of study is reason relations. In the end, the pragmatics first order of explanation (the primacy of giving and asking for reasons) remains nonnegotiable to Hlobil and Brandom. One may also wonder whether the conciliation survives conflict. Given two contents, an inferentialist might claim that they are (normatively) incompatible while a representationalist denies that they are (alethically) impossible. A Moore paradox might lead to such a situation, as it is normatively precluded but alethically possible. To resolve disagreement about a common subject matter of reason relations, perhaps either normative or alethic relations must take priority. The authors seem to disagree here. Hlobil’s epilogue contains a derivation of “the world” as setting an alethic standard of correctness. Brandom dissents in an endnote.Besides these grander implications, neopragmatists will also benefit from (finally!) possessing a rigorous notion of content, as some problems related to the former lack of such a notion may now be answerable. For instance, neopragmatists are pressed to say not just what it is to believe or assert some content (or otherwise use it in the game of giving and asking for reasons) but also what it is to hope, fear, or regret that same content. They now have a fighting chance.Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons is thus a key achievement in neopragmatism, presenting a long-desired formal treatment of its version of the doctrine. Its formal innovations, especially the notion of content and the conciliatory project it enables, are apt to reshape the debate in semantics. This work improves our understanding not just of meaning but of the study of meaning itself.

articles.t: Kantian Dignity and Its Difficulties
articles.ab: The Kantian notion of universal human dignity has become a mainstay in contemporary liberal societies. But it was not always so, and even now it faces criticism and threats from a variety of sources. In this work, Karl Ameriks traces the long, winding road the Kantian ideal of dignity took to get to its current prominence, scrutinizing the various ways it was, after being formulated by Kant, taken up, interpreted (and often misinterpreted), or added to by other influential historical thinkers. Ultimately, Ameriks concludes that, properly understood and adhered to, it remains a forceful and worthwhile ideal with continuing progressive potential.The work consists of an introduction and eight chapters, as well as an afterword.Chapter 1 introduces the Kantian understanding of dignity, discussing and refuting some of the misguided charges that have been levied against it, as well as taking up some controversies within current Kant scholarship, engaging especially with recent works by Richard Dean and Paul Formosa. Ameriks defends what he calls the “‘mainline interpretation’ of Kant’s basic concept of dignity as an unconditional, all-or-nothing, and inviolable feature of all human beings, one that deserves universal respect” (16).Chapter 2 contrasts Kant and Herder, arguing that much is to be gained by complementing Kant’s emphasis on necessity and universality with Herder’s keen eye and sensitivity for the importance of particularity, diversity, and historical contingency. Ameriks argues that the views of Herder and Kant are nonetheless closer and more readily combinable than is often thought, and he explores how their different foci influenced later authors.Chapter 3 takes up the question of Kant’s racism and his influence on fascism, paying special attention to the historical role played by Houston Stewart Chamberlain and his distorted interpretation of Kant. Though Ameriks emphasizes that the way Chamberlain and the Fascists construe Kant is wholly untenable, the chapter ends in a rather damning evaluation of Kant’s person, arguing that, though he never denied the dignity of any person, regardless their race, and made a point of making his respect for various Jewish scholars public, he did maintain many highly objectionable views typical of his time about the abilities of different groups and expressed these prejudices in very disparaging terms, thus making it all too easy for the Fascists to later distort his philosophy and use it to their own nefarious ends.Chapter 4 examines the fact that Kant never seemed to have shown much interest in the American Revolution or the political thought of the Founding Fathers. This omission is particularly glaring as Kant did engage directly with the later French Revolution and generally paid close attention to the international developments of his day. Ameriks deems this neglect a momentous failure on Kant’s part, both because the Founding Fathers were particularly astute political thinkers and because they shared Kant’s emphasis on the special status of the individual human being. Ameriks ascribes this oversight to hubris and narrow-mindedness on the part of Kant, before going on to link this to Kant’s views on colonialism more broadly and criticizing Kant for not having paid more attention to the fact that the Königsberg area was once subject to a kind of colonizing project itself. Ameriks argues that if Kant had been less narrow-minded on these and related topics, he could have prevented many of the more unfortunate turns of later German philosophy and history.Chapter 5 continues the theme of Kant’s neglect of contemporary thinkers who argued for positions similar to his own, focusing on the figure of Richard Price. Ameriks compares several aspects of Kant’s and Price’s practical philosophy, before putting special emphasis on the notion of self-evidence in its connection to the equal dignity of every human being. In doing so, Ameriks again emphasizes Kant’s personal failings, and Price is presented as the person who in many regards succeeded most in living up to the ideal of human dignity.The last three chapters focus on the person of Thomas Mann. Mann is worth studying, Ameriks argues, not just because as a highly influential public intellectual he played a notable role in the way universal human dignity became a central fixture of democratic life, but also because of the intellectual road he traveled. Mann came to properly appreciate the importance of universal human dignity only relatively late, holding more achievement-oriented and chauvinistic views in his early years. In discussing Mann’s intellectual journey, many other influential thinkers are surveyed, including the Early Romantics, Hegel, Kierkegaard, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Whitman. Mann’s life personifies, as Ameriks puts it, “an example of how a surprising positive reversal in philosophical orientation is possible even after a long period of being committed to deep-seated errors” (155).When evaluating the work as a whole, I confess to remaining of two minds. Professor Ameriks displays a tremendous knowledge of historical authors and their intellectual context that few will be able to rival. Moreover, the book is organized in a highly original fashion, recounting the history of the ideal of human dignity through various influential authors who simultaneously serve more or less as archetypes—the flawed messenger (Kant), the irredeemably corrupted villain (Chamberlain), the hero (Price), the redeemed sinner (Mann). This provides a narrative arc that supports the work’s central message: the Kantian ideal of universal human dignity remains worth striving for, however often we personally or collectively fall short of it. Thus, the book is both original and informative, as well as skillfully crafted.This narrative strategy also comes with a significant drawback, however, as it means that the historical figures discussed are not only relevant for their philosophical positions but also serve as exemplars of the various ways one can fail to live up to the ideal of dignity. Thus, a considerable amount of effort is put into highlighting and seeking explanations for their personal shortcomings. Indeed, a recurring theme in the book is how to explain why Kant failed so often (in Ameriks’s view) to live up to the implications of his own philosophy. This inevitably involves a significant amount of psychologizing speculation and conjecture, and passing judgment over historical persons’ character in this way is not very considerate of their personal dignity. Though Ameriks regularly emphasizes that the worst charges that have been levied against Kant’s person cannot be sustained, his verdict often remains very uncharitable, especially in instances where Kant fails to rise above the prejudices of his time and/or expresses himself in ways that conflict with the reigning attitudes and preoccupations of our own time.The double feeling the book gives rise to can perhaps best be illustrated by chapter 4, which laments Kant’s disinterest in the American Revolution. The chapter makes several points I fully endorse: the American Founding Fathers had very similar views to Kant regarding the dignity and importance of the individual human being; they indubitably included some of the most perspicacious political-philosophical minds in history; and bringing their political philosophy together with Kantian thought on dignity is a most worthwhile and promising endeavor for us to pursue. But Ameriks does not stop there: he regards it as a blameworthy and baffling failure on Kant’s part that he did not himself do this. Since Kant did deem the French Revolution worthy of his attention, Ameriks attributes this neglect to Kant’s arrogance and narrow-mindedness toward colonial matters. To further emphasize the unforgivable flaws in Kant’s character, Ameriks also accuses Kant of not paying sufficient attention to Prussia’s own colonial past, at one point even suggesting that Kant failed to fully grasp and respect his own identity because he did not attend to the possibility that he may have had some Sambian ancestors, thereby “suffer[ing] from a self-incurred loss of cultural autonomy” (101).These charges are highly questionable in many respects. The purported analogy between transatlantic colonialism and the German conquest of parts of the Baltic appears rather anachronistic. To demand that someone base his sense of self on his ancestry similarly is to project (rather dubious) present-day ideas and preoccupations on bygone times. The suggestion that one should link culture to genetics or bloodline seems especially unpalatable. Most importantly, however, it is a bit odd to fault a philosopher for choosing not to write about something: one of the fundamental features of academic freedom is that we may freely choose what to write about and what not, and we owe no one an explanation or justification for these choices—one may simply not fancy a given topic, or think that one has little to contribute on it, or be too busy with other things one happens to find more interesting, pressing or promising, and so on. Even if some such reasons were to prove mistaken in hindsight, that remains a far cry from indicating a serious character flaw.Moreover, concerning the American and French Revolutions, there are good reasons to believe that Kant’s own philosophical commitments naturally made him more interested in the latter. Despite some superficial similarities, the two revolutions were radically different in character. Where the American Founding Fathers explicitly sought to improve, but also build on, the received political wisdom of the ages, effectively advocating a modernized version of the ancient doctrine of the mixed constitution, the French Revolution was much more an attempt to remove all that was there and start anew from scratch, based on, among other influences, Rousseauian ideas about the unerring and unconstrained will of the people. Even though Kant’s political philosophy is much more restrained than Rousseau’s, it remains heavily influenced by Rousseauian ideas, and hence it should come as no surprise that Kant found the French Revolution more philosophically interesting than the American one. Indeed, one need only look at Federalist 10, with its focus on competing interested and impassioned factions as the quintessence of political freedom, to see how fundamentally different the Founding Fathers’ political outlook was from Kant’s.Thus, even though I agree with Ameriks that the cause of human dignity would be furthered by combining insights from Kant and the American Founding Fathers, I see no reason to jump to anti-colonial narrow-mindedness or other character flaws on Kant’s part to explain why he chose not to write about the American Revolution. At the very least, more charitable interpretations are available—especially since Kant appears to have shown similarly little interest in other titans of political thought like Machiavelli or Montesquieu, who advanced views more akin to those of the Founding Fathers.In sum, there is much to agree with in Ameriks’s book as to its main message regarding the importance and difficulties of living up to the Kantian ideal of universal human dignity, and readers will find many interesting facts and observations in it. At the same time, in its zeal to save Kantian dignity from its detractors, the work is perhaps a little too eager to impugn Kant’s personal dignity as a means to this end.

articles.t: Phenomenology and the Norms of Perception
articles.ab: Doyon’s book aims to demonstrate that perceptual experience is oriented by norms of coherence and optimality, and that it is in virtue of this orientation that perceptions count as perceptions in the first place. Doyon contends that these norms should not be understood merely as epistemic norms but instead as sui generis, belonging to the internal structure of perceptual experience itself and constitutive of what it is to be a perception at all (xiv–xv). Perception is structured by the norms of coherence and optimality, not because this is conducive to knowledge but because of what perception itself is. The main source of evidence for the book’s claims comes from detailed descriptions of a diverse range of perceptual experiences, and the majority of the book is devoted to showing how coherence and optimality structure experiences of different kinds, including experiences of our own bodies and other minds.The book draws its main conceptual resources from the phenomenological tradition. One of the book’s attractions is its clear, textually grounded exposition of a broad swathe of conceptual machinery from phenomenology. Here, the two main sources are Husserl and Merleau-Ponty, who are joined by many others, including classical figures like Edith Stein and contemporary figures like Shaun Gallagher. The book’s most distinctive achievement, however, lies in its synthesis of these phenomenological resources with an impressively broad range of literature on perception from outside the phenomenological tradition, showing where individual phenomenologists can be placed in relation to significant contemporary debates. The book shows how phenomenological analyses can fruitfully inform current discussions about perception in psychology, cognitive science, and analytic philosophy, offering critical responses, amplifications, and clarifications. Throughout, the book offers precise formulations of its claims and is very detailed without being dense. It presents clear, easy-to-follow arguments and well-chosen examples that provide evidence for its phenomenological claims about experiential structure while helpfully illustrating key concepts.Let me briefly characterize the two norms, beginning with coherence. As Doyon puts it, “Coherence … serves as the measure for what counts as perception at all” (6). His contention is that perceptions are constituted by experiences that progress more or less normally given the type of object we are perceiving and the conditions under which we are perceiving it. (The relevant concepts of normality and type are given substantial attention and developed out of Husserl.) Doyon emphasizes that the constitutive role of the coherence norm is tied up with the temporal structure of perceptual experience. When experiences are unmasked as illusions, it is typically because they “break with the temporal laws regulating normal (i.e. successful) experience,” as when a patch of sunlight, initially mistaken for a stone, “does not modify its appearance in progressive and expected ways when I move around it” (48). This example also illustrates the tight connection between perception and awareness of possibilities for bodily action: as the appearance of a stone gives way to the appearance of a patch of sunlight, so too does my sense that I could walk over and stand on it. The coherence of experience is, in this way, connected with our bodily sense of agency. Perception of stones is indexed to my sense of what I can do with my body; by contrast, “illusions are marked by an ‘I cannot’” (49). The coherence of our experiences is a constitutive condition of perception, since, to the extent that it is lacking, we begin to lose our grip on whether we are truly perceiving at all. Doyon’s careful consideration of the temporal structure of perception is a refreshing break from much philosophy of perception, which often overlooks the significance of its diachronic structure.The second norm is optimality. Those of us who have visited an optometrist will be quite familiar with this norm: the optometrist swings the many-lensed phoropter in front of your eyes and flicks between lenses of different refractive indexes, asking ‘Which is better: one or two?’ Our sense that a given perception could be better or worse depends on its relation to an optimum that serves as a norm, a better such that “no further improvement is possible” (13). Here, too, the norm shows up in relation to our bodily agency, insofar as “optimality has a motivating force” (33). As Doyon explains, “seeing things … is accompanied by an awareness of … movements I could produce with regard to the object in order to optimize my perspective” (81). This is apparent, Doyon notes, “when one goes to a concert with no seating and continually tries to improve one’s view of the stage by moving one’s head around and craning one’s neck” (86). Often, we don’t notice that we are making these adjustments, and Doyon uses this as evidence that the motivating force of optimality does not require us to reflect on our perceptions and make judgments about them in relation to the normative optimum. Instead, perception is constituted by norms that are already at play in prereflective awareness. In prereflective awareness, “one feels the ‘tension’ toward the norm or the optimum … one literally feels it in one’s body” (86). Since all perception occurs in light of better and worse, it is constituted by the norm of optimality.The book itself is split into three main parts.Following a brief introduction outlining the book’s project, part 1 lays out the key phenomenological analyses and core conceptual resources that frame the book’s central thesis. Chapter 1 focuses on Husserl and chapter 2 on Merleau-Ponty. In motivating and positioning his own view through these initial chapters, Doyon offers a phenomenological account of illusion and hallucination, as well as critical commentary on Hubert Dreyfus’s account of absorbed coping and Sean Kelly’s interpretation of the concept of maximal grip from Merleau-Ponty.Part 2 focuses on embodiment and its significance for perceptual normativity.Chapter 3 focuses on the structure of embodied experience, defending a phenomenological analysis that ties prereflective awareness to the experience of bodily agency through the body schema, which presents worldly objects in relation to the body via possibilities for bodily action. On the basis of this analysis, Doyon argues that “most of our daily perceptual activities are not epistemic but pragmatic in nature” (69), providing a phenomenological counterpoint to views of perception, like John McDowell’s, that conceive perception as a “rational capacity to represent what there is” (69).Chapter 4 offers phenomenological grounds to think that all perception is multimodal and subject to norms of integration between sense modalities. For Doyon, perception is always indexed to the body, integrating kinesthetic experience of the body’s position and movement with experience of other objects. Vision, for example, presents distal objects as “over there” in relation to the zero-point of the body that sees them. Since the body that sees is also a body that moves, experience of the body’s “I can” is intrinsically connected with a systematically structured, anticipatory “it will.” The experience of bodily agency is structured by a ‘horizon’ of further experiences that we expect to result from bodily movements, a horizon whose exploration through action and perception is subject to the norms of coherence and optimality. Doyon concludes that insofar as all perception makes reference to the body, “the loop of bodily sensations, perception, and movement that co-constitute the subjective space of the body is an intermodal achievement” (120).Chapter 5 carves out a phenomenological position on the nature and scope of perceptual learning. Doyon argues that Husserl’s concept of type points to an important form of perceptual learning, as it involves “long-lasting perceptual change that results from practice or experience” (129). For Husserl, types are experiential structures present in all perceptual experience that allow us to recognize objects of different kinds and furnish us with more or less determinate expectations about how experience will unfold given the kind of thing we are perceiving. For example, “Based on the dogs I have experienced in the past, sensory contents associatively partaking to the type ‘dog’ generate expectations of what legitimately constitutes a dog” (136). Types are shaped and reshaped over the course of our lives through experience of associations and dissociations between apparent qualities. Crucially, types lack the perfectly defined logical boundaries of concepts, making them essentially vague, even as they suffice for a measure of empirical generalization. This allows phenomenologists to stake out a distinctive nonconceptualist position regarding perception, while acknowledging the richness of its contents. Perception is not conceptual through and through; instead, it is structured by types, which furnish the basis for later intellectual activities that regiment the vague structures already present in types into the logical structure of the fully general concepts that figure in our judgments. Doyon’s examination of types in this chapter provides an excellent introduction to genetic phenomenology, which aims to describe structures in experience that change over time, by contrast with the static structures emphasized in many discussions of Husserlian phenomenology.Part 3 turns to normativity in perceptions of—and with—others. Chapter 6 begins with a detailed survey and comparison of Husserl and Edith Stein on empathy, showing how normativity is at work in perceptual experiences of others, while chapter 7 develops and defends a view of the necessary conditions for shared intentionality, as when we watch a film with another person or play a team sport like soccer.I will conclude with a brief comment on the book’s Husserlian commitments. Chapter 6 closes with a Husserlian rebuttal to critical phenomenologists, like Lisa Guenther, who argue that classical phenomenology’s focus on universal and necessary structures of experience prevent it from fully reckoning with “contingent, historical and social structures” (Guenther 2020: 12) like “colonialism, anti-Black racism, and heteropatriarchy” (Guenther 2021: 6) that profoundly shape the structure of experience in ways that go beyond the production of experiences with specific contents. Doyon argues, correctly, that existence of structural variation does not, by itself, imply that there are no universal structures at a more fundamental level. This response falls short, however, of establishing the positive claim that “certain features …really are a priori or universal” (208). Although it remains open to the Husserlian phenomenologist to try to place contingent experiential structures within a system of (presumed) universal invariants, the argument that there remains conceptual space for this possibility despite variation is not a demonstration that there are structures that are universal and necessary. Absent a positive argument for our entitlement to claims about universality and necessity, it remains that phenomenology can be conceived differently, as a more local and situation-specific endeavor, even if it is possible for us largely to agree on, for example, the basic structure of time consciousness. Husserl’s contention was that making concessions of this kind would be fatal for phenomenology qua rational inquiry into evidential norms, turning it into anthropology or psychology. Sartre, Beauvoir, and even Merleau-Ponty, however, seemed more sanguine about the prospects for a phenomenology capable of accepting a thoroughgoing contingency, one that allows that “existence precedes essence.”

articles.t: Rights and Right-Holding
articles.ab: Matthew Kramer is the foremost contemporary proponent of the Interest theory of rights, and his latest monograph is a definitive statement and defense of that theory. While some of the arguments in Rights and Right-Holding are familiar to rights theorists, some novel ones are introduced in order to complete his account of right-holding. Since it is impossible to do justice to this rich and carefully argued book in such a short review, I will focus on the fresh ideas presented here.Let me start with a short exposition of the two main accounts of right-holding. The literature on rights is divided between theorists who subscribe to the Hohfeldian framework of deontic relations and those who don’t; Kramer is firmly in the first camp, while many other interest theorists explicitly or implicitly reject it. Within this Hohfeldian camp, however, there is a long-standing divide between Choice theorists and Interest theorists.One of Hohfeld’s main insights was that rights are deontic relations between two parties. Thus, the legal position of a right-holder correlates with a legal position of another party, where ‘correlativity’ should be understood as mutual entailment; each of the two positions in this relationship logically entails the other.The most discussed deontic relationship is that between a claim-right and a duty. While Hohfeld’s followers agree that claim-rights and duties always come together, they disagree about what binds them together. Take my contractual duty to deliver this book review. Presumably this duty is owed to (the editor of) this journal to whom I promised that I would. According to the Choice theory, this is so because the editor has control over my duty, in that they could release me from it or demand compliance with it. On the competing, Interest theory this is so because my contributing the review would benefit the journal and therefore its editor. The standard Interest theory of right-holding claims that the party that holds the (claim-)right correlative to a duty is the party that stands to benefit from the performance of this duty. This expounds the widely held intuition that rights are advantageous to their holders.But contracts or promises such as the one above pose a problem to this view. Imagine, if you can, that my review will also benefit the readership of the journal. It would be strange to claim that the readership of this journal has a right against me that I deliver the review, especially since, if the editor releases me from my duty, the duty ceases to exist. Yet this is what the Interest theorist may be committed to.Interest theorists have proposed various solutions to this third-party beneficiary problem. The test for the success of such a solution is whether it can resist an outlandish proliferation of right-holders without restricting the class of right-holders too much. Kramer’s new formulation of the Interest theory aims to do just that: “Individually necessary and jointly sufficient for the holding of a claim-right by X are (1) the fact that the duty correlative to the claim-right deontically and inherently protects some aspect of X’s situation that on balance is typically beneficial for a being like X and (2) the fact that X is a member of a class of potential holders of claim-rights” (179). It may be worth noting how the first condition differs from Kramer’s (1998: 62) earlier formulation of it, whereby “necessary but insufficient for the actual holding of a right by a person X is that the right, when actual, preserves one or more of X’s interests.” Of particular importance are the additions of ‘inherently’ and ‘typically beneficial’ ‘on balance’. Both are effectively meant to respond to the third-party beneficiary objection mentioned above. While the first rules out as right-holders parties that benefit fortuitously from a duty, the second allows the interest theorist to ascribe a right to someone even when they do not perceive the protection offered by the duty as a benefit and would perhaps waive the duty if possible. A masochist, for instance, might find that an unwaivable duty against assault offers them no benefit, but they would still be counted as a holder of the correlative right under this version of the interest theory since such a duty is on balance, typically beneficial to human beings.This version of the Interest theory also allows Kramer to offer a renewed defense of the Correlativity Axiom. According to Kramer, the Correlativity Axiom posits that every claim-right has (at least) one correlative duty and every duty has (at least) one correlative claim-right.1 The second part of this axiom in particular is widely disputed since there seem to be many (legal or moral) duties that do not correlate with rights, such as the legal duty to pay taxes or the moral duty of benevolence or charity. The former, Kramer maintains, like every legal duty, “is correlated with a legal claim- right vested in the system of governance that has imposed the duty” (Kramer 2022: 392). He emphasizes elsewhere that “this thesis about every legal duty, a thesis that is sufficient to sustain the Correlativity Axiom, is a straightforward corollary of my version of the Interest Theory of right- holding” (Kramer 2022: 392). Strictly speaking, this is only so when combined with the assumption that a system of governance is the kind of (collective) entity that can have rights.The second type of duty is more difficult to accommodate, and here Kramer proposes a novel yet highly loaded solution. Duties to give to charity—or eleemosynary duties, in his terminology—are owed to several different parties. First, they are owed to different charities disjunctively; second, they are owed to the system of governance (if imposed by the law); and third, they are owed by each bearer to themselves! This might strike the reader as bizarre and at odds with the interest theory since it doesn’t seem to be in one’s interest to have duties at all, let alone duties that are often seen as quite demanding. Nevertheless, Kramer maintains that it is typically beneficial on balance for human beings to act in conformity with the requirements of morality.This ingenious defense of the Correlativity Axiom may be a step too far for some. Arguably, it goes against the spirit of Hohfeldian correlativity, which was meant to highlight that rights are deontic relationships between two different parties. Moreover, it’s unclear that the second part of the axiom, as formulated by Kramer, was envisaged by Hohfeld, as there is no evidence for it in Hohfeld’s text. What he was at pains to emphasise was that X’s claim-right against Y is equivalent to Y’s duty toward X but not necessarily that every legal, let alone moral, duty has a correlative claim-right; in other words, that every claim-right correlates with a directed duty and vice versa.We can now turn to the second condition for the holding of a claim-right, which requires that the right-holder be a member of a class of potential holders of claim-rights. We should start by noting that Kramer’s rather complex account only spells out the conditions under which someone can be a right-holder; it is silent on whether these potential right-holders should be ascribed rights, by law or morality. Like most Interest theorists, and in contrast to Choice theorists, Kramer wants to include in this class many creatures that are not full-blown moral agents, such as dead and unborn people, fetuses, permanently comatose people, anencephalic infants, and some nonhuman animals.A law that prohibits walking on the grass may seem to benefit blades of grass, and, inasmuch as the grass has interests, legal rights could be ascribed to blades of grass. Kramer does indeed take an expansive view of what counts as an interest, and, on that view, insentient and inanimate creatures can have interests. Yet not all creatures with interests can have rights; a separate necessary condition needs to be fulfilled.Here Kramer joins many other theorists (e.g., Joseph Raz and Frances Kamm) in thinking that only creatures that possess ultimate value can be right-holders. “Such value is possessed by beings if and only if (1) they are êtres pour eux-mêmes and (2) the furtherance of their interests is intrinsically valuable” (317). He chooses the Sartrean French phrase, he explains, in order to avoid reference to consciousness and thus leave open the possibility that artificial intelligence, for instance, might be a potential right-holder.Kramer ultimately finds that key to having such value is the possession of a “level of self-reflective attunedness that is characteristic of conscious engagement with oneself and the world” (318). It might seem like this would rule out many of the creatures mentioned above. But, while Kramer concedes that “myriads of human beings” are not êtres pour eux-mêmes (323), they are ultimately included in the class of potential right-holders by way of an explicit embrace of speciesism.According the Kramer, the two requirements above “apply as generics, rather than universally quantified propositions” (327) to the species, rather than to each individual member of that species; in other words, they ascribe to human beings “a property which is characteristic of them but is not universally shared by them” (324). Note that this does not apply to all nonhuman animals; this is because an ‘ethically pregnant commonality’ only obtains between human beings.But if these conditions are met by the entire species rather than by individuals, it seems that the right-holder is the species as a whole, not individual members of it. This is a problematic conclusion in two ways: first, because it is debatable whether the human species, which is an unorganized collectivity, can hold rights as a single entity, and second, because what we would ultimately want is to ascribe rights to individual human beings not the species as a whole.I take it that Kramer would reply that humanity, as an ethical community, can hold rights as a whole because the ascription of a right here involves aggregative universal quantification even though the ascription of value did not involve a universal quantifier. Moreover, he also claims that individual members of the species can hold additional homologous rights at least when the inherent protection bestowed by a duty is “typically advantageous on balance” for them as individuals (382–84); this is to say that, when a duty is beneficial for most but not each member of the species, not every individual will be a right-holder. So it’s not clear to me that this argument actually succeeds in ascribing rights to all human beings, including comatose people and anencephalic infants.2 Those dissatisfied with the Choice theory because it cannot ascribe rights to creatures who are not agents may have to look elsewhere for an alternative.Many of the complex and sophisticated arguments in this impressive book had to be left aside in this short review, but they would repay careful reading. The first book-length defense of the Interest theory of rights, Rights and Right-Holding is required reading for any rights theorist.

articles.t: Laws of Nature and Chances: What Breathes Fire into the Equations
articles.ab: This rich and thought-provoking book should set the agenda for discussion about Humean approaches to the metaphysics of laws and chances for years to come. Its aim is an overhaul of the Lewisian Best System Account (“BSA”) that allows the systematization itself to deliver the fundamental ontology and space-time structure in addition to the laws. The view, which Loewer calls the Package Deal Account (“PDA”), will be familiar in broad strokes to those who are acquainted with his articles on the topic over the last several decades. Still, there is plenty here to think about, even for readers familiar with his work.I won’t try to summarize the entire book. Rather, I’ll focus on some key motivational issues and how they inform the structure of the PDA. I’ll use this discussion to develop an objection, which I’ll call the Value of Standards (“VoS”) problem, that concerns me as a Humean who is otherwise highly sympathetic to Loewer’s overall project.Loewer’s PDA is a development of David Lewis’s (1973) BSA, which Loewer elaborates in chapter 3. The BSA has two main components. First is the Humean mosaic—-the collection of particular matters of fact that constitute the world. For Lewis, these consist of space-time points instantiating perfectly natural properties, which are the metaphysically elite properties that play multiple roles in his metaphysics, epistemology, and philosophy of language.Second is a set of systematizing standards, which we might call the Nomic Formula. These standards are supposed to be the epistemic standards physicists use to decide among competing physical theories; Lewis thought that they consist of a balance of simplicity and informativeness. The laws of nature, for Lewis, were the results of applying the Nomic Formula to the Humean mosaic; doing so generates a systematization of the entire mosaic, the regularities of which are the laws. This makes scientists’ epistemic standards into standards that are constitutive of lawhood, and given the particular Nomic Formula that Lewis advocated, it makes the laws into an efficient summary of the entire mosaic.The BSA has a long history of defenders and dissidents, and in chapter 4 Loewer takes on some of the latter. Space forbids a detailed survey, but this chapter is surely a highlight. Objections are presented and dispatched in rapid succession—-Loewer cuts straight to the point—-and more than once his treatment revealed new angles on issues I thought I knew. This chapter should be required reading for anyone looking to contribute to the debates between Humeans and non-Humeans.With those objections cleared away, Loewer pivots to his central constructive aim: developing the PDA. Earlier I noted that he wants the systematization to deliver not just the laws (as on Lewis’s account) but also the fundamental properties and the space-time structure. Here we should consider both why that result is desirable and how to secure it.Chapter 5 answers the “Why” question. In it, Loewer presents his main criticisms of the BSA, which focus on its reliance on perfectly natural properties. Given the variety of roles they play on Lewis’s approach, they must satisfy a battery of metaphysical requirements—-for example, they must be local, intrinsic, and categorical. Moreover, to avoid a trivialization worry, Lewis also required that the laws be expressed in terms of these properties for the purposes of assessing how well they satisfy the standards in the Nomic Formula.Loewer raises several worries about the metaphysical posit of perfectly natural properties. For our purposes the relevant one is the problem of missing value, lodged by Shamik Dasgupta (2018), who asks, effectively, why we should care about expressing the laws with reference to perfectly natural properties. What value is there in this? What if physicists delivered us a final “theory of everything” that referred to properties that don’t match the profile of Lewisian perfectly natural ones? What would be wrong with that?This worry leads Loewer to suggest that the fundamental properties should not be an independent ingredient that is fed into the Nomic Formula but rather should be a result of the systematization process just like the laws. Ultimately, he proposes that the systematization process itself will deliver the fundamental properties, space-time structure, and laws as a “package deal.” This does away with the brute metaphysical posit of perfectly natural properties and instead ties their value to the value of the systematization itself: as long as the systematization is valuable, there will be value in expressing the laws in terms of whatever properties they reference.Next, we need to consider how to structure the view to achieve this. Loewer addresses this issue in chapter 7. The main obstacle here is that if the fundamental properties and the space-time structure are a result of the systematization process, it is not clear what is left to be systematized by the Nomic Formula in the first place.Loewer’s answer is Quinean: physics begins in medias res with the motions of familiar macroscopic objects—-planets, pendula, projectiles, and so on—-and iteratively develops its ontology as it proceeds. A first pass yields a theory that systematizes those macroscopic phenomena; a second pass systematizes both the macroscopic phenomena and the posits of the first theory; and so on. At the limit, a final “theory of everything” would knit together every ontology introduced along the way, together with the macroscopic facts we started from, into a single set of fundamental laws, properties, and space-time structure.1This gives us a basic overview of the PDA’s motivations and structure. Now I want to suggest a worry, which is that it’s not clear that the PDA solves the problem of missing value. Recall: as long as the systematization itself is valuable, there will be value in the individual components of that systematization, such as the fundamental properties that it posits. But what is the value of the systematization itself?Loewer gestures at an answer in chapter 3, where he outlines—-but does not fully spell out—-the standards and the goal they serve: “An optimal systematization of the Humean mosaic … organizes and unifies facts so as to enable [us] to understand the world.” Moreover, the systematization should “explain what [we find in the world] in terms of fundamental ontology and fundamental laws” (27). The goal, then, is understanding, where this involves an explanation of the phenomena we find in the world in terms of fundamental ontology and laws. This seems reasonable—-of course we value understanding—-but, as I’ll argue, the proposal sits uneasily with the rest of the PDA.Imagine an alien civilization that likewise engages in the project of systematizing the mosaic, but they systematize according to different standards. (For example, maybe their standards weigh simplicity more than ours do.) As a result, their final theory differs from our own: it posits different fundamental properties, space-time structure, and laws. What is the value of adopting our standards over theirs?Loewer, I think, wants to claim that our standards are valuable because they provide a systematization that facilitates understanding of the world. But what is understanding? The aliens’ standards would likewise provide a systematization that facilitates something like understanding, which we might call understanding*. Still other sets of standards would provide us with understanding**, understanding***, and so on. What is uniquely valuable about understanding as opposed to these alternatives?One tempting answer is intimated by Loewer’s comments about the fundamental explanations provided by the optimal systematization. You might think that our actual standards provide us with genuine understanding (as opposed to faux understanding) because they illuminate the world’s fundamental structure, whereas other standards do not. But this plainly won’t work: according to the PDA, the systematization process itself is what underwrites the truths about the world’s fundamental structure. So it cannot be on account of illuminating that structure that the standards provide us with understanding; this would effectively define “understanding” as that which the standards provide, but it would not tell us the value of the standards.Chapter 7’s solution therefore reopens the very gap it meant to close. To recap: Loewer escapes Dasgupta’s problem of missing value by letting the system choose its own fundamental properties, so their value now rests entirely on the value of the systematizing standards themselves. But why adopt these standards rather than any rival that would yield a different package deal? Pointing to “understanding” does not help, because each rival set of standards would confer its own analog of understanding. One might reply that our standards are privileged because they alone reveal the world’s fundamental structure, and that revelation is essential to understanding. Yet on the PDA the standards themselves determine the fundamental structure; branding the result “understanding” therefore adds no justification—-it just gives a name to whatever package those standards happen to deliver without showing why those standards are privileged. In short, the missing value problem has reemerged one level up, now targeting the standards themselves. This is the Value of Standards (“VoS”) problem.I think the VoS problem is a worry for the PDA, but I don’t think it’s damning. Resolving it will require, first, a fuller catalog of the systematizing standards and, second, an independent account of why the kind of understanding they yield is uniquely valuable—-perhaps by showing that any community of inquirers, alien or human, must converge on these standards to maximize some sort of pragmatic payoff.2The book’s remaining chapters merit more space than I can give them here. To mention just a few: chapter 8 shows how David Albert and Loewer’s “Mentaculus” fits into the PDA framework; chapter 9 considers how the PDA would treat laws of the special sciences; and chapter 10 defends the view from charges of relativism. Each chapter brims with thought-provoking arguments and novel perspectives. Loewer’s talent for finding fresh angles on long-standing issues makes the book a delight even when one disagrees. Whether or not the PDA can ultimately resolve the Value of Standards problem, Loewer has set a demanding research agenda. Anyone working on the metaphysics of laws and chances will need to engage with this bold and imaginative work.

articles.t: What Is Togetherness and Why Is It Good?
articles.ab: To be together with other people, truly together, is a social good. Perhaps it is deeply entwined with other social goods that have been subjected to sustained philosophical discussion such as friendship. Still, in its own right, the topic of the nature and apparent value of togetherness has been largely neglected. This article advances three claims: (1) that togetherness of a certain relevant sort consists in sharing a sense of the meaningfulness of things; (2) that this sort of togetherness is a lead candidate for being the internal goal of personal relationships as such; and (3) that togetherness so understood is valuable because senses of the meaningfulness of things are to be shared. The argument of the article articulates a sense in which even solitary meaningful experiences have a social structure.

articles.t: Fractured Goodness: Aristotle’s Response to Plato’s Form of the Good
articles.ab: In the first book of his Nicomachean Ethics (EN), after his remarks on different ways of life in 1.5, Aristotle interrupts the discussion of happiness, the highest end, and turns to ‘universal’ goodness (1.6), by which he means to the Platonic Form of the Good. Against the existence of a Form of the Good, he sketches a series of technical arguments to the effect that the good is not, in fact, something universal. Most of these arguments point to a relevant diversity among goods—a diversity that is, in Aristotelian terms, incompatible with the good’s being ‘universal’, ‘common’, and ‘one’ (1096a28). Perhaps the most important diversity is that the good is not univocal: it is said in as many ways as ‘being’ (1096a23–24). Aristotle adds that, even if there were a Form of the Good, it would be of no use for ethics. Then he returns, without much ado, to the zêtoumenon agathon, the highest end he has been discussing in 1.1–5.Aristotle’s readers are usually at a loss with this chapter, which looks like a foreign body in EN 1; and while some tend to regard it as a failure, others downplay its relevance for Aristotle’s ethical project. Against both of these tendencies, Christopher Shields’s Fractured Goodness (FG) offers a welcome antidote. First, the book defends the relevance of EN 1.6 by arguing that the attack against Plato reveals a challenge that Aristotle has to answer himself: If goods are so diverse that the good is not univocal, then how can they be compared qua goods? And how can there be anything like a science of goodness? As Shields argues, the answer to these questions lies in the concept of core dependent homonymy (chap. 9.2), which makes possible both comparisons among goods, based on a causal perspective (chap. 9.3), and a science of goodness qua goodness, modeled after the science of being qua being (chap. 10). Readers familiar with Shields’s work will notice the close connection to his Order in Multiplicity (1999). In a way, FG is a sequel to this influential study. Second, FG insists that the arguments against Plato are not in fact a failure. Instead of being ‘partisan’ (chap. 2.3) toward Aristotle, however, Shields aims at a fair assessment that does not ignore the problems those arguments raise but nonetheless identifies their valid points. This is done in a careful and detailed study of EN 1.6. This meticulousness, the persistence that Shields both shows and expects from his readers, is one of the main virtues of his book.As this is not the place to follow Shields into the details, I will confine myself to some observations that might help to characterize his project. I will also try to raise a worry that I think is likely to arise for readers of FG.The core of FG is a close reading of EN 1.6, devoting one chapter to each of Aristotle’s arguments against the ‘Platonist’ (chaps. 2–8) (see chap. 1.1.7 on the identity of Aristotle’s target). The strategy of those core chapters might be put as follows. After presenting the argument at stake in the sketchy form of EN 1.6, Shields explains why that argument is not convincing, as it stands. As it turns out, the different objections of EN 1.6 raise different problems. Some seem to rest on equivocations, to be unspecific, or to beg the question; others do not specify what the charge exactly is, or they fracture goodness to an extent that Aristotle could hardly find attractive. To pick out just one example, the argument from the diversity of the sciences (1096a29–35) seems to rest on observations concerning actual sciences, which are, as Shields asserts, insufficient to establish the impossibility of a unified science of goodness (chap. 5.1).In the next step, Shields suggests a ‘development’ of the argument as presented in EN 1.6, drawing on other parts of Aristotle’s writings. Again, this development takes different routes in different cases; and by following these routes, Shields turns his interpretation of EN 1.6 into a study of some fundamental aspects of Aristotle’s philosophy. Thus in the case of the argument from the sciences he considers Aristotle’s conception of the ‘requisites’ of a science from the Posterior Analytics (chap. 5.2), and develops, in a veritable tour de force, what he calls the “predicational purview” of that science (135).Finally, Shields concludes his reading in each case with a reassessment, pointing out that, in its developed form, the argument makes a valid point against the Platonist (which does not mean that the latter might not have an answer to it).There is a lot to learn from, and a lot to ask about, these chapters. What stands out is how consistently they correlate the argument of EN 1.6 with the topic of nonunivocity, sometimes to an extent that might appear strained, given the highly compressed nature of Aristotle’s objections (the argument from the sciences is a good example). This brings me to an observation that I take to be crucial for a proper assessment of Shields’s perspective. The chapters of FG just mentioned are, as it were, engaged in a reconstructed debate, for they confront a developed version of the Aristotelian arguments with a comprehensive account of the Form of the Good. Now, it surely is an important lesson that such a developed version can make a point that should make the Platonist think. One might worry, however, that by leading that reconstructed debate, FG tends to lose sight of what Aristotle is actually doing in EN 1.6, what he thinks he has achieved, and how that affects the course of EN 1. In contrast to Shields, Aristotle draws on a biased and selective view of Plato’s theory. He apparently wants to make a specific point against Plato and ignores many aspects that the latter’s partisans would find indispensable. If this selectiveness is no accident, then it seems natural to ask, Why does Aristotle turn to the Form of the Good at this point of EN 1, and why does he treat it in that peculiar way? On these questions, FG is obviously less informative.A similar observation can be made concerning Shields’s account of the relevance of EN 1.6. As already mentioned, he argues that the variety of goodness spells a problem for the comparison of goods that Aristotle himself is engaging in, for this comparison requires a common standard.1 While a Platonist approach finds that standard in the “propinquity metric” (195), Aristotle’s solution lies, as Shields holds, in the tool of core dependent homonymy.
