The problem is of course that ‘core dependence’ (pros hen) is only one of the tools mentioned in EN 1.6 and that Aristotle does not develop the respective theory. The ambitious agenda of FG, chapters 9–10, is hence (1) to show that core dependence, not analogy, is in fact Aristotle’s answer to the question how the different goods are related, (2) to spell out this core dependence, and (3) to outline how it makes possible a science of goodness qua goodness and a comparison among goods.I cannot do justice to this extremely subtle discussion, so let me just note that it again deals with a reconstruction, for it asks, What would a science of goodness qua goodness, which Aristotle nowhere develops, look like? Drawing on Aristotle’s remark that going into details would be the matter of a “different philosophy” (1096b29–30), one might characterize FG as being about that different philosophy rather than about the importance of (the proposed reading of) EN 1.6 for the aims of EN 1. To be sure, this is a perfectly legitimate and important project. But it is obviously less interested in what we can learn about Aristotle’s engagement with the Form of the Good from the very context in which it appears. I believe, however, that this context throws a different light on some of Shields’s assumptions.Throughout EN 1.1–5, Aristotle conceives of goods as ends and of the highest good as a highest end. This teleological outlook grounds his general remarks on the ethical project as well as his discussion of ‘opinions’, because all candidates for happiness treated in EN 1.1–5 are (highest) ends. When he turns to the Form of the Good, Aristotle does not just introduce a “contender” (176) for the highest good but a different way to conceive of it: not as a highest end but as something that possesses goodness to the highest possible degree. A question lying behind this “interlude” (17) is thus whether it is right to think of goods as ends. Aristotle does not raise this question as explicitly as in EE 1.8, but since the overall dialectic of EN 1 is still shaped by it, one might want to describe that dialectic differently than Shields: not in terms of ‘normative’ versus ‘axiological’ (chap. 1.3), nor ‘circumscribed’ versus ‘absolute’ (chap. 1.2), but in terms of a ‘teleological’ versus a ‘paradeigmatist’ view of the best good.A related difference can be observed with regard to the comparison of goods. Shields is right in claiming that EN 1.6 offers a challenge to Aristotle’s own project of comparing goods. But this challenge is more specific than Shields assumes, because Aristotle has already spent five chapters on that project. He has explained how goods can be compared if they are conceived as ends. So the specific question seems to be whether this teleological account of the highest good is in any way affected by the results of the anti-Platonic argument. And although it is impossible to be sure on that matter, one might find this specific question present in the ‘Platonic Rejoinder’ that Shields discusses in chapter 7, for the intrinsic goods are here characterized as being pursued for their own sakes (1096b10–11). If they, too, are different qua good, one might worry that a teleological account of the good leads into an irreducible plurality of (highest) goods. However that may be, given the context of EN 1, Shields would have to explain why Aristotle should find problematic something that he has been doing all along: comparing goods.Relating EN 1.6 to the context of EN 1 might finally affect our position toward the alternative between analogy and core dependent homonymy. Putting aside the question whether analogy really reintroduces “Platonic univocity, simply at a higher level” (212) (I think it does not), it can hardly be denied that the argument of EN 1.1–5 is shaped by the language of analogy—that is, by the remark that the good-as-end is different in different cases (1095a23) (see Brüllmann 2011). It is this remark that reappears in 1.6 when Aristotle sketches what an analogy is (1096b29) and in 1.7 when he returns to the teleological perspective (1097a20). If we take this observation seriously, then the option ‘analogy’ (or a combination of analogy and core dependence: 210n32) should not be dismissed so easily. In this case, we might also take a different stance on the alternative ‘absolute’ versus ‘circumscribed’ goodness. For whatever Aristotle’s position on the existence of absolute goodness might be, his very choice of a teleological approach—at least as laid out in EN 1.1–5—seems to imply a circumscribed perspective.These observations do not diminish the achievements of this absorbing book, which covers new ground in scholarship and combines passion for details with an impressively wide scope. They rather show how stimulating it is.

articles.t: The Anatomy of Justice: On the Shape, Substance, and Power of Liberal Egalitarianism
articles.ab: On the opening page of John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice, readers are told that “justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.” If a social arrangement is unjust, then it must be abolished or reformed. It cannot be redeemed by its realization of other values or ideals. These famous remarks, which are immediately qualified by Rawls as expressed too strongly, are perplexing on reflection. Either the remarks express a kind of fanaticism, whereby one value ‘justice’ is taken to trump every other value, or they express a certain tautology, whereby justice is construed to reflect all the relevant values of political morality, and hence must be the first virtue, as it encompasses all the others. Gina Schouten’s engaging book The Anatomy of Justice, which is in many respects a sympathetic extension of Rawls’s project, responds to this conundrum by arguing that we need two distinct notions of justice, one that applies narrowly to distributions of social goods and one that encompasses all sources of political value and provides an overall evaluative ranking of social arrangements. The former notion, which Schouten terms “aspirational justice,” is but one important input into the all-things-considered evaluation provided by the later notion, “verdictive justice.” Inattentive readers of Schouten’s book might suspect that she has renamed G. A. Cohen’s much-discussed distinction between justice and rules of regulation. But that suspicion would be a mistake, since Cohen’s rules of regulation respond not only to all relevant political values but also to considerations of feasibility and to expected shortfalls of political will and human motivation to do what should be done. Verdictive justice is a purer account of what fundamentally matters from the standpoint of political morality than Cohen’s more prescriptive and action-guiding, but thereby less evaluatively pure, rules of regulation. Still, “aspirational justice” is what Cohen sought to rescue from Rawls’s constructivism, and Schouten’s agreement with Cohen that fairness in the distribution of social goods should not be identified with the distribution favored by Rawls’s principles of justice will give more orthodox Rawlsians pause. For Rawlsian justice, conceived verdictively, may not be fair, even under the best of conditions, and thus “justice as fairness” would not be an apt slogan for Rawlsian justice.So, while Schouten’s anatomy of justice is Rawlsian in spirit, it does not aim to reproduce or vindicate Rawls’s views. By articulating a framework of the things that matter fundamentally from the standpoint of political morality, it provides a way of capturing certain key Rawlsian ideals while also providing critical distance on them. As an illustration, consider Rawls’s signature distributive principle, the difference principle. That principle, Schouten contends, is not compelling as a principle of distributive fairness. It is better thought of as a compromise between two aspirational values—distributive fairness and efficiency. Distributive fairness, in turn, is expressed by the luck egalitarian principle that Rawls called “the principle of redress,” whereby undeserved inequalities call for correction. But the principle of redress applies to all goods, natural and social, and not just to the social primary goods that are the currency of Rawlsian distributive justice. Accordingly, the principle of redress, although Schouten does not highlight this point, does not sit well with the general Rawlsian social contract approach under which the goods subject to distribution are those produced by social cooperation. The anatomy of justice, or at least Schouten’s favored articulation of the anatomy, in this way appears to pull us beyond political contractualism.Whereas verdictive justice is the all-encompassing value of political morality, and aspirational justice is one important input into it, the star of the show in Schouten’s anatomy is not justice but legitimacy. Legitimacy constrains the pursuit of aspirational justice and other aspirational values, and it takes strict priority over all conflicts with them. Schouten claims that legitimate political arrangements manifest mutual respect among citizens, and nothing can further verdictive justice by flouting its demands. Legitimacy is here understood in politically liberal terms, making the anatomy of justice a version of Rawlsian political liberalism.The Anatomy of Justice consists of an introduction and seven chapters. The introduction and the first chapter helpfully outline the structure of the anatomy and explain its pluralistic character. The next three chapters discuss the demands of distributive equality, both as they relate to aspirational justice and to legitimacy, as well as the demands of legitimacy, including both its procedural and substantive elements. These three chapters also show how the anatomy of justice is responsive to both distributive and relational egalitarian commitments. The final three chapters address egalitarian critics of liberalism, especially radical feminist egalitarian critics, and they argue that liberalism, as the anatomy of justice illustrates, has the critical resources to address problems that the critics charge it cannot address. Among other topics, these chapters engage with debates over basic income proposals, the site or subject matter of liberal justice, and the adequacy of reflective equilibrium for political and social critique. The concluding chapters are also an extended exercise in liberal egalitarian applied theory, showing how the ideals and values in the anatomy of justice can inform criticism, including radical criticism, of existing institutions and culture under present conditions.The Anatomy of Justice is an excellent book. It will be primarily of interest to Rawlsian political liberals and feminist critics of liberal egalitarianism. But it should interest political philosophers more generally as well, as it makes significant contributions to a number of important debates in contemporary political philosophy, including those related to distributive and relational egalitarianism, ideal and nonideal theory, the possibility and nature of legitimate injustice, and the relationship between justice and culture.The book is filled with interesting arguments and insightful discussions, two of which can be highlighted here. The first concerns the strict priority that the anatomy of justice assigns to legitimacy. Schouten is admirably clear on the stringency of the priority. “When pursuing distributive equality or any other aspirational value comes at a cost to legitimacy, that pursuit always leads to a less valuable social arrangement on the whole, no matter the magnitude of the gain or loss in question” (6). As Schouten notes, many will find this kind of trumping priority to be deeply implausible. Surely, the thought goes, a large enough gain in aspirational justice or some other aspirational value overrides a very small deficit in legitimacy. Schouten has two responses. First, we must attend to the role that legitimacy plays in the anatomy. It is the value (or more precisely the value of mutual respect that undergirds it) that adjudicates conflicts between other political values and ideals. If we treat legitimacy as just one political value to be balanced or weighed against other political values, we misrepresent its character as an adjudicatory value. Second, and responding in particular to the alleged implausibility of assigning strict priority of legitimacy over aspirational justice, Schouten argues that the distributive requirements of legitimacy are considerably more demanding than they are normally taken to be. Within political liberalism, standards of legitimacy delimit the set of reasonable conceptions of justice, but such standards impose, in addition to priority for the basic liberties and the securement of a basic minimum of all-purpose means, a demanding egalitarian requirement on the distribution of social goods. “To be reasonable,” Schouten claims, “a conception of justice also must recognize a baseline of equal shares and deem talent unfit to justify deviations from that baseline” (94). The strong egalitarian demands of legitimacy ensure that the magnitude of aspirationally unjust material inequality that is compatible with legitimate arrangements will not be excessive, thereby making the strict priority of legitimacy over egalitarian aspirational justice easier to stomach.This line of argument will reassure strong egalitarians that legitimacy is not an unacceptable constraint on the pursuit of aspirational justice. But it comes with a significant cost. By packing more egalitarian content into the standard of legitimacy than Rawls envisioned, the set of reasonable (i.e., legitimate) conceptions of justice contracts. That means that the anatomy of justice makes political liberalism less accommodating to pluralism, including otherwise reasonable pluralism. The parochial character of political liberalism, which is already alarming to some critics, is exacerbated when the parish to which it applies narrows. Schouten allows that citizens with less robust egalitarian commitments can be committed to public reason and to the burdens of judgment and yet err in their judgments about the distributive demands of legitimacy. They are not, she says, unreasonable in virtue of that kind of mistake. Yet this concession prompts a worry (94n4). If such citizens were indeed granted membership in the justificatory community, and if their views were to prevail in democratic debate, then the resulting arrangement would be legitimate; and if it were legitimate then its relatively inegalitarian character would raise the worry about the strict priority of legitimacy over egalitarian aspirational justice that Schouten’s argument was intended to silence.The second of Schouten’s arguments that I will highlight here concerns the legitimacy of the state’s promotion of autonomy. Autonomy is, on the standard political liberal reading, a comprehensive ideal, one that the state should not favor, even if it is granted that it is a key component of living well. Against this standard picture, Schouten argues that if actual social conditions are such that they make it costly to realize comprehensive autonomy in important areas of one’s life by, for instance, institutionalizing sex-based work specialization, then there can be a politically liberal argument for valuing, and favoring in political deliberation, comprehensive autonomy. Under these conditions, those who realize comprehensive autonomy, Schouten claims, provide valuable assurance to others that “each of us could acquire the capacities involved in using our moral power to revise our conception of the good” (139). The argument here is focused narrowly on the issue of overcoming the gendered division of labor, but its form is general. When actual social conditions militate against the realization of comprehensive autonomy, there is an instrumental argument for state support for this ideal. Just as sex-based work specialization can “affront” the value of autonomy, so too, presumably, can other social conditions. The distance between the political liberal and the comprehensive liberal who champions autonomy thus seems to close considerably on Schouten’s argument. It can be said in reply that there remains the crucial difference that the political liberal, in contrast to the comprehensive liberal, values comprehensive autonomy only instrumentally as a means to reciprocity and stability, and not as a key contributor to the human good. But that reply sits in tension with the political liberal claim that the social conditions necessary for the adequate development of the moral power to form, pursue, and revise a conception of the good, the very conditions to which the value of autonomy purportedly contributes to instrumentally on Schouten’s argument, are themselves a means to our good. Accordingly, if Schouten’s intriguing argument is sound, then the difference between comprehensive autonomy-based liberalism and political liberalism may boil down not to a difference over whether the state should promote autonomy, and not whether the state can do so in the name of promoting the good of its citizens but whether its doing so is a only a means to, or also a constituent element of (as the comprehensive liberal claims), their good.Let me conclude by mentioning an interesting puzzle that arises from Schouten’s anatomy. The puzzle centers on the primary value of legitimacy and it arises from the following claims that Schouten makes about it. First, legitimacy is a matter of the moral permissibility of political action; and, second, legitimacy is a scalar value, one that has multiple dimensions and can be realized to different degrees. Now, permissibility is normally taken to be a dual operator. We ask, Is this arrangement permissible to impose and enforce or not? But what exactly would it mean to say that two social arrangements are each legitimate, but that one is more permissible to impose and enforce than the other?Schouten briefly contrasts legitimacy with authority. She allows that a political arrangement can have authority and thus be such that those subject to it are obligated to comply with it, while not being fully legitimate. A partly illegitimate, but still legitimate to some threshold, political regime may enjoy authority. But this helpful clarification does not dispel the puzzle. We turn to legitimacy because we are interested in understanding the permissible exercise of political power, but authority, not legitimacy, now seems to answer to that question, even if justified authority must meet a legitimacy threshold.Rawls sometimes described his liberal principle of legitimacy in terms of the moral permissibility of the exercise of political power, but he also, at other times, employed the more obscure idiom of propriety. The exercise of political power is only fully proper, he claimed, when the liberal principle of legitimacy is satisfied. Talk of propriety fits well with a scalar notion of legitimacy, but it leaves us in the dark as to how exactly assessments of greater and lesser degrees of legitimacy bear on the rights and duties of citizens. Progress on that issue would be a welcome development for the political liberal project, and the structure and clarifications provided by Schouten’s anatomy of justice prove useful here. We can say, on Schouten’s anatomy, that when we judge one social arrangement to be more legitimate than another social arrangement that also meets the threshold standard for legitimacy, we have moved beyond the issue of the moral permissibility of the exercise of political power. After all, by stipulation both arrangements can be enforced permissibly by authorities. We are now just expressing an evaluative ranking. The more legitimate arrangement, we are saying, is the more verdictively just arrangement. Legitimacy is a special value because it adjudicates conflicts with other political values. Full propriety is a matter of getting that adjudication fully right.

articles.t: The Scope and Limits of Partiality
articles.ab: This is a wide-ranging yet thorough investigation of the justification and limits of partiality. The author’s engaging style makes the book a pleasure to read. However, I wish she had told us how this book relates to her earlier book Rationality and Moral Theory: How Intimacy Generates Reasons.We are all partial to those we love—our friends, our families, and even our pets. We feel justified in paying for a family trip even though we know that we could have done more good by spending that money on the impoverished family down the street. We spend more on our children than on other people’s children even if the latter are much worse off. Indeed, we would criticize parents who left their own sick child untreated in order to help their neighbors’ three sick children.But how can we justify our partiality? We have fundamental—that is, nonderivative—reasons to care for our intimates, but we also have fundamental reasons to care for other people. When should our reasons to care for other people take priority over our reasons to care for our intimates?Consequentialist theories hold that we ought to try to maximize intrinsic value, hence our reasons for being partial must be justified as a means to such maximization. According to act-consequentialism, every action ought to be justifiable by this principle. But this is certainly not how we justify our partiality toward our intimates. Nor is the attitude needed for such justification compatible with the intimacy of loving relationships. Jeske rightly complains, “If one were to behave and deliberate [like a consequentialist] … it seems that one would not to be able to form or to sustain intimate relationships. Intimacy seems to require emotions and attitudes of special concern and also actions that express that special concern” (50).Peter Railton (1984: 149), however, has argued that sophisticated (or objective) act-consequentialism is compatible with the pursuit of intimate relationships and the dispositions it requires. He argues that we can and should develop the ordinary attitudes of special concern for intimates, because actions motivated by these attitudes in fact typically result in the greatest good. It is only if our partialist dispositions cease to promote the overall good that they cease to be justified and must not be acted upon.Jeske notes that the objective consequentialist’s friendship is justified only “insofar as it brings about the best consequences in the long run” (59). For the consequentialist, the only fundamental reasons are agent-neutral reasons to promote the good.I agree with Jeske, having myself argued that on Railton’s theory “whether I ought to be true to my friendship or betray it, preserve my dispositions of friendship or sacrifice them, depends on which choice produces the most good in the long run” (Badhwar 1991). Hence, if I accept consequentialism, the moral justification I must give for acting like a friend and preserving my friendship is instrumental. And this is incompatible with regarding my friendship as an end in itself—that is, as intrinsically good and justified because it is intrinsically good. As a consequentialist friend, I must think two logically incompatible thoughts: “As your friend, I place a special value on you out of friendship and not out of consequentialist considerations—but as a consequentialist agent I do so only so long as … valuing you thus promotes the overall good” (Badhwar 1991: 493).Jeske thinks I’m confused, objecting that (1) “I can continue to subjectively care more about my friend and my relationship with her even if … I am required to make a choice contrary to [her] … well-being,” and (2) the intrinsic good of a friendship is part of the overall good, not an instrumental means to it (58).However, (1) valuing a friend is not just a matter of having certain thoughts and feelings, but also of acting like a friend. And acting contrary to a friend’s well-being, or betraying her, is not exactly acting like a friend. And (2) while the intrinsic goodness of my friendship is, indeed, part of the overall good, if I can justify it only if it promotes rather than detracts from the overall good, then my justification of it is instrumental.What, then, is the best justification for being partial to our intimates? Jeske’s answer proceeds within the framework of three different kinds of reasons for action: “the objective agent-neutral (grounded by objective intrinsic value), the subjective agent-relative (grounded by subjective value relative to the agent), and the objective agent-relative (grounded by special relationships of the agent)” (39).We all have objective agent-neutral reasons for helping people in certain situations, such as during natural disasters; objective agent-relative reasons of intimacy with our friends; and subjective agent-relative reasons, such as those grounded in our projects. Jeske examines three views of why we have reasons of intimacy with our friends: the projects view, the individualist view, and the view she defends, the relationships view.The projects view holds that our reasons of partiality are grounded in our most important intrinsic (noninstrumental) goals, those that are commonly called ‘projects’. These are goals that “are embedded in and permeate our lives,” goals to which we have long-term commitments (86). Our intimate relationships are among our projects. So they give us fundamental, agent-relative reasons to care for our intimates, which “provide counterweight to the consequentialist reason” (90).But, Jeske argues, our intimate relationships can’t be understood simply as projects, because projects don’t have to be objectively valuable to give us reason to pursue them. They might be only subjectively valuable, their value entirely dependent on the fact that we care about them. But friendships also give us objective agent-relative reasons—that is, what most of us would call moral reasons or obligations—to care for our friends. Hence, although giving up a project when it interferes with other projects we are more interested in can be painful, doing so does not (usually) violate a duty to anyone. But neglecting or abandoning an intimate relationship when it becomes inconvenient or somewhat burdensome does. We have objective, agent-relative reasons not to do so. So the projects view is not a sufficient explanation for our reasons of intimacy. “Our friendships give us reason to try to maintain them as projects beyond the point at which our subjective attitudes cease to do so” (105). Thus, it is because Marnie and Anne are old friends that Marnie has an obligation—an objective, agent-relative reason—to care for her when she falls ill, even at the cost of giving up many of her own interests and pleasures.The individuals view of partiality articulated by Simon Keller and others claims, by contrast, that Marnie’s obligation is based on the fact that Anne has objective intrinsic value. Marnie’s reasons to care for Anne would exist even if Anne were not Marnie’s friend (112). But if Anne were not Marnie’s friend, Marnie’s reason to care for Anne would not be a reason of intimacy. It would be an objective, agent-neutral reason.Keller tries to show that friends have special agent-relative reasons to care for each other because their friendship is an enabler; that is, it enables them to act on the reason that the friend’s value gives them. Others who hold the view that the reason to act for the friend’s sake is based on her objective intrinsic value give similar reasons in order to secure agent-relativity.I find these views somewhat mysterious. In what sense does friendship “enable” one to care for a friend? How does a lack of friendship disable one from doing so? Obviously it doesn’t, since without the friendship you would still have objective, agent-neutral reasons to help, depending on your circumstances. So I agree with Jeske’s relationships view that it’s friendship that gives us a fundamental, objective agent-relative justification to care for our friends even when, subjectively, we no longer value them as much. In everyday language, friendship requires that we continue to care for our friends as a matter of loyalty.However, Jeske now argues that even when we do value a friend subjectively, we don’t have subjective, agent-relative reasons of care, because friendship is a historical relationship of mutual caring, in which the acts of mutual caring are motivated by subjective states but are not reducible to these states (111).I find this argument puzzling. A caring act is necessarily an act that expresses love, concern, loyalty, regard, or some other positive subjective attitude, even though it is not reducible to any of these subjective attitudes (since no act is reducible to a subjective state or attitude). Motivation by these subjective attitudes gives us subjective agent-relative reasons for acting in caring ways toward our intimates, reasons that those who don’t have intimates lack. Jeske recognizes this in her discussion of intimate relationships as projects and again in chapter 5, so it’s hard to understand why she changes her mind here.The relationships view itself comes in two varieties: the values-based view and Jeske’s non-values-based view. But since the arguments for and against the value-based view are similar to the arguments about the individuals view, I will not rehearse them here.In chapter 5, Jeske provides a rich picture of close friendship, the sort that gives us reasons of intimacy without glossing over the difficulties and flaws of even such a friendship. In a close friendship, the two friends have mutual affection and concern, and deep mutual knowledge—both knowledge-that and knowledge-how—thanks to their shared history. Our relationships with our companion dogs and cats have much in common with our human friendships, although perhaps they cannot love us for who we are, but only instrumentally (chap. 6). In both these chapters, Jeske draws from her own human and animal friendships, thus giving authenticity to her discussion.In chapter 7, Jeske argues that the legal and cultural importance given to marriage is unjustified, because although many people find a good marriage necessary for their happiness, the intimacy that makes it valuable can be found in close friendships also. Marriage is not uniquely valuable.In the last chapter, Jeske returns to the issue of the demands of intimacy versus the demands of people in general. She argues that if I have reason to save Marcy from drowning rather than a stranger, I also have those reasons in more complex real-world cases (266). I find this argument both original and compelling. Of course, having good reason to prefer your intimates over strangers doesn’t tell us how much preference is rational. Do those of us with flourishing lives have an obligation to spend less time and money on ourselves and our intimates, both human and animal? Jeske rightly argues that what it is rational for any given agent to do is a function of her causal placement vis-à-vis the promotion of intrinsic value and her intimate relationships. Philosophy helps us raise questions about the weight we place on those we love vis-à-vis others, but it can only give a general answer.Jeske worries that “continuing our current patterns of partiality is likely … to continue to widen the gap between the rich and the poor, thereby making the poor even worse off” (62; cf. 263). But a widening gap doesn’t by itself make the poor worse off if, while the rich get richer, the poor become less poor. This has indeed been the case with economic growth in poor countries. In 1990, 2.31 billion people lived in extreme poverty; in 2025, 808 million do.1 Likewise, spending a lot on our children’s development and thus giving them a “competitive advantage” over children whose parents can’t afford to do the same is not, contrary to Jeske, a harm to the latter (269). This zero-sum outlook ignores the fact that not all worthwhile jobs or careers in life require the support of rich parents. Again, the claim that having children means creating more people with needs overlooks the fact that people have not just needs but also capabilities: as the slogan goes, we come with two hands for every mouth.But these are small problems in the context of the book’s many virtues. Everyone interested in intimate relationships and their justification will benefit from reading it.

articles.t: Omnisubjectivity: An Essay on God and Subjectivity
articles.ab: In this engaging and sharply written book, Linda Zagzebski thoroughly explores an underdiscussed question for classical theistic metaphysics: whether and how God is ‘omnisubjective’, perfectly grasping creaturely conscious states as they are experienced by their subjects. She argues that theists have several strong reasons to suppose that God is omnisubjective; offers four ways one might understand this divine capacity, each with pros and cons; rebuts arguments that it is inconsistent with six other standard divine attributes; argues that it extends to all possible (and not merely actual) creaturely subjective states; applies it with novel implications to the Christian doctrines of Trinity and Incarnation; and argues that subjectivity is primary in God, with God’s ‘objective nature’ depending on God’s choice to create a world with an objective nature. She also briefly suggests some implications of the foregoing to the problem of evil.Zagzebski opens chapter 1 by stating, “What I mean by subjectivity is consciousness as it is experienced by the subject of conscious states, not consciousness as an object of personal reflection or empirical investigation or theoretical description.” (1) She allows that physicalism might be true, conceived as a thesis about either the fundamental objects or all the objective facts in the world. But that would not reduce subjectivity to a physical phenomenon since, in her view, “the objective does not exhaust reality” (8). The idea of subjectivity is absent from Descartes’s theory on which mental properties or powers are wholly distinct from physical properties and born by a distinctive sort of object, the I, the conscious substance. Though dualist, this ontology represents the mind as no less objective than physical reality. It posits a mental substance but no self (later described as “the inside of a person” 145). Indeed, according to Zagzebski, the very idea of subjectivity was unknown to Descartes or any of his predecessors in human history, emerging only in subsequent philosophical critiques of Descartes’s theory.Such bold claims raise many questions. But for the moment, let us merely note that they set a high bar for accounting for God’s omnisubjectivity. It is not enough that God should know all the facts about the subjective states of all His creatures; He must also grasp perfectly what each such state is like for its subject. God must perfectly grasp the qualitative character of bat echolocative experience, despite not having echolocative sensory apparatus. Further, He must grasp what it is like to have such experience within the biological and cognitive confines of bathood, and further still, within the narrative trajectory and other idiosyncrasies of a particular bat. Most challenging of all, He must be able to distinguish the irreducible ‘for-me-ness’ of two qualitatively duplicate bats (150–51). How might this go? Zagzebski notes that two natural proposals, on which God has an idealized imaginative empathy for, or a more-direct-than-sense perception of, a creature’s experiences, will inevitably fall short, insofar as they maintain some kind of epistemic gap between God and creature. “Provided that there is any distance at all, God as knower does not really grasp what you are experiencing in the way you experience it as the subject of the experience.” (72) She then notes that one might close the gap by rejecting classical theism in favor of panentheism, on which every created thing is within God (as a part), although God is more than the totality of created things. But panentheism is saddled with the burden of explaining how particular evils can be parts of a perfectly good God, and it forces us to reconceptualize the dynamics of prayer, the very religious practice that made pressing the project of accounting for God’s omnisubjectivity. The final (and to this reviewer, most promising) approach that Zagzebski considers is to tease out implications of the idea that God is (continuously) First Cause of the world. As Thomas Aquinas famously contends, God does not know created reality ‘after the fact’. Rather, He knows each created thing in the first instance by knowing His own creative power that continuously gives being to the thing in all its particularity: its qualities, powers, and thisness. Zagzebski suggests that we think of creation as streaming forth like light, such that each creaturely subjective state is a distinctive color in the full rainbow contained within the uncreated white light of God’s creative consciousness. In this way, the divine light “bathes and infuses objects without being identical to them” (81).On most accounts, the actual creation does not exhaust the scope of what might have been. In knowing created things by knowing Himself, then, God must fully grasp counteractual things and their states no less than the ones He contingently willed into being. (‘Counteractual’, not ‘counterfactual’, because subjectivity is not a subdomain of objective facts and cannot be fully expressed propositionally [116]). Here Zagzebski’s usual clarity falters. She emphasizes the role that imagining possible subjective states (of actual persons or fictional characters) plays in our own lives, and on this basis she suggests repeatedly that the line between the actual and possible is blurred in some way that is underappreciated in canonical possible-worlds theorizing. In some instances, she qualifies her point, as when she writes that “there is not a sharp line separating actual and counteractual in the imagination” (124; emphasis added). If this means only that our imaginative representations of counteractual states make a difference to actuality and you cannot understand our own subjectivity without taking into account the role that such episodes play in our own personal narratives, it will be entirely unobjectionable. However, other passages strongly suggest that she wants to make the stronger claim that the line between the actual and the possible is itself blurred, with the imagination serving as a portal between them: “The human imagination connects actual and counteractual subjectivity and the line between them is vague. When we think about our counteractual self, the actual and the possible blend and merge” (129). For example, “I imagine something funny that does not exist in the actual world and that makes me laugh” (130). What is the referent here of “that”—Zagzebski’s entirely actual imaginative state or the possible situation? As best I can judge, she intends the latter, but she fails to provide a clear case for the necessity of such a possibilist thesis over the actualist alternative.Zagzebski then turns to God’s grasp of actual and counteractual subjectivity. She sharply distinguishes imagination, with its representation and productive creativity, and intellect, characterized by abstract thought (134–35). She argues that imagination is “the only appropriate faculty for grasping subjective possibilities and it is a faculty superior to the intellect for grasping objective possibilities” (136). But missing is an argument that there is an either/or choice to be made. Certainly, in us these capacities have complementary roles in grasping either kind of possibility, with the intellect discerning the lineaments of essences and logical relations. As many philosophers and cognitive scientists emphasize, perception and imagination are infused by cognition. What would the former be without the shaping role of concepts and propositional understanding? Zagzebski might argue that for God, with a perfect intuitive (‘imaginative’) grasp of all possible things and their interrelations, the need for intellectual abstraction falls away. But why is it not more appropriate to say instead that there is a unitary mode of knowing that has both imaginative and intellectual aspects? Leaving that question aside, we may ask how God’s knowledge of all possibilities impacts the issue of actualism versus possibilism. Zagzebski writes that “all possible objects exist in the divine imagination, and in the creation, some objects go from the darkness of the possible to the light of the actual” (139). This way of conceiving the matter is noncompulsory. We may instead say simply that God has the unexercised power (or unactualized potentiality, if we are in the mood for provoking Thomists) to create any of innumerable kinds of beings in any of innumerable kinds of circumstance, and He represents these possibilities in fully determinate ways within His perfect imaginative/intellectual mode of knowing. Notice, too, that the objects so represented need not be (as Zagzebski seems to suppose) determinately individuals, preloaded with thisness in a way that gives rise to vertiginous and possibly paradoxical barely distinct possible individuals with the exact same qualitative profiles across possibility space.I turn, finally, to Zagzebski’s seemingly radical suggestion that there is a deep distinction between subjectivity and objectivity in God and that in God subjectivity is primary and alone uncreated. She equates objective nature with essence (144) and tells us that the divine essence or objective nature includes “attributes such as omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, and perfect goodness” (144). God’s subjectivity, on the other hand, “is not a component of the divine nature” because it cannot be “taken objectively” (145), which is to say grasped “from outside” and “communicated from one mind to another” (178). God’s subjectivity, however, is not bare subjectivity, since “God’s states of willing, knowing, and loving are subjective states” (145). But we (inevitably) conceive these “from outside” as omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence, and this perspective “leaves aside the first-person aspect of these attributes” (145). The primacy of subjectivity in God thus appears not as radical a claim as it initially sounds. It amounts to saying that (1) unlike us, there is no unconscious aspect or capacity in God and (2) while we may truly say of God that He is, for example, omnipotent, we are precluded from grasping that power as it is in itself (infinitely creative subjectivity) and are confined to thinking of it ‘from outside’ as a theoretical quality analogous to ones we experience in and around ourselves. While there is much that is contentious in classical theistic metaphysics, this pair of claims is not. Zagzebski links (178–79) the primacy of subjectivity doctrine to Thomas Aquinas’s doctrine of divine simplicity, on which God is being itself (ipsum esse), such that there is no distinction in God between essence and being. That is a radical claim indeed. But her thesis and Aquinas’s seem wholly independent. She offers her primacy thesis as an interpretation of a couple of passages from Aquinas propounding the simplicity thesis, but this interpretive move is odd, given that she told us earlier that the very idea of subjectivity was unknown prior to the post-Cartesian era.Space precludes my remarking on her intriguing discussions in chapter 6 of maximal subjective and intersubjective consciousness among persons of the Trinity and her use of subjectivity as the basis of the unified person of the dual-natured, incarnate Christ. Grappling with her proposals and arguments throughout the book was fruitful for developing my own thinking on several matters, and that is strong commendation for a work of philosophy.

articles.t: Inquiry Under Bounds
articles.ab: All theories of rationality face a challenge. Our intuitions about rationality make unrealistic demands of us. So how can a theory take our imperfect reasoning to be rational while at the same time preserving our unrealistic intuitions? David Thorstad has written a book that tries to square this circle. His questions are pressing and important. His grasp of the relevant literature is enviable. His ability to bring a wide range of philosophical and empirical considerations to bear in support of his view is impressive. And his final theory has many virtues. But does he manage to vindicate both our imperfect reasoning and our unrealistic intuitions? Let’s take a look.The Standard Picture reflects our unrealistic intuitions. Rationality on this picture is reserved for ideal agents unburdened by pesky human limitations. The attempt to apply Standard Picture expectations to real people has “bleak implications” for human rationality (Nisbett and Borgida 1975). Thorstad rejects these bleak implications—at least with respect to inquiry.Consider an example. This morning, I randomly chose a pair of gym socks from my sock drawer. I didn’t conduct an exhaustive survey to find the best pair of socks. Was my behavior rational? For Thorstad, it was—but not because I reasoned like an ideal agent. I didn’t. In fact, on the Standard Picture, my sock-choosing behavior was just more confirmation that, rationality wise, I’m a big disappointment. For Thorstad, however, my sock-choosing behavior was rational because it satisfied two conditions. First, it was my best option. Of all the ways I might have chosen gym socks this morning, random choice maximized expected utility, where this is calculated using a wide range of values (more on this soon) and probabilities derived from my available evidence. And, second, my behavior was prompted by considerations that made it the best option: I chose randomly because I’ve got better things to do with my morning than search for the perfect pair of gym socks. Thorstad’s Reason-Responsive Consequentialist View (or RRCV) is a theory of bounded rationality. It accounts for a reasoner’s limitations, if any, from the get-go. It’s a unified normative framework for all agents, bounded and unbounded.RRCV takes rationality to be environment-relative (or “ecological,” in the jargon of psychologists). Random choice was rational because—not to get too braggy—my sock drawer is always full of comfy gym socks. Random choice wouldn’t have been rational had the drawer been mostly full of mittens. This is a simple but important point. A large literature in psychology shows that in typical (but not all possible) environments, several of our default heuristics are surprisingly effective, despite the scorn heaped on them by the Standard Picture.RRCV delivers a vindicatory epistemology: Our inquiries are typically rational. They are rational far more often than the Standard Picture allows. This is because we work smart, not hard. We seldom use expensive ideal strategies (e.g., closely evaluating every sock in the sock drawer). We usually use cheap heuristics (e.g., random choice) that deliver good (and occasionally ideal) results. If we focus on the consequences of a single episode (e.g., choosing this pair of socks), we’ll usually get somewhat better results with ideal strategies. But the benefit of cheap heuristics is that they free us to do other valuable things with our finite resources (like drive the kids to school, go to the gym in socks that are plenty, if not perfectly, comfy, and still get to work on time). If we tried to live up to the ideals foisted on us by the Standard Picture, the juice just wouldn’t be worth the squeeze.That’s the basic outline of Thorstad’s theory. Now let’s dig into the details. His overall strategy is to defend a theory of practical rationality, apply that theory to inquiry, and establish that human inquiry is typically rational (203). The theory consists of three elements.It’s worth noting that utility-maximizing theories are prototypical Standard Picture theories. But since RRCV doesn’t require agents to calculate expected utilities, it is a theory of bounded rationality. The sock example illustrates that RRCV provides a natural way to account for how limited creatures engage in rational inquiry. It illuminates how we ought to select topics, seek evidence, sift evidence, halt inquiry, and arrive at conclusions. Curiously, however, Thorstad does not apply RRCV to the products of inquiry.Thorstad does not discard the Standard Picture. Instead, he apportions part of our cognitive lives (inquiry) to a theory of bounded rationality and another part of our cognitive lives (the attitudes that result from inquiry) to the Standard Picture. This is how Thorstad tries to square the circle. He vindicates human rationality with RRCV and our unrealistic intuitions with the Standard Picture. Thorstad’s theory takes our inquiries to be rational more often (and perhaps far more often) than the products of our inquiries (178).It’s worth noting just how much tradition Thorstad preserves. Even his theory of bounded rationality has the look and feel of a Standard Picture theory. As I see it, this philosophical conservatism leads to three problems. The first is caused by level separation. For level separation to work, there needs to be separation between what’s rational and what’s irrational. But there’s not. Suppose RRCV says that it’s rational for Robin to inquire using a heuristic that employs a fraction of their total evidence. The heuristic’s final step, the decision rule, says: Accept p. But suppose that the belief that ∼p is rational given our preferred Standard Picture theory (e.g., it’s best supported by Robin’s total evidence). There’s a tension: It’s rational for Robin to accept p (RRCV) but believe ∼p (Standard Picture). This problem is exacerbated by the fact that Thorstad takes rationality to be deontic: One is rationally required to X just in case one ought to X (32). Every time inquiry is rational but the result of that inquiry is irrational (or vice versa), Thorstad’s theory yields a pair of ‘ought’ claims that cannot both be satisfied. This is especially problematic given that Thorstad accepts the ‘ought’ implies ‘can’ principle (128). (Level separation causes analogous problems for practical inquiry. And insofar as practical attitudes, such as preferences and intentions, turn out to be irrational, it’s hard to see how this irrationality doesn’t bleed into a lot of theoretical inquiry.)The second problem for RRCV is that it seems to be self-defeating. By its own lights, it’s too unwieldy to inform rational inquiry into rational inquiry. RRCV evaluates each choice-point in an inquiry by comparing its expected utility to the expected utilities of other possible choices. And all those expected utilities are a function of the inquirer’s total evidence and every value in Thorstad’s rich axiology. This is not a theory humans can use. Compared to RRCV, the models of rational inquiry psychologists build are absurdly simple (162). Thorstad takes these models to be simplified applications of RRCV. And that’s fair, but it doesn’t really address the objection. To see why, consider that Thorstad is a philosophical lumper. Lumpers prefer fewer large categories, whereas splitters prefer a larger number of small categories. A philosophical splitter will propose different, but related, normative frameworks for empirical inquiry, prudential inquiry, aesthetic inquiry, moral inquiry, and so on. Thorstad lumps all these disparate kinds of inquiry into a single framework. Splitters seem to be in a much better position to develop frameworks for specific types of inquiry (empirical, prudential, moral, aesthetic) that we can use to understand and predict the behaviors of real rational agents. What’s more, it’s possible that a splitter’s frameworks could be applied to improve how people reason about (say) causation, sunk costs, moral obligations, or film. By taking us so far away from the action, by its own lights, RRCV risks being far less rational than more specific and useful splitter theories.The third problem for RRCV concerns normative dilemmas. Here’s a classic dilemma: Epistemic considerations pull Alex to believe p while moral considerations pull Alex to withhold judgment and seek more evidence. Splitters can explain dilemmas (“Moral values versus epistemic values!”) but have trouble resolving them. Lumpers resolve dilemmas so efficiently that they have trouble explaining them (“Just believe that p, what’s the dilemma?”). But this isn’t my worry. Thorstad’s framework has resources to explain normative dilemmas. My worry has to do with the way RRCV resolves normative dilemmas. It lumps values together and then swamps some of them in its expected utility calculations. For example, Robin’s use of a cheap heuristic might not maximize expected epistemic utility, but it’s rational because it maximizes overall expected utility. This explanation is a signature success of RRCV. But there’s a dark side to values getting swamped in the consequentialist maw.Consider Draper, a sexist living in a sexist culture. Some of Draper’s heuristics reflect his sexist attitudes. For example, he automatically infers that unfamiliar women at work are secretaries, and in his environment, this heuristic is highly accurate. Thorstad regards “it as a non-negotiable datum” that this sort of stereotype-based inference is rationally impermissible, despite its “resemblance to structurally similar cases of rational heuristic inference” (99). A classic objection to consequentialism is that it delivers fewer non-negotiables than we’re comfortable with, and that’s the problem here. The consequentialist machinery that swamps epistemic values (to vindicate Robin’s epistemically imperfect inquiries) will just as efficiently swamp moral values (to vindicate Draper’s sexist inquiries). In fact, this swamping is a practical certainty in Draper’s sexist environment. A lumping-swamping theory of rationality is not going to make Thorstad’s “non-negotiable datum” stick. Splitters, on the other hand, are better positioned to prevent moral values from being swamped in the evaluation of Draper’s inquiries.Let me pause here to emphasize that I don’t take these objections to be disqualifying. Remember, I think that every theory of rationality carries significant costs. Every theory has to pick its poison. So when I push Thorstad to be a splitter or to abandon the Standard Picture, he can (with justification) push back by noting that this means flouting some very robust intuitions. And, in fact, that’s exactly what he does (58–60, 178–86). Ultimately, the issue for Thorstad’s theory—and, really, for any theory—is whether the juice is worth the squeeze.Philosophers interested in rationality have a choice. We can have a theory of bounded rationality that explains how we can be both rational and imperfect. Or we can have a Standard Picture theory that respects our unrealistic intuitions. Thorstad tries to do both. The result is a book that’s admirable, impressive, and in some ways successful. But in philosophy, as in life, we tend to get ourselves into trouble when we try to have it all.

articles.t: Autonomy and Legitimacy: An Internal Refutation of Consent Theory
articles.ab: Consent theory claims that political legitimacy rests on the consent of the governed. The theory has been marginalized in political philosophy due to the success of Hume’s objections, which observe that consent theory entails anarchism, as almost nobody has consented to be governed. However, these standard objections leave the foundations of consent theory untouched; the consent theorist, confident in the appeal of these foundations, can endorse anarchism in response. This article offers an objection that focuses on what makes consent normatively appealing in the first place, the value of individual autonomy. On almost any plausible reading of that foundation, one should not be a consent theorist.

articles.t: The Abstract and the Concrete: Further Essays in Ontology
articles.ab: The Abstract and the Concrete is a collection of nine essays (eight of which have been previously published) on a variety of different topics in ontology and metaontology. The essays in metaontology broadly defend a “neo-Quinean” approach to metaontology by critiquing various alternative approaches. The essays in ontology mostly focus on defending a particular theory of abstract objects, which van Inwagen calls “Lightweight Platonism.”A central component of Quine’s metaontology is that there is only one way to exist. The goal of the first essay is to defend this view against “ontological pluralism,” which says that there is more than one way to exist. The kind of ontological pluralism at issue in this chapter can be thought of as endorsing the fundamentality of at least two existential quantifiers, which we can symbolize as ∃1 and ∃2. These distinct quantifiers nonetheless function grammatically like the standard first-order existential quantifier, in that they bind variables in nominal position (as opposed to the kinds of quantifiers in higher-order logic).Van Inwagen argues that the “generic” existential quantifier, which ranges over absolutely everything across different ways of being, is indispensable for the ontological pluralist. For example, if the ontological pluralist wishes to state that everything exists in one of two ways, they would seem to need a generic quantifier. Van Inwagen also argues that in order to construct a satisfactory logic that accounts for the validity of “mixed” inferences that use different fundamental quantifiers, the ontological pluralist must (either explicitly or implicitly) appeal to generic quantifiers. The fact that generic quantifiers are indispensable for ontological pluralists (while “specific” quantifiers are not indispensable for neo-Quineans) is, van Inwagen argues, a reason to be skeptical of ontological pluralism. This kind of argument against pluralism has since been further discussed and defended by Trenton Merricks (2017) and David Builes (2019). Finally, van Inwagen also argues that the primary motivation behind ontological pluralism is not persuasive. Although it is true that (say) numbers and tables are extremely different entities, that is not a good reason to think that they exist in different ways. One only needs to appeal to the vastly different properties had by numbers and tables to capture how different they are.The goal of the second essay, as well as the eighth, is to defend neo-Quineanism against “neo-Carnapianism.” A central component of Carnap’s metaontology is that many ontological debates can be trivially or analytically settled by appealing to a “linguistic framework.” For example, one might argue that there are conceptual truths that guarantee the existence of numbers, properties, mereological sums, propositions, and so on. Such conceptual truths might include, for example, “If there are no dinosaurs, then the number of dinosaurs is zero,” “If an apple is red, then it has the property of redness,” or “If there are particles-arranged-table-wise, then there are tables.” Van Inwagen raises a number of initial difficulties for this view. Here are three of them. First, the kinds of conceptual truths that lead to the existence of properties quickly lead to contradictions that are similar to Russell’s paradox. Consider the predicate “non-self-applicable.” The property of wisdom is non-self-applicable, since the property of wisdom is itself not wise. But, if the property of being non-self-applicable exists, is it non-self-applicable? Either way, a contradiction follows. Second, how exactly are truths about numbers supposed to be guaranteed by adopting a particular linguistic framework? Given Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, it seems like any finitely specifiable list of linguistic rules will fail to capture all the truths of arithmetic. So it’s hard to see how the truths of arithmetic could be guaranteed by the adoption of some linguistic framework. Third, even if the bare existence of these various entities is guaranteed by linguistic rules, there seem to be many questions about these entities that are not settled by linguistic rules. For example, what are the persistence conditions of tables? What kinds of de re modal properties do tables have? More generally, accepting the existence of an entity results in the theoretical burden of assigning a consistent and complete (and preferably nonarbitrary and independently motivated) set of properties to that entity.Of course, there are ways to resist these initial problems. Philosophers have developed many different ways to resist Russell’s paradox, there are ways to defend the determinacy of arithmetic without giving up on neo-Carnapianism (e.g., see Warren 2020), and there are ways to deflate questions about the temporal and modal properties of objects (e.g., via temporal or modal counterpart theory or via a plenitudinous ontology that contains objects with “all possible” temporal and modal profiles). However, each of these further replies comes with its own distinctive set of philosophical challenges. A last and more general point that van Inwagen raises is that philosophers have given many different arguments against the existence of numbers, properties, mereological sums, and so on. Appealing to conceptual truths does nothing to show where these arguments are supposed to go wrong (if anywhere).The third and final topic in metaontology that van Inwagen discusses is whether we should adopt a “hierarchical” model of ontology, according to which some entities are more fundamental than, and metaphysically ground, other entities. Van Inwagen’s main criticism of this kind of view is methodological. Oftentimes a hierarchical model of ontology is motivated by giving some intuitive examples of entities that are supposed to ground other entities, such as Socrates grounding {Socrates}. Van Inwagen instead argues that we should be deciding on the merits of a hierarchical model of ontology by comparing global systematic metaphysical theories that utilize a hierarchical model of ontology with global systematic metaphysical theories that do not utilize such a hierarchical model. A second point that van Inwagen makes is that eliminativist views about Fs have important advantages over views that recognize the nonfundamental existence of Fs. For example, van Inwagen argues that the various philosophical puzzles that come with giving a full theory of events are avoided if one is an eliminativist about events, whereas recognizing the nonfundamental existence of events doesn’t seem to do anything to address those puzzles.Although these two points are well taken, I would have liked to hear more about how van Inwagen addresses the usual paradigmatic examples of metaphysical grounding. Van Inwagen’s preferred ontology does not include sets, so the example of {Socrates} will not get off the ground. But van Inwagen does accept the existence of composite living organisms. The defender of metaphysical grounding would say that there is a systematic correlation between the kinds of properties that composite living organisms have and the intrinsic properties and relations of the simples that compose that living organism. Moreover, this systematic correlation seems to hold of metaphysical necessity. It is natural to think there should be an explanation of this systematic necessary correlation. Proponents of metaphysical grounding will say that what explains this necessary correlation is that the properties of composite objects hold in virtue of the properties of their constituent parts, where this “in virtue of” tracks an important kind of explanation that is ubiquitous in metaphysics. In the absence of an explanatory connection of this kind, the necessary connection between a composite object and its parts can seem mysterious.Moving on to “first-order” ontology, three of the essays in the book (essays 4, 5, and 6) defend and describe van Inwagen’s preferred theory of abstract objects, while one essay (essay 7) critiques a rival account of “fictionalist nominalism.”Van Inwagen’s primary motivation for believing in abstract objects is a familiar Quinean reason. Much of what we say in ordinary life seems to quantify over abstract objects, and there doesn’t seem to be a successful way to “paraphrase away” this ontological commitment. One nominalist response to this challenge is to say that, although much of what we say in ordinary life might be strictly speaking false, the “nominalistic content” of what we say (roughly: how the concrete world would intrinsically have to be in order for our sentences to come out true) is still true, and this is good enough both for ordinary life and scientific purposes. One criticism of this view in the literature, defended by Mark Colyvan (2010), is to argue that this kind of view cannot account for the explanatory role that mathematics plays in science (just as scientific antirealists cannot account for the explanatory role of unobservable scientific posits). Van Inwagen comes close to this kind of criticism in his seventh essay, “Fictionalist Nominalism and Applied Mathematics,” where he argues that nominalists cannot account for why applied mathematics is so successful at letting us draw conclusions about the concrete world. However, by now there are several existing replies to this explanatory challenge by nominalists in the literature, which, unfortunately, van Inwagen does not address (e.g., see Leng 2012).With respect to his own positive views, van Inwagen defends a theory of abstract objects with several different components. First, he argues that abstract objects are all necessarily existent. Although this view is fairly standard, it has its detractors. For example, one could think that “haecceitistic” properties like being Socrates are abstract objects that only exist in worlds where Socrates exists. In response, van Inwagen argues that denying that properties exist necessarily leads to the implausible view that the accessibility relation among possible worlds is not symmetric (103–4). A second component of van Inwagen’s view is that abstract objects do not stand in any causal relations. This view is also standard, although again it has its detractors (e.g., one might think that fictional characters are abstract objects that are causally brought into existence by their authors). Third, he argues that all abstract objects are “universals” rather than “tropes,” where the relevant conception of universals is “transcendent” rather than “immanent,” in that universals do not in any way depend on the concrete world for their existence. Fourth, van Inwagen rejects the idea, defended by David Armstrong, that universals are explanatory posits that are meant to explain (say) facts about objective similarity. He also rejects the idea that (say) an apple is red in virtue of or because it instantiates the abstract property of redness. For van Inwagen, the only explanation for why an apple is red will be a scientific causal explanation, not a metaphysical explanation.One of the more distinctive aspects of van Inwagen’s view of abstract objects is that they are all relations. Here, “relations” is meant to be understood broadly to not only include n-place relations where n is greater than 1, but also 1-place relations (“properties”), 0-place relations (“propositions”), and variably polyadic relations. Van Inwagen describes his version of Platonism as a “truth-centered” ontology, since all these abstract objects are closely connected to the concept of truth. Propositions are of course things that can be true or false, and properties and relations are things that can be true or false of some other thing(s).Van Inwagen’s truth-centered ontology does not include ordinary mathematical objects like numbers and sets. So how does van Inwagen account for mathematics? He does this by introducing a structurally similar “replacement” for set theory that he calls “proxy set theory,” or “proxet theory” for short. The rough idea behind proxet theory is to replace sets with properties and membership with instantiation. {Socrates} is associated with the haecceity of Socrates, or the property of being Socrates. So “Socrates is a member of {Socrates}” is translated as “Socrates instantiates the property of being Socrates.” More generally, a nonempty set of things is associated with a disjunctive property, which is the disjunction of the haecceities of its “members,” so {Socrates, Plato} will be associated with the disjunctive property of being either Socrates or Plato. Finally, the empty set can be associated with an arbitrary impossible property that is not instantiated by anything, such as the property of being non-self-identical.Overall, this collection of essays contains many interesting and important arguments in ontology and metaontology, and I would recommend anyone interested in those topics read it. In some cases, the essays feel a bit dated and not responsive to the contemporary literature on the relevant topics, but that is only to be expected since the volume contains many essays that were written roughly a decade ago. For example, recent discussions of “higher-order metaphysics” are, of course, very relevant to both metaontology and the reality of abstract objects, but they are not discussed in any detail in the present volume. Readers interested in what van Inwagen has to say about higher-order quantification (and, in particular, why he finds such quantification unintelligible if it is not paraphrased away) can find his thoughts on the topic in chapter 5 of his previous book, Being: A Study in Ontology.

articles.t: The Complex Tapestry of Free Will: A Philosophical Odyssey
articles.ab: This book is a comprehensive presentation of Robert Kane’s important views about free will and moral responsibility. Kane is a proponent of libertarianism about free will (and moral responsibility), the conjunction of two claims: (1) the incompatibility of causal determinism with free will/moral responsibility, and (2) our freedom and moral responsibility. Some incompatibilists, such as Carl Ginet and Peter van Inwagen (among others), focus primarily on establishing (1) but do not pay so much attention to (2). Kane is distinctive in giving both core claims of libertarianism considerable attention.In defending (1), Ginet and van Inwagen emphasize what van Inwagen dubbed “the Consequence Argument,” which employs primarily principles expressing the fixity of the past and natural laws. Kane accepts these principles but does not explicitly employ this argument as the driver of his incompatibilism, although I would claim the intuitive ideas and principles involved in the Consequence Argument do play a role in Kane’s argumentation. Similarly, while some incompatibilists, especially about causal determinism and moral responsibility, such as Derk Pereboom, emphasize Manipulation Arguments, Kane does not explicitly invoke them as central to his rejection of (1), although, again, I would note that manipulation concerns do play a role in Kane’s critiques of compatibilism. Kane’s distinctive arguments for (1) rely primarily on consideration of examples and more general kinds of circumstances and facts about human nature and behavior, and the application of inference to the best explanation.In his defense of (2), Kane offers a detailed account of indeterministic free will. He avoids appeal to “extravagant” and “obscure” elements in this account, arguing that it is entirely consistent with naturalism and science. It is not committed to any sort of dualism about the relationship between the mind and body, nor to different “realms” or “perspectives,” as in Kantian views about agency. Kane also presents critiques of other approaches to these topics (compatibilist, incompatibilist, and skeptical) and defenses of his views against objections offered over the years. These further clarify and sharpen both Kane’s defense of incompatibilism and his account of indeterministic free will/moral responsibility. Kane’s critiques and ruminations throughout the book are insightful and illuminating.Kane is one of the most important and influential contemporary philosophers working on this cluster of topics of ancient as well as contemporary interest. Unfortunately, he passed away a few months before the publication of this book. Bob was a generous and supportive mentor and a sympathetic interlocutor, even with those with whom he had fundamental disagreements—a role model for writing clearly and doing philosophy in a collegial way.I confess: I am one of those philosophers with whom Kane has had fundamental disagreements, and I will sketch some of them here, even as I worry that it may seem a bit ungracious. I’ll start with Kane’s defense of incompatibilism (1), then turn to the development of his particular account of indeterministic freedom, as it relates to (2).(1) The Defense of IncompatibilismA central feature of Kane’s overall theory of free will and moral responsibility is his notion of “self-forming actions (SFAs)” (12–13). He observes that many of the seemingly intractable debates (including much of the contemporary discussion) are misguided in focusing solely (or primarily) on the notion that moral responsibility requires alternative possibilities, the AP condition. Rather, Kane holds that there is a deeper and more important requirement for moral responsibility, “ultimate responsibility,” the UR condition (11–14). He contends that a necessary condition of our moral responsibility is that we are the ultimate sources of our behavior (in the first instance, our will or choices) in the way captured by UR: to be ultimately responsible for an action, an agent must be responsible to some degree for anything that is a sufficient reason (a sufficient condition, case, or motive) for the action’s occurring (11).Kane believes that UR implies that, if we are to legitimately attribute moral responsibility to an agent for an action, we need to trace back to some point at which there is indeterminism. The indeterminism enables SFAs. For Kane, it is a mistake to focus solely on what he calls “freedom of action.” Rather, a more basic (though obviously related) issue is “freedom of the will,” which requires an SFA (13–15). Crucially, Kane takes the claim that SFAs require alternative possibilities (freedom to will/choose otherwise) and causal indeterminism to be intuitive. I don’t, however, see an argument for it, apart from the idea that genuine “depth” of human moral responsibility and value depends on such freedom.The problem is that all Kane is entitled to, based simply on intuition, is that there be an exercise of “freedom” or “free will” at some point along the action-generating path, but it is contentious (and not decided by intuition alone) whether this is alternative-possibilities freedom or an actual-sequence freedom. Harry Frankfurt (1969, 1971) distinguished between freedom to do/choose otherwise and acting freely. This distinction, or something like it, goes back at least to Chrysippus and is noted by philosophers such as Bramhall and Locke, as well many contemporary philosophers (in addition to Frankfurt). I contend that, at this point in the dialectic, that is, the analysis of the intuitive and pre-theoretic idea of an “SFA” (a character-forming choice that helps to ground moral responsibility), Kane is not entitled to the idea that SFAs require alternative-possibilities, rather than actual-sequence, freedom.One could put it this way. Kane and I agree that moral responsibility for an action requires an exercise (or, at least, possession) of freedom along the path to the action, but we disagree about the kind of freedom: alternative-possibilities or actual-sequence. We all want a deep interpretation of the free will required for moral responsibility, but it is not justified, at an intuitive level of argumentation, to assume that actual-sequence freedom cannot be deep. If, as I contend, there is nothing in our intuitive and pre-theoretic idea of an SFA that points to alternative-possibilities, rather than actual-sequence, freedom, much of Kane’s argumentation becomes problematic. Throughout his various arguments for incompatibilism, he does not give sufficient weight to the possibility of actual-sequence freedom. (He does offer such an account of voluntariness, but not of freedom.)Consider his discussion of B. F. Skinner’s Walden Two (26–28). Frazier, one of the designers of the “utopian” community, behaviorally conditioned people (in a causally deterministic way) from childhood to want and choose only what they could have and do (26). Frazier described the community as “the freest place on earth, the freest place imaginable” (26). Of course, Kane thinks this is false; the people are free only in a superficial sense (“freedom of action”) but not in a deeper sense (“freedom of the will”). He holds that this deeper sense requires an SFA, and thus indeterminism. Kane writes: “…the worry [about the freedom implicated in moral responsibility] grows to the extent that the conditioning may be completely determining …” (28).I agree that B. F. Skinner’s community is not the freest place on earth. It is more like a “gangster’s paradise,” as in the song sung by Coolio and L.V. I deny, however, that the only way to capture this “deeper” kind of freedom is to accept AP and UR. Actual-sequence freedom can fill the bill. There are various plausible accounts of such freedom, and my point here does not depend on accepting any particular account of actual-sequence freedom, only that such freedom exists (and can be separated, at least analytically, from alternative-possibilities freedom).I adopt a “guidance control” model of actual-sequence freedom. On my view, an agent acts freely only if she exhibits guidance control—that is, she chooses/acts from her own appropriately reasons-responsive mechanism (Fischer 1994; Fischer and Ravizza 1998). The people in Walden Two lack the capacity for guidance control and thus lack actual-sequence freedom. They do not act freely. They lack not merely the freedom to want and do what they do not in fact want or do (perhaps as the result of deterministic conditioning by other people or other clandestine compulsion). It is deeper than this: one must choose and act from one’s own reasons-responsive mechanism. The people arguably fail to act from their own mechanisms, and those mechanisms may fail to be reasons-responsive in the relevant sense.I contend (although I cannot argue for this here) that guidance control is compatible with causal determinism (Fischer and Ravizza 1998). Thus, even if alternative-possibilities freedom (freedom to choose and do otherwise) is incompatible with causal determinism, actual-sequence freedom need not be. We should not then infer that the problematic status of the denizens of Walden Two must be explained by causal determination qua causal determination; it might be explained by the kind of determination that precludes guidance control.Kane writes that some compatibilists would insist that the difference between deterministic control by others (such as Frazier) and such control by natural processes of heredity and environment (and “ordinary” human interaction) is relevant here. He claims that these compatibilists would resist attributing responsibility to the citizens of Walden Two, but not necessarily to any agent causally determined to choose and act as she does.
