Mill, meant when they styled the utilitarian philosophy and its progressive agenda as “utilitarianism.”The book concludes with a discussion of some of the standard criticisms of utilitarian consequentialism that Darr boldly argues might well have been moot had it retained its former theological cast, notably the view of an omniscient and providential God who wills the maximal happiness of all human beings. For example, the “cluelessness” problem, the impossibility of accurately comparing and quantifying pains and pleasures, the fact that the theory can be employed to justify abhorrent actions—namely, the sacrifice of the innocent to serve the interests of others—the deflection from one’s own projects and commitments required when utilitarian outcomes demand a different course of action, and the sheer “demandingness” of the theory which requires that every person do as much as possible to maximize universal happiness, each may be avoided or overcome in Darr’s view by the belief in a benevolent God and acceptance of the logic of divine providence, with its appeal to divine sanctions to cover cases in which ordinary psychology looks insufficient. Morality, on this view, does not require that we do anything that is not ultimately for our own happiness (here and in the afterlife), including sacrifices of our own interests for the good of others. However, Darr recognizes some limitations to his proposition. For example, we can have little confidence that divine providence solves the problem of abhorrent actions, since we cannot know with certainty that abhorrent actions are not sometimes the best way for God to maximize happiness. Also, the idea that we naturally have a sufficient motive to maximize happiness in most instances is doubtful, since we cannot always know what it is that maximizes happiness. With these caveats granted, what are we to make of Darr’s speculation that a revised version of Anglican utilitarianism might yet overcome these deficiencies (252)? At a time when religious belief in Western societies is in a long-standing retreat, it is doubtful that the enriched theologizing necessary for this recommendation to gain purchase will resonate with contemporary moral theorists.Might we be convinced by Darr that a theological consequentialism akin to that of More and Cumberland is more promising, since they posit a more expansive picture of goodness that God aims to maximize, one that includes human perfection as well as pleasure, and an account of motivation that is not limited to private happiness but also encompasses being motivated simply by what is good (252)? Other intrinsic goods may also be “consequentialized,” such as beauty, knowledge, and autonomy, but Darr acknowledges that the simplicity of consequentialism is obfuscated, and the strength of its appeal is watered down by such philosophical maneuvers. Should consequentialism, which seems most “natural” to us in reasoning about moral questions, be abandoned in favor of a different way of looking at the nature of goods, ends, and agency? Darr examines the trolley problem to suggest that outcomes or states of affairs are not the only thing at stake and invites us to consider the good and the rights, and hence the value, of the persons involved; even if we cannot save everyone, there is a virtue in trying, perhaps by crying out in alarm, calling for help, frantically searching for alternatives, rushing into the aftermath looking for signs of life, calling for emergency services, grieving their deaths, consoling loved ones, or honoring the dead by the way we conduct our own lives, all crucial to a morally appropriate response (258–59). This raises the question, however: Are any of these possibilities not available to the actor concerned with producing the best outcome? Certainly, Mill’s view of the utility value of the nobleness of “character” might be counted on to produce similar actions with similar results. This brings me to another issue.The commonplace objections to utilitarianism discussed by Darr are based on a version of utilitarianism in which totalizing the aggregate of pleasures over pains is all that matters. This is a misleading view of utilitarianism as it was developed by Bentham and Mill. For instance, revisionist interpretations of Bentham have emerged over the past forty years based in part on the availability of writings hitherto confined to manuscripts, setting Bentham’s ideas in new contexts and revealing subtleties in his thought that demonstrate an awareness of the some of the objections rehearsed by Darr. The sacrifice of the innocent proposition, for example, can be addressed by a version of utilitarianism that is not a crude maximizing theory but rather contains safeguards against forfeiting the basic interests (Mill would say “permanent interests”) of vulnerable or innocent persons simply to increase the pleasure or good of others, no matter how large a majority the latter may be. On this view, Bentham’s utilitarianism is maximizing but posits the equal security of every person’s life, liberty, property, and legitimate expectations as foundational to the greatest happiness (“everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one,” in Mill’s phrasing). Nor did Bentham think that optimal utilitarian outcomes were to be achieved by requiring that every individual dedicate themselves absolutely to universal benevolence (the so-called demandingness of the theory), but rather that in the ordinary run of things the prudent pursuit of self-interest, which may encompass the interests of family, friends, neighbors, and, quite possibly, for some, whole communities, and which is not harmful to the basic interests of others, could be counted on as the best way to enhance the greatest happiness.Despite these concerns, Darr’s book deserves to be read as an important contribution to the history of moral and theological ideas. It is well written, well structured, and richly sourced, with detailed notes and a comprehensive index, though the absence of a bibliography is regrettable.

articles.t: Advancing the Boltzmann Brain Skeptical Challenge
articles.ab: Some leading cosmological models predict that in the future history of the universe, there will be vast numbers of Boltzmann Brains (“brains” formed by chance in otherwise empty space), including many that are physical duplicates of your own brain and that (arguably) have conscious experiences indistinguishable from your own experiences. This article advances the skeptical challenge posed by this prediction in two ways. First, the author challenges the common assumption that scientific evidence for Boltzmann Brain superabundance presents a serious skeptical worry only if that evidence gives one reason to assign significant credence to the hypothesis that one is a Boltzmann Brain. On this assumption, Boltzmann Brain–related skeptical worries are easily swept aside. The author develops a new and more formidable Boltzmann Brain skeptical argument that is not committed to this assumption. Second, the author takes up recent objections to Center Indifference, a principle underlying Boltzmann Brain skeptical arguments. Sinan Dogramaci and Miriam Schoenfield have argued that Center Indifference imposes absurd constraints on one’s credences for certain scientific theories. The author shows that their arguments turn on some subtle confusions and that Center Indifference does not have the absurd implications that they attribute to it.

articles.t: Responsibility and Desert
articles.ab: Generally, harm is bad. Is it always bad? Some retributivists—axiological retributivists—think not. They think that harm to people who are responsible for wrongdoing can be good, for they deserve it. In his excellent, intricate, and humane book, Michael McKenna defends a wimpy and qualified axiological retributivism. His retributivism is wimpy in that wrongdoers, on his view, only deserve proportional harm that arises from blame—the harms of having a hampered ability to engage in some spectrum of social intercourse, of a lack of freedom to live a personal life as she wishes, and the unsettling of her emotional stability (61). These harms are not (just) instrumentally good for McKenna—they are good noninstrumentally as part of an organic unity that is intrinsically good. The organic unity consists in the harm occurring in the course of the wrongdoer responding appropriately to their wrongdoing.McKenna’s retributivism is qualified in that it is good for responsible wrongdoers to be harmed in these ways only as a result of being blamed, where blame is part of a conversation that responds appropriately to the wrongdoing of the responsible person. Wrongdoers deserve appropriate blame, and appropriate blame aims at harming responsible wrongdoers in these ways. And his retributivism is wimpy in another way—McKenna admits uncertainty about whether the conditions for desert can be satisfied in particular cases, or in general (chapter 10). And he has concerns about the role of conversational responsibility and desert in socially unjust circumstances (chapter 9).Nevertheless, McKenna defends a retributivist theory of punishment as well as blame along similar lines, though he is uncertain whether states can punish for retributivist reasons (see 90; I was left a bit unclear about the difference between state actors and nonstate actors that might make the latter but not the former permitted to punish on retributive grounds, and McKenna’s view is the converse of the standard, though I think also mistaken, view that states have the unique right to punish). Punishment extends beyond blame in that it involves intentional harm, which blame need not, and it involves imposing sanctions. These sanctions aim at ensuring that wrongdoers recognize that they have acted wrongly and fostering their understanding that they deserve the consequences imposed on them by the sanction. The sanction provides an external source of the kind of harm that it would be appropriate for the wrongdoer to experience if she felt guilty. If she then feels guilty, she will come to see these harms as deserved.Blame, and the harm that results from it, for McKenna, can be fitting. They are appropriate responses to responsible wrongdoing. And, for him, this is the best way of interpreting the Strawsonian project of understanding responsibility for wrongdoing as a feature of interpersonal communicative and emotional practices (chap. 6). He considers the possibility that the hostile emotions such as indignation and resentment involved in blame are by their nature destructive—they can be destructive, he admits, but suitably tempered and qualified, they need not be (chap. 8).This is a terrific book. McKenna’s conversational theory of responsibility is highly attractive. His discussion of desert is nicely integrated into that view. His arguments are careful, often deeply thought out, and humane. And he shows admirable modesty and doubt about the role of desert, even when he is attracted to it. He shows not only great philosophical skill but also a real connection with the emotional lives of wrongdoers and victims of wrongdoing. He is attentive to the significance of historical injustice and the potential harm that endorsing retributivism in the real world can cause. And the wimpiness and qualifications to his retributivism make it in some respects more appealing and less barbaric than other forms of retributivism.In the remainder of this review, I put pressure on McKenna’s retributivism. One weakness of McKenna’s book is that he does not fully consider the merits of other proposals about the moral implications of responsible wrongdoing that are, like retributivism, essentially backward looking but that do not rely on the idea that harm suffered by wrongdoers is noninstrumentally good. These alternatives strike me as better than the retributivist view.Consider one of the harms that McKenna claims wrongdoers deserve—lack of freedom to live one’s personal life as one wishes. First note that such freedom is not an unqualified good on any sensible view. I might wish to live my life as a serial killer. My freedom to do so isn’t good—not for me or anyone else. Why not? Because where I am required not to v, I am already morally unfree to v. If I am morally unfree to v, there is often no value in my being practically free to v. Practical freedom to do something that I am already constrained by duty not to do lacks value. I wish to lie but don’t have the opportunity, so I lack the freedom to do so. No loss!Now, uncontroversially, wrongdoers acquire duties to respond to their wrongdoing. Their wrongdoing results in their being morally less free. The fact that they are made practically less free when they have acted wrongly is then not bad for them. We need not appeal to the noninstrumental goodness of their being unfree to explain this. So we have a straightforward nonretributivist explanation of the intuitive idea that wrongdoers are not free to live their lives as though they had not acted wrongly.Now compare the idea that it is good that wrongdoers feel the pain involved in guilt with a close alternative. It is good for wrongdoers to understand that they have acted wrongly. Understanding this is painful. But the pain is just an inevitable intrinsically bad side effect, in those who are psychologically typical, of the good thing—understanding. And although pain is intrinsically bad, it is instrumentally good because it helps the person to comply with their duties in the future. As understanding is very important, and pain is instrumentally good, it is typically overall better that the person feels guilty as a result of their wrongdoing, even though the pain they suffer is intrinsically bad.McKenna is aware of this alternative but doesn’t do enough to defend the retributivist view against it. How might we adjudicate between McKenna’s retributivism and this alternative? Intuition is a bit unhelpful. When we react negatively to the fact that a responsible wrongdoer is not suffering pain, are we reacting to the fact that it is bad that they don’t understand, or to the fact that is bad that they are not suffering? And how successful are we at screening out the instrumental value of the pain of guilt to focus on its intrinsic qualities? Not very.How do we make progress? McKenna does this by comparing grief. He claims that it is good when a person feels the pain that is involved in grief from losing a loved one. I didn’t have this reaction—I think that the suffering involved in grief is just bad. It is a bad consequence of something good—understanding loss. When one understands the importance of the loved one, and the role that they played in one’s life, one understands the loss at their passing. And this understanding, which is good, inevitably results in the person feeling pain. But I find it quite implausible that the suffering involved is itself good, even as part of an organic unity. Were it so, we would react by valuing the suffering, but we don’t.Here is another way of making progress. We can imagine psychologically unusual people who can fully understand that they are responsible for wrongdoing but who do not suffer the pain of guilt. And we could also imagine that these unusual people suffer no loss in motivation from their lack of pain—understanding does the trick without any additional psychological support. I don’t find it so hard to imagine people like this, but when I do, I don’t feel the loss of anything good. McKenna, of course, responds otherwise.Is there more to say? One thing in favor of the instrumental view is that it is just intuitive in itself that pain is always intrinsically bad. Of course, the idea of organic unities, familiar since G. E. Moore, shows that retributivism is coherent. But it does no more than that. And there is something metaphysically extravagant about organic unities. Where we find alternative explanations for our intuitions, these should be preferred. Finally, we might explore how understanding that one is responsible for wrongdoing leads to the feeling of pain. I cannot outline how best to do this here, but I have done so in other work (see Tadros 2011: 44–51). My suggestion is that once we recognize the source of the pain, we also find it harder to vindicate the view that pain is noninstrumentally good. McKenna could have done more to explore this line of argument to make progress beyond the bare intuitive response to the suffering of wrongdoers.Finally, let us focus on the relationship between McKenna’s retributivism and his conversational theory of responsibility. McKenna thinks that harms to wrongdoers are good only if they result from the kinds of blaming conversations that follow from wrongdoing. This struck me as in one way appealing, in that desert does not float free from human interaction, but in another way less plausible than unqualified retributivist alternatives.Retributivists often focus on our intuitions about the suffering of serious wrongdoers. But many people have these intuitions (or at least initial reactions) in cases where conversation does not, and cannot, occur. Consider: Hitler’s Island: Hitler did not die at the end of World War II but escaped to a remote island where his diaries have been found by an explorer. On reading the last entries, the explorer realizes that he showed no remorse about his conduct after the war. He is yet to find out about the weather on the island. If it was rainy, Hitler was miserable; if it was sunny, he was happy. As the explorer knows that no one else has found out what happened to Hitler, and that he was alone for the rest of his life, what happened to him had no effect on anyone else.I think it better that Hitler’s island was sunny. But many retributivists find this view absurd. McKenna’s view has a similar implication to my anti-retributivist view. However, most of us recognize at least the initial reaction that it is better that Hitler’s island is rainy. To that extent, both anti-retributivism and McKenna’s wimpy retributivism are revisionist. But if we endorse revisionism in this case, why not go all the way? McKenna implies revisionism in this case but not across the board, without fully explaining why we should be more confident in our retributivist inclinations in conversational cases than in this case.Furthermore, the conversational view has surprising implications. Consider: Hitler’s Island II: You are an explorer who arrives on Hitler’s island and you discover that Hitler has fallen into a deep pit. He doesn’t yet know that you are there. As a result of being in the pit, he is suffering. He might come to recognize that this suffering is good. You can engage Hitler in conversation or leave him alone. If you leave him alone, he is more likely to recognize that he acted wrongly and consequently believe that his suffering is good, than if you engage him in conversation.McKenna’s view seems to provide you reasons to engage Hitler in conversation, for only by doing that can you make his suffering good. If he suffers without the conversation, that suffering is just bad. This strikes me as an unappealing implication for retributivists. At least in this respect either full-blown anti-retributivism or unqualified retributivism fare better.There is, of course, much more to say, and I haven’t done justice to the many excellent arguments and ideas in McKenna’s excellent book. While I am yet to be convinced of McKenna’s retributivism, his is perhaps the most humane and thoughtful version on offer.

articles.t: Hegel’s Logic and Metaphysics
Love and Its Place in Virtue
articles.ab: Love and Its Place in Virtue expands and refines the view of virtue ethics Christine Swanton has developed in such influential works as Virtue Ethics: A Pluralistic View and Target-Centered Virtue Ethics. Her wide-ranging discussion touches on a diverse range of topics, so let me acknowledge up front that in this brief review I will not be able to do it justice. I will focus on the issues that strike me as most interesting and most problematic, issues that tend to pop up repeatedly, in one form or another, throughout the book.As the book’s title indicates, Swanton argues that love, along with the more general emotional orientation she calls “lovingness,” is significantly related to virtue. ‘Lovingness’ is what Swanton calls a Grundstimmung, a term she borrows from Heidegger to refer to an “emotional orientation to the world at large … necessary for the disclosure of the world as having a moral dimension” (x–xi). It is, essentially, an inclination to love in particular cases, in accordance with the demands of the situation.Swanton’s focus is squarely on impartial, universal love rather than the more familiar forms that clearly embody partiality: romantic love, friendship, and love for one’s children and other relatives. Indeed, love, in Swanton’s treatment of it, comes across as a placid and rather bloodless affair. (One would not know, from reading this book, that such a thing as sex existed, let alone that it had any connection with love.) Of the nine features she identifies as having been viewed as “essential or important to love”—this is as close as she comes to defining love, claiming that love is too complex and contested to be defined—only one, “a passion for union or fusion,” suggests any form of passion, desire, excitement, or intensity (7).In its general avoidance of intense, let alone turbulent personal feelings, Swanton’s list of features feels tailored to fit her interest in impartial, universal love. Consider her treatment of another alleged central feature, “coming close.” One might naturally expect this to connect with passion, intensity, or intimacy. But the metaphor never becomes very clear, and it is often deployed in quite impersonal contexts. Swanton shows little interest in what it might be like to come close to a child, friend, or romantic lover. She follows Kant in speaking of universal love as “a beneficent coming close” that is a “duty to all human beings merely as human beings,” and in insisting that the motive of such love must have nothing to do with desire, or with delight, pleasure, attraction, affection, or other such feelings (164). Her less extensive positive characterization mentions such mild-sounding states as well-wishing and satisfaction in others’ well-being. As for what lovers do, Swanton’s go-to example is offering assistance. The reader often gets the sense that for Swanton, the paradigmatic loving act consists of giving aid to a needy stranger.Swanton’s focus on the impartial and impersonal, and her lack of attention to the personal and the passionate, will have some readers wondering whether the phenomenon she is interested in is really love at all. She frequently emphasizes how little love requires, writing that it need not involve intense feeling but “merely a lack of indifference” (166), approving of Kant’s notion of “practical love” which “requires not so much the presence of emotion but the absence of unloving emotion” (104), stating that the identification relevant to universal love “merely requires … that we do not treat the members of the relevant group (humans in this case) with indifference, let alone callousness and hatred” (100–101), and endorsing Kant’s claim from The Metaphysics of Morals that “when I say that I take an interest in this human being only out of my love for all human beings, the interest I take is as slight as an interest can be. I am only not indifferent with regard to him” (166).Swanton’s intent seems to be to defuse the anticipated objection that universal love will be excessively demanding by emphasizing how undemanding it actually is: embodying universal love, she claims, does not mean becoming a moral saint. But such remarks set a distressingly low bar: Avoiding callousness and indifference is one thing; loving someone is surely another. And while writing regular checks to Oxfam might well show an admirable concern with the plight of needy others, it hardly seems sufficient to establish that you love them. Moreover, her concern with avoiding the ‘sainthood’ objection prompts her to impugn those individuals whose capacity for loving strangers exceeds the norm. Her criticism of Paul Farmer, whom she accuses of being misled and rendered less than truly virtuous by a “false conception of universal love,” struck me as both uncharitable and unnecessary: Even if we agree that universal love does not require such strenuous efforts, those who engage in them sincerely surely are loving, and surely merit our admiration (106).Other comments throughout the book also suggest that Swanton’s conception of love is unusually undemanding. “One form of love,” she asserts, “is the admiration of a sports fan for a player” (3). “Lovingness” turns out to be consistent with hating some people; universal love is compatible with holding some people in contempt; and we are informed that you can love somebody you are trying to kill: “A ruthless determination to assassinate Hitler (or Putin) as a dangerous enemy or let him die is arguably compatible with universal love. We are to love our enemy but that does not mean that we should not protect ourselves and others from them” (111). (To be fair, Swanton does acknowledge that loving places some limits on such conduct: I am not allowed to enjoy killing Hitler.)Thus, there are two unpalatably low bars here. One concerns what love requires of us, both in terms of aiding the needy and in terms of our attitudes and conduct toward truly bad people. The other concerns what is required for love: Swanton appears to hold that there is nothing a person can do that would render them unworthy of or ineligible for love. Merit, she holds, is irrelevant both to forgiveness and to universal love generally.These issues are significant in her discussion of forgiveness. Many would say that Hitler is unlovable precisely because he performed unforgivable acts. But in Swanton’s view this presupposes an objectionably “backward looking view” of forgiveness, which holds that the propriety of forgiveness is determined largely by the nature of the transgression (184). Admittedly, her account of forgiveness is complex and at times unclear. What does seem clear is that she thinks forgiveness should be “forward looking” and “a virtue of unconditional universal love” (184–85). The ‘unconditional’ element seems to imply that ultimately it really does not matter what the transgressor has done. In principle, all acts are forgivable and ought to be forgiven. She follows Martha Nussbaum (in Anger and Forgiveness) in assuming that the backward-looking view requires us to see forgiveness as merely “transactional,” that it involves “‘a list keeping inquisitorial mentality’ and a ‘retentive and unloving’ attitude,” and that it “speaks to an anger-driven retributive culture where there is demand for payback” (184).To my mind, there are a great many more options available than the extreme unconditional view Swanton seems to favor and the extreme hyper-retributive view she rejects. One need not be either unloving or inquisitorial to think that what the transgressor did matters fundamentally. (Indeed, refusing to forgive an evildoer might sometimes express love, concern, and compassion for their victims.) Nor does refusing to forgive Hitler for killing millions of innocent people imply that one views forgiveness as merely “transactional.” Admittedly, Swanton allows that the severity of the crime might affect how long it takes a person to forgive, and that successful forgiveness “may not be within one’s voluntary control” (187). Her most interesting suggestion is that the amount of time it would take to work through the process and reach a state of forgiveness might sometimes exceed a human lifespan. In this weak sense, then, some actions may be unforgivable. But this weak sense is insufficient. For one thing, the limits here seem to be purely psychological: Swanton avoids asserting that people ought to take a long time to forgive extreme wrongs, stating only that, given how we are constituted, it will take a long time. She sems to offer no grounds for thinking there would be anything wrong with a person who was able to forgive Hitler instantly, and who did so. But in my view there are some acts that should never be forgiven. If there is an afterlife, and Hitler and I both end up there, I do not plan to make it one of my moral goals to figure out how to forgive him for the Holocaust. Frankly, if refusing to forgive Hitler is wrong, I don’t want to be right.These various issues all connect with two fundamental questions. The first is, What role does love play in the judgment of the practically wise agent? For Swanton, the connection between love and virtue is made out via practical wisdom, which she takes to be necessary to all virtues: even with good intentions, virtues can misfire in the absence of practical wisdom. This general claim about the connection between virtue and practical wisdom seems (to me) plausible enough. But though she approaches the issue in several places and from several different directions, Swanton never really gets around to offering a satisfyingly fleshed-out argument for the claim that only loving agents can possess genuine practical wisdom. Yet this claim is necessary to her overall argument.The second fundamental question is, I think, closely related: In what ways, if at all, does love respond to the nature of the love object? Swanton describes lovingness as “a set of predispositions of openness or receptivity which makes one liable to loving responses to any individual” (3). But the particulars of her view often push against this. She frequently suggests that rather than being about receptivity, openness, and genuine responsiveness, love works primarily in the other direction and is fundamentally expressive: “One does not love for reasons. Rather love as a mode of response … embodies expressive loving responses rather than responses for reasons, whether we are dealing with affectional loves or agapeic love” (85). Thus, we are to be ready to love anyone, no matter what (even if they are thoroughly evil), and we ought to forgive everyone, no matter what (even if they perpetrated mass murder). Such dispositions indicate, and their associated actions express, the sort of genuinely generous and loving nature that could not, in Swanton’s view, be possessed by a person who is hung up on such unseemly matters as merit and good behavior. When reasons do matter, they usually turn out to be reasons concerning a person’s needs and their predicament, decidedly not reasons based in their personality, character, or qualities. For Swanton, the reasons that matter—where reasons matter at all—have nothing to do with what a person is like.The view of love that results feels oddly impersonal, on top of being cool and dispassionate. Admittedly, it is hard to be clear about just how much Swanton means to emphasize this side of things. Again and again she flirts with the language of accuracy and getting things right, only to (appear to?) back away from such claims and retreat to a position that disavows any notion of love’s epistemic advantages or merits. (There is a rich recent literature on the relevant issues, oriented around the notion of ‘epistemic partiality’ in love relations; it would have been helpful for Swanton to engage with that literature and locate her position in terms of that terrain. In general, the book does not engage with the current philosophy of love literature as much as one would have liked.)Swanton’s discussion of Iris Murdoch in chapter 4 is a case in point. She seems to agree with Murdoch that a “generous loving gaze penetrates deeper into [a person’s] nature” than a “jealous hostile gaze” (90). But she goes on to allow that both ways of seeing respond to real features, and at least seems to say that the real problem with the hostile gaze is that it “is likely to be expressive of psychological shortcomings of [the observer] such as jealousy, and her conventional weddedness to problematic cultural expectations” (90). So it is not clear that the explanation of why “lovingness is central to right emotional construal, and we must be rightly emotionally oriented if practical wisdom is to guide us to correct action” has much if anything to do with the idea that more loving gazes are more likely to depict reality accurately (88). Still, as is often the case here, the discussion is somewhat unclear, so it’s hard to be sure.In the end, I can’t help but wish that Swanton had spelled out the connection between lovingness and practical wisdom in greater detail, and clarified the sense(s) in which love is, and is not, receptive, open, and responsive to reality. Such clarifications might have lessened, to some degree, my worry that Swanton’s account of love—universal love in particular—sometimes diminishes or cheapens that emotion by turning it into a form of dispassionate concern that lends itself naturally to being universally and impartially directed. Such a view, from the perspective of someone who wants love to be an ethical phenomenon through and through, might well seem attractive. But I think it risks omitting or distorting a great many of the facts about love’s actual nature and the roles it plays in our lives.

articles.t: Could the Truths of Mathematics Have Been Different?
articles.ab: Could the truths of mathematics have been different than they in fact are? If so, which truths could have been different? Do the contingent mathematical facts supervene on physical facts, or are they free floating? This article investigates these questions within a framework of higher-order modal logic, drawing sometimes surprising connections between the necessity of arithmetic and analysis and other theses of modal metaphysics: the thesis that possibility in the broadest sense is governed by a logic of S5, that what is possible holds in some maximally specific possibility, and that every property can be rigidified. The investigation will distinguish sharply between platonic contingency—contingency about whether particular abstract platonic mathematical objects are arranged in a certain way (e.g., in the structure of the natural or real numbers)—from a deeper variety of structural contingency concerning what holds of objects whenever they are arranged in that way.

articles.t: Lottocracy: Democracy Without Elections
Reasoning with Attitude: Foundations and Applications of Inferential Expressivism
articles.ab: Semantic orthodoxy since Frege has it that the content of a sentence (in context) is given by its truth conditions, and that the content of a subsentential expression is given by its contribution to the truth conditions of the sentences in which it may occur. This semantic paradigm is widely adopted in contemporary philosophy of language as well as in linguistics departments. However, widespread and successful as it is, it has long been challenged on a number of grounds. Intuitionists have objected that it makes the content of mathematical sentences radically disconnected from mathematical practice. Anti-realists have charged that it delivers an unworkable, irredeemably circular account of understanding. Deflationists have accused it of relying on hopelessly obscure conceptions of truth and reference. Expressivists have lamented that it delivers a deeply flawed account of normative vocabulary. Inferentialists have attacked it on the grounds that it turns metasemantics into a mystery and that it makes semantic content unnecessarily complicated. Yet none of these critical voices has been able to offer a viable alternative semantic paradigm that can actually be used to deliver a workable semantics for fragments of natural language. As Timothy Williamson (2007: 282) famously put it, anti-realists, inferentialists, and unorthodox semanticists more generally “preferred to polish their formulations of the grand programme rather than getting down to the hard and perhaps disappointing task of trying to carry it out in practice.”In their superb book Reasoning with Attitude, Luca Incurvati and Julian Schlöder take up the challenge of providing an alternative to semantic orthodoxy head on. They set forth a novel, unorthodox semantic paradigm, inferential expressivism, as they call it, and go on to (1) show how it can be applied to key fragments of natural language—to wit, epistemic modals, moral vocabulary, attitude verbs, semantic vocabulary, conditionals, and probability talk—and (2) argue that inferential expressivism altogether avoids some of the problems that have been plaguing existing accounts, both orthodox and unorthodox, of these natural language fragments. The book is divided into ten chapters. The first two introduce, respectively, expressivism and inferentialism, and briefly discuss the main challenges they face. The third argues in favor of combining expressivism and inferentialism into inferential expressivism. The next six chapters work out in a fair amount of detail inferential expressivist accounts of the six fragments of natural language mentioned above. The tenth chapter briefly discusses areas of future work.The book is admirably written and argued. It is impossible, in such a short space, to do justice to its wealth of detailed philosophical arguments and semantic analyses. The first three chapters are largely philosophical: They provide concise and yet informative and engaging critical introductions to inferentialism and expressivism, clearly articulating the main arguments in their favor and the problems they face. Along the way, Incurvati and Schlöder also briefly introduce truth-conditional semantics as well as the now familiar distinction between semantics, postsemantics, and metasemantics, correctly observing that, whereas on the orthodox picture facts about reference and truth conditions are conceptually prior to facts about validity, on the inferentialist picture it is rather the other way round. The remaining chapters lie at the intersection between the philosophies of language and logic, logic proper, and formal semantics. Their subject matter is more technical, but the presentation is always engaging and accessible. Technical proofs are relegated to appendices.The main metasemantic principle Incurvati and Schlöder rely on when arguing in favor of their own inferential expressivist framework is what they call the Pragmatist Razor—that is, the injunction to “avoid semantic explanations that are not needed to account for the functional role of an expression or sentence” (9). For instance, if one’s account of the functional role of moral role of moral predicates—that is, of the point of having such predicates in the language—doesn’t require that those predicates have extensions, then one’s semantic account of moral predicates should not assign extensions to them. Incurvati and Schlöder’s semantic framework is thus strongly inferentialist: The meaning of an expression is not to be explained in terms of reference but is rather given by the basic rules for its correct use. More precisely, Incurvati and Schlöder’s starting point is a bilateralist account of logic (Smiley 1996; Rumfitt 2000; Warren 2020), according to which the basic rules for an expression e comprise both rules for asserting and rules for rejecting sentences in which e figures (for instance, the rules for negation include rules that allows one to move from the assertion of ¬φ to the rejection of φ, and vice versa). Incurvati and Schlöder generalize the standard bilateralist framework along two dimensions. First, they differentiate between strong, weak, and moderate forms of both assertion and rejection. Whereas the strong assertion of φ (linguistically realised by the answer ‘Yes’ to the question whether φ) can be seen as a proposal to add φ to the positive common ground (the set of sentences that are believed by the speakers in a given context), the weak assertion of φ (linguistically realised by the answer ‘Perhaps yes’ to the question whether φ) can be seen as a proposal not to add φ to the negative common ground (the set of sentences that are disbelieved by the speakers in a given context). As for moderate assertion (linguistically realised by the answer ‘Probably yes’ to the question whether φ), it is interpreted as a tentative proposal to add φ to the positive common ground. Similarly, mutatis mutandis, for strong, weak, and moderate rejection. The framework becomes a multilateralist one, in which several speech acts figure among both the premises and conclusions of basic principles. Second, Incurvati and Schlöder consider attitudes beyond those expressed by assertion and rejection, such as approval and disapproval, and take them to figure among the basic principles governing predicates such as ‘right’ and ‘wrong’.The framework is doubly expressivist: It allows the expression of attitudes toward contents to figure among the premises and conclusions of basic inference rules, and it also takes the point of the logical vocabulary to be the expression of certain basic attitudes—for instance, the point of negation is to express disbelief, the point of ‘might’ is to express one’s refraining from expressing disbelief (107), the point of ‘wrong’ is to express disapproval, and so on.The question immediately arises whether Incurvati and Schlöder’s framework faces a version of the Frege-Geach problem. According to traditional expressivism, ‘Killing is wrong’ doesn’t really have content; it simply expresses disapproval of killing. But, as Frege and Geach pointed out, embedded occurrences of expressions that are accounted for in expressivist terms cannot be plausibly taken to express attitudes—after all, the assertion of sentences such as ‘Killing isn’t wrong’ don’t express disapproval of killing. Inferential expressivists avoid the problem altogether. Sentences of the form ‘Φ-ing is wrong’, Incurvati and Schlöder argue, don’t express disapproval of Φ-ing but rather have a content that’s given by their basic inference rules (such as the principle ‘From disapproval of Φ-ing, infer that Φ-ing is wrong’ and its converse). These rules sanction the interderivability of disapproval of Φ-ing and the strong assertion of ‘Φ-ing is wrong’, but they don’t require that ‘Φ-ing is wrong’ be interpreted as a mere expression of disapproval of Φ-ing. The solution generalizes to epistemic modals, conditionals, and so on. Incurvati and Schlöder do an excellent job at suggesting that the view avoids the pitfalls of traditional expressivism while retaining its benefits (for instance, inferential expressivism accounts for the motivating character of moral judgements and avoids postulating problematic semantic values such as moral properties).The hero of the book is the basic multilateral logic BML, whose rules involve strong assertion, strong rejection, and weak rejection. Extensions of BML, which include rules for ‘wrong’, ‘might’, ‘true’, ‘probable’, and ‘if’, constitute the semantic frameworks in terms of which the inferentialist semantics for the six case studies considered in the book is given. However, BML isn’t fully classical. For reasons that we don’t have the space to review here, Incurvati and Schlöder maintain that inference rules need not preserve evidence and that their validity is to be accounted for in terms of preservation of one’s commitments (78). They then argue that meta-rules are valid only if their subproofs are evidence-preserving. As a result, the subproofs of any meta-rules are restricted so as to disallow the application of principles that don’t preserve evidence. Crucially, according to Incurvati and Schlöder, the naive rules for the truth predicate (which sanction the interderivability of any sentence and its truth predication), and semantic rules more generally, are cases in point, whence meta-rules such as classical reductio, ¬-I, →-I, and ∨-E are restricted along familiar supervaluationist lines so as to disallow the use of semantic rules within their subproofs. The output is both a diagnosis of what goes wrong in the semantic paradoxes, that they all rely on non-evidence-preserving instances of naive semantic rules, and a cure—namely, that rules that are not evidence-preserving may not be used within subproofs. This, Incurvati and Schlöder argue, suffices to block the semantic paradoxes, including the so-called revenge paradoxes (205–15).Incurvati and Schlöder’s approach to the paradoxes isn’t an essential part of their semantic framework. It is also the least convincing. For one thing, the question whether their approach is revenge-free cannot be assessed: their diagnostic machinery, which relies on notions such as evidence and evidence preservation, simply isn’t present in the object language of the theories they consider. And yet revenge paradoxes typically arise precisely when one tries to formulate in the object language a diagnosis of what goes wrong in paradoxical derivations.1 For another, their diagnosis of the paradoxes seems forced. Their main argument for thinking that semantic rules fail to preserve evidence is that instances of those rules involving definite descriptions, as in ‘It will be sunny tomorrow; therefore, what Ursula said yesterday is true’ are typically not evidence-preserving (one may have evidence that it will be sunny tomorrow while failing to know that this is what Ursula said). The problem here is that this gives us no reason for thinking that the instances of the semantic rules involved in the paradoxes, which need not involve definite descriptions, fail to preserve evidence. The problem also appears in Incurvati and Schlöder’s approach to the paradoxes of weak rejection (216–17). Incurvati and Schlöder argue that certain principles for the use of a weak rejection predicate must be restricted to sentences we understand. But they are then forced to maintain that the instances of those principles involved in a certain Liar-like paradox violate this restriction, which is tantamount to saying, implausibly, that we do not understand a Liar-like sentence that can be unproblematically formulated in the language of arithmetic with the addition of a weak rejection predicate. It should be stressed, however, that Incurvati and Schlöder’s approach to the paradoxes is but an added bonus to their overall semantic framework. The framework should be judged in the way it deals with moral terms, epistemic modals, conditionals, and other expressions. And here it certainly succeeds in setting a new standard—one that makes Williamson’s objections to critics of semantic orthodoxy, fair at the time in 2006, unfair and passé now.This research was funded in part by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) [10.55776/COE3 and 10.55776/PAT2449425], whose support I gratefully acknowledge.

articles.t: Movements of the Mind: A Theory of Attention, Intention, and Action
articles.ab: In his book Movements of the Mind, Wayne Wu presents a theory of agency. While the book focuses on mental action, the theory is meant to cover all forms of agency. At the center of this theory is attention and its interaction with intention.Wu’s book is a significant contribution to current action theory. While the book can be challenging to read, it raises many hard questions and is chock-full of interesting, provocative theses. Wu’s steadfast endorsement of an empirically based approach deserves praise. And having one of the prominent figures in current action theory draw attention to the connection between working memory, executive control, and human agency does the discipline a major service. The book is bound to engender much discussion.Part 1 contains chapters 1 and 2, which lay out Wu’s accounts of attention and action, respectively. Part 2, containing chapters 3 and 4, presents a theory of intention-in-action. Chapters 5–7 (pt. 3) apply the account to bias and skill, deduction, and introspection. The book’s first four chapters present the “core of [Wu’s] theory of agency” (149). I focus on these in what follows.In chapters 1 and 2, Wu presents his account of attention and action. Attention is selection-for-action, in Wu’s technical terminology, a stimulus’s being coupled to (and guiding) a response. Action, in turn, is a response coupled to a stimulus. The two notions are interdefined.To use Wu’s illustration, if you kick one of two balls and can do so with one of two legs, you must select, and thereby couple, one of the balls to one available response—that is, kicking it with one of two legs.Is all attention/action like that? Isn’t it possible for us to act inattentively? When I walk across the hallway while speaking on the phone, I do not seem to attend to my walking. And can’t we attend without necessarily acting on what we attend to? If my attention is captured by a bright light, might I not attend to the light before going back to my reading, without otherwise responding? Commentators have pointed to examples like these, taken from everyday life, and cognitive science (Watzl 2011; Jennings and Nanay 2016; Buehler 2018b; Lange 2023). Wu suggests that such cases draw on unreliable intuitions. In his technical sense, even these cases feature attention and action. And cognitive science, he claims, supports this view as against intuition. We should go with science in our theorizing.What, then, do his technical terms mean? And how does cognitive science support his claims? Wu seems to have settled on this: a stimulus is coupled to a response just in case they both occur at the individual level, they both are processed nondeviantly, and the coupling might not have occurred. Responses are exercises of action-capacities. That may seem to be tight circle, if the aim is to provide an account of action. But Wu’s action-capacities are not the familiar ones. They include, for instance, the “sharpening of one’s visual experience” (179) and “improved cognitive access” (76). What, then, are these capacities? The notion remains unspecified. This allows Wu to handle challenging cases: paradigm passive episodes like captured attention, for example, turn into “passive actions” (79). Purported cases of inattentive action become attentive, since some action-related information-processing usually occurs. And yet, without substantive constraints on these central notions, one may wonder how they relate to the target-explananda.Wu’s theory, in any case, is revisionary. Why should we adopt it? Wu’s central argument revolves around the claim that cognitive science is committed to:Wu notes that cognitive science studies attention through paradigms like, for example, visual search, which operationalize attention as selection of a search-target for a response. He contends that this implies that all of cognitive science is committed to (ESC). But, for one, these paradigms are carefully designed to investigate attention. From the fact that they study attention, it does not follow that all processing of stimuli in a task-setting involves attention. Many experimental tasks do not investigate attention. For another, even if (ESC) were true, moving from it to a claim about all attention and action outside experimental settings requires argument.Most importantly, however, cognitive science does not appear to be committed to (ESC). There are several avenues of work that explore the possibility of processing information for a task—coupling it to a response—without attending to it. Thus scientists ask whether scene gist, certain object-categories, or statistical learning require attention. They design sophisticated experimental paradigms—the attentional blink, multiple-object-tracking, and others—to probe whether these stimuli can be reported, despite attention’s being allocated elsewhere. While establishing that all attention is absent from some task is practically extremely difficult, scientists treat claims like (ESC) as an empirically open matter (Buehler 2022b). Wu nowhere satisfyingly engages with these points (see also Wu 2019, 2025). But if Wu’s theory conflicts with both common sense and cognitive science, some other, powerful form of support is needed to lay the foundation for the rest of the book.Part 2 discusses the connection between working memory, executive function, and action. Theorists have previously explored this connection (Carruthers 2015; Buehler 2014, 2022a, 2023; Christensen et al. 2016; Watzl 2017), and Wu draws on this work. The precise relationship with that work could be more clearly articulated.Wu’s own take on the connection consists in a theory of intention-in-action as practical memory, presented in chapter 3. His central claim is that there is a “functional equivalence between executive control in working memory and intention[-in-action] (94).” From this he appears to infer that intention ‘is’ practical memory (190).The exact nature of the target claim is not fully specified. Wu writes that intention-in-action is working memory (109); that working memory constitutes (3, 46); underwrites the dynamics of (104); parallels (103); is the basis of (98); realizes, or implements intention-in-action (104, 106). These ideas would benefit from further clarification. Standard theorizing in cognitive science describes occurrent intentions as held in working memory. It is unclear how to square this with some of the claims that Wu seems to make.Be that as it may, Wu’s argument apparently proceeds from the mentioned claim of a functional equivalence. To establish such a functional equivalence, one would have to provide a characterization of the purportedly equivalent items, and then show that they indeed are equivalent.What is the characterization of intention-in-action that Wu is working with? Maybe he takes the observation that intention “sets” (roughly, directs) attention to identify the functional role of intention? If so, then his characterization is nonstandard. Work on intention’s functional role does not emphasize the setting of attention but points to other features as central to intention’s functional role (Searle 1983; Bratman 1987; Mele 1992; Pacherie 2006, 2008; Fridland 2019; Mylopoulos and Pacherie 2017, 2019; Shepherd 2021; Grünbaum and Kyllingsbaek 2020). Wu’s argument here would benefit from more engagement with extant conceptions of intention(-in-action).Regarding executive control and working memory, Wu largely relies on an article by Alan Baddeley (1996). Wu reports as functions of the central executive the “coordinating performance during dual task cases, coordinating search strategies during random generation of words from long-term memory, controlling attention to one stimulus and suppressing distraction from another, manipulating and maintaining items in long-term memory as needed in working memory tasks (e.g. span tasks)” (102). Wu emphasizes that “one function consistently tied to the central executive is that it regulates attention” (102).However, if all the cited functions constitute the executive’s functional role, then it is unclear how the functional equivalence with intention is established: Standard characterizations of intention’s functional role do not mention them. And if only the regulation of attention is relevant, then an argument is needed for focusing on this function over others, in characterizing the executive’s functional role.One might have also hoped for some discussion of why Baddeley’s, and not one of the many other characterizations of executive control, is the right one. Research on executive function, working memory, and cognitive control is vast and complicated. It has rapidly grown and developed since Baddeley wrote thirty years ago (Buehler 2018a, 2025). More engagement with this literature would have been welcome.Overall, one feels that the chapter’s central claim about functional equivalence would have benefited from more discussion and support.Chapter 4 builds on this link between intention and working memory. In it, Wu claims that the agent’s intending—her acting with an intention —itself is “an action of practical reasoning as she acts” (125). More specifically, “intending-in-action is constituted by fine-tuning of practical memory in practical reasoning” (129).Wu’s example is that of eating cake. As I intend to eat cake and see this cake, I fine-tune my intention by forming the further intention to eat this cake. The updating of my intention through working memory-updating in light of incoming visual information constitutes the fine-tuning. But “fine-tuning in turn is basic practical reasoning” (139). “Updating of memory [is] a type of thinking” (133). Thus “the dynamics of working memory reveal the dynamics of intention in practical reasoning” (135).Dynamic aspects of intention-in-action have been discussed in prior work, notably by Elisabeth Pacherie and Myrto Mylopoulos (cf. their dynamic hierarchical theory: Pacherie 2006, 2008; Mylopoulos and Pacherie 2017, 2019). These authors describe sources of dynamics and fine-tuning beyond working memory, such as motor processing. If they are right, how can working memory dynamics constitute fine-tuning? Wu does not discuss this work. Does he reject this idea? Or is his claim rather that working memory-updating sometimes fine-tunes intention? If the latter, how is the proposal different from those available in the literature?Maybe the answer lies in Wu’s broader claim that fine-tuning of intention is a form of practical reasoning. That plausibly is often the case. And attention often plays an important role in such reasoning (Grünbaum 2013). Yet Wu apparently aims for a stronger claim, on which all fine-tuning, certainly all working memory-updating, constitutes practical reasoning. This claim would set Wu’s account apart from others in the literature. But working memory-updating through, for example, encoding perceptual information about the cake does not always appear to be practical reasoning. Philosophical accounts of reasoning tend to impose conditions—that reasoning must be propositional and rule-guided, must involve a taking, or some such—that working memory-updating does not always meet. What recommends the stronger claim?Where, finally, does all this leave attention? The emphasis on working memory and executive control may suggest that we here find the locus of agential control. For Wu, this would be too quick. On his view, “attention is everywhere” (80). Working memory encoding, maintenance, updating, output-gating, all are episodes of selection, hence attention, hence action. This puts attention right back at the heart of the account. Whether or not we find this outcome plausible, it raises the question of whether the notion of attention at play here is too thin to do much explanatory work. The explaining rather appears to be done by appeal to working memory and executive control, as I’ve argued elsewhere (Buehler 2014, 2022a, 2023).Thanks for their feedback to Thor Gruenbaum, Myrto Mylopoulos, Elisabeth Pacherie, and Josh Shepherd.

articles.t: The Joy of Consent: A Philosophy of Good Sex
articles.ab: Eight years after the eruption of the #MeToo movement into public discourse, relations between men and women appear to be in a bad way. Manosphere influencers and incel forums have driven extreme misogyny into the mainstream. Straight women have found inspiration in the 4B movement emerging out of South Korea, which swears off partnership with men. Pundits have decried the ‘male loneliness crisis’. The widespread return to conservative values evident in tradwife content and Christian nationalism reveals the depth of the problem. What began with a discussion about the pervasiveness of men’s sexual violation of women has blossomed into full-on heteropessimism.One might be excused for thinking that the conversation that #MeToo started has ended—not because it achieved its aims but because it was foreclosed, whether by the unrelenting violence of its enemies, sheer exhaustion, or the devolution of public discourse in the United States. Yet Manon Garcia’s The Joy of Consent: A Philosophy of Good Sex suggests that this conversation is far from over. In a sense, it might not even have begun, for a genuine public discourse about sexual ethics should both propose a positive vision for what makes sex good and foster the conditions for achieving it. This involves a robust understanding of why sex is so often bad, in being shaped by unjust social norms. It is a matter, then, of an education in “the art of erotic conversation” (204).Garcia’s book was first published in French in 2021 as La conversation des sexes: Philosophie du consentement, where it received a wide readership and public acclaim. As Garcia notes, the long French tradition of the art of love involves celebrating a largely amoral approach to seduction, seeing sex as beyond the ethical realm altogether (39). It is common in France to think of discussions of sexual ethics, including around consent, as a product of the influence of American puritanism. In this context, Garcia serves in La conversation des sexes as a kind of ambassador for a feminist ethics of sex, which has predominantly flourished up until now in Anglo-American cultural settings. The attention her book has received in France attests to the success of this project, and the book is now being translated into numerous other languages. Garcia has also been a key intellectual voice in France in the recent high-profile case of the sexual assault of Gisèle Pelicot.In an American context, the book provides the most comprehensive, lucid synthesis of feminist critiques of sexual consent in a single volume to date. While feminist philosophers are likely to be familiar with many of these critiques, the breadth of Garcia’s citations and the engaging character of her prose render the book extremely useful as a compendium of them in all their variety. She deftly explains and ties together not only a wide range of scholarship within feminist theory but also legal theories of consent, approaches from BDSM, and more. In contrast with perhaps its closest cousin in recent feminist philosophy, Amia Srinavasan’s (2021) The Right to Sex: Feminism in the Twenty-First Century, which is thin on engagement with contemporary positions in feminist philosophy, The Joy of Consent is steeped in the rich debates and nuances of this subfield. Feminist philosophers will find this book highly rewarding as a result, and those unfamiliar with these decades-long debates will find that the book is an excellent introduction. Garcia, a French scholar who has also lived and worked in the United States, translated the book from French herself, and the result is highly successful.First and foremost, The Joy of Consent is a critique of the liberal view of consent, originating in the work of John Stuart Mill. While the liberal view may be helpful for distinguishing rightful from wrongful sex, Garcia contends that it is not up to the task of distinguishing good from bad sex (38). Garcia explains how the mainstream view of consent is rooted in liberalism, and that the recent public calls for more robust consent norms on college campuses and beyond—including affirmative, enthusiastic, and ongoing consent—are therefore insufficient. Indeed, while consent has become more and more popular in public discourse around sexual ethics in recent years, feminist philosophers have questioned its fittingness as a norm guiding sexual ethics. For Garcia, we need to move beyond liberal consent toward a view of consent as conversation. On the way, she finds a surprising ally in Kant (38).The liberal view is essentially individualistic, Garcia points out. It treats social relations, including sex, as encounters between individuals who are each pursuing their own vision of the good life by the means that they wish, barring infringing on the rights of others (46). Within Mill’s liberal framework, consent is “the criterion for the legitimacy of actions implicating multiple individuals, defeasible only by harm” (51). If permission is given, then the sex should escape state intervention (50–51). The deeply rooted social norms that may undergird sexual encounters are outside the purview of the liberal view of consent. Consent is a formal criterion for the permissibility of sex—but whether the sex is good is a different question (52).Like Mill, Kant views consent as enabling the expression of individual autonomy (37). However, the Kantian picture of consent places ethics at its center. Garcia draws on the Kantian idea that the consent of one’s sexual partner is inseparable from treating them as an end, rather than as a means (201). “The fundamental question,” she writes, “is not how to ensure that everyone takes only pleasure from sex but rather that each of us has only sexual experiences that are wanted and valued” (194). Recognizing others as subjects of desire and pleasure “is at the heart of a Kantian vision of good sex,” which she advocates (196). This, then, enables us to understand what makes sex good.Garcia states that the book aims to foster an understanding of good sex. She means ‘good’ in the double sense of (a) not being impaired by unjust social norms, such as female submission, and (b) fostering a good life (186). However, the book is most successful as an extended account of the problems with taking consent to be the guiding norm for sexual ethics. The positive account of good sex, while promising, is sketched out only in the final chapter of the book and is largely proposed rather than argued for. I’d like to turn now to this view of consent as conversation.The solution to the problems of gender injustice in matters of sex, Garcia suggests, is to “talk to each other” (187). Rather than conclude that sexual consent is a dead end, Garcia advocates rethinking consent as erotic conversation (187). On this view, consent is relational, shared between all parties. It is not something we have but something we do—in fact, we do sex, and reframing sex as a conversation highlights its character as activity (191). “In a conversation,” she writes, “we progressively lose track of the authorship of ideas, as the conversation becomes something generative that steers participants in unforeseen directions” (204). This counters the mainstream view that consent is a sort of permission giving, with an asymmetry between the giver and receiver of consent. It also emphasizes that consent is ongoing and requires respect for one’s partner(s).The advantages of this approach over the liberal view are clear. But consent as conversation also has advantages over other related proposals for rethinking sexual consent in recent feminist philosophy. Garcia points out that her view is less agonistic than Quill Kukla’s (2018) argument for conceiving of consent as negotiation. And, while Linda Martín Alcoff (2017) has helpfully proposed rethinking sexual subjectivity, Garcia’s account better highlights the relationality of sexual ethics. Additionally, conversations, like sexual encounters, are temporally delimited situations that end, whereas subjectivity is a general and pervasive feature of experience. Finally, one advantage of the conversation model is that it is applicable in both private and public contexts: Garcia shows that consensual sexual encounters are conversations of a sort, but so too should our educational model around sex be conversational. We must be able to speak openly about the features of good and bad sex, including the unjust social norms that shape sex. Only in doing so will we build the skills needed to improve our erotic conversations.At the same time, Garcia’s analysis of the unjust social norms that shape sex give reason to wonder whether the solution can really be as simple as talking to each other. What might talking to each other, or having an erotic conversation, look like between men and women socialized under patriarchy? Extensive research on patterns of communication between women and men reveals that men are generally dismissive of women’s invitations for conversations about challenging interpersonal issues, in part due to a lack of education in speaking about their emotions (see Anderson 2023). Gendered oppression is more recalcitrant within intimate relationships than in other domains of life in purportedly egalitarian societies (Gunarsson 2014: 99). One way that this appears is in the widespread expectation that women interpret both their own feelings and those of male partners, taking on un undue burden of what I have called hermeneutic labor (Anderson 2023). Given this, it is likely that erotic conversations, even when explicitly welcomed by sexual partners, would most often involve further exploitation of women.This is the opposite of what Garcia desires: she suggests that the asymmetry of labor should actually go the other way in order to push against patriarchal expectations. That is, the person with more power in the encounter, who is most often the man in heterosex, should be the one to establish the erotic conversation (188). But it seems impossible for that goal to be achieved without a profound transformation of the conditions that drive this gendered imbalance to begin with (see Gavey 2005: 223–24). It is unclear that further skill building in erotic conversation would achieve it. This is not to say that Garcia is wrong but rather to highlight the challenges we face under current sociosexual conditions. The discursive register of conversation, even understood broadly, may not be radical enough.Granted, Garcia recognizes that there is a chicken-and-egg problem at work. “How can we have good sex if good sex requires an art of erotic conversation that we do not already possess?” she asks. However, she states that this is precisely “where consent could be emancipatory” (204). By practicing erotic conversation, we get better at it over time. Although sex under current conditions is unlikely to happen between equals, the care of the more powerful sexual partner can to some extent provide a corrective and enable a conversation between “near-equals” (205). “My hope,” she writes, “is that the more people practice erotic conversation with partners, the more comfortable they will become at talking about sex, during sex and outside of it” (204). Although that is likely true, I have to wonder who will be doing most of the teaching, and who most of the learning.

articles.t: Depth: A Kantian Account of Reason
articles.ab: Depth develops a Kantian account of reason. On Zinkin’s interpretation, “reason itself is valuable because it is the source of our deep, rather than superficial, engagement with the world” (1).1 Human beings are “intrinsically deep … since it is we who have the capacity for such deep rational thought—about artworks, nature, and ourselves” (2). Zinkin sees reason as a unitary capacity; its principle is systematicity. Systematicity enables “our deep cognition, and comprehension” (16) of the world, our duties, and ourselves.Zinkin takes up a central puzzle left by Kant: Just what is reason? The Critique of Pure Reason refers to “reason’s common principle” as still undiscovered (Axx). The Critique of Practical Reason hopes that “some day” we might “attain insight into the unity of the whole rational faculty (theoretical as well as practical) and derive everything from one principle” (5:91; see also 4:391; 253). Later works develop no such insight or principle.Some points are clear. Reason is the supreme capacity of human beings. In the first Critique, reason is crucial to scientific and philosophical knowledge but also deeply prone to error. Reason requires critique; since there is no higher capacity, reason must be its own severest critic. In the second Critique, reason is the basis of morality. “Pure practical reason” lays down principles of right action. It motivates us to act rightly by means of respect, the only feeling “self-wrought by a rational concept [= duty]” (4:401n). Again, however, reason is fallible. We often give undue weight to “the dear self” and its inclinations (4:407); we sometimes “rationalise” (156; Sticker 2021) over our duties and fall into “self-conceit” (197).Zinkin emphasizes a less obvious point: “Reason has an aesthetic component, which is what I call depth” (17). Although unmentioned in the title, reason is central to Kant’s Critique of the Power of Judgment: “The power to judge autonomously—that is, freely (according to principles of thought in general)—is called reason” (7:27; 1). Kant insists that a critique of this power belongs to the critique of pure reason (27): Pure reason is our “capacity of judging in accordance with a priori principles” (5:168). Principles spin in empty space, if a thinker or doer cannot connect principles to particulars. Or if someone only makes such connections mechanically, by rote, the result is a “plaster cast of a living human being” (A836/B864; 14, 201, 248). Such a person is shallow; reason is not their own active power.This is the core of Zinkin’s book. Reason is nothing unless it is a matter of meaningful judgment and genuine commitment. Kant’s readers often miss these aesthetic and affective aspects: the satisfactions of comprehending the world, the communicable pleasures of taste, the feeling of respect. Zinkin places special weight on Kant’s articulation of respect in the later Metaphysics of Morals. Our moral personality rests on four affective preconditions: “moral feeling,” “conscience,” “love of human beings,” and “respect for oneself” (6:399; 16f, 197). Thought, judgment, and action demand our personal engagement (128); choices or decisions should be matters of personal commitment (187). Only then does our activity have depth.At the same time, Zinkin follows Kant’s emphasis on cognition. Two points are key. First, cognition is not just about what is the case; it also judges what we should do. In Kant’s terms, cognition is both “theoretical” and “practical.” Second, cognition comes in grades or degrees. At the simplest level, we merely “represent something.” At the highest level, we “comprehend” it; that is, we “cognize something through reason or a priori to the degree that is sufficient for our purpose” (9:65; quoted at 13, 37, 99; see also A320/B376). Since pure practical reason is Kant’s final judge of our proper purposes, one might say: Comprehension is cognition that is thoroughly oriented by reason, both in its exercise (“through”) and its aim (“our purpose”).For Zinkin, systematicity unites these claims about reason. This is a bold proposal. Apart from the gap in Kant’s own work, there are several competing positions.Some interpreters argue there is no unifying principle. For example, Colin McLear (2025: 172) holds that “we have no basis for comprehending the connection between [theoretical and practical reason] in some more basic intellectual act. There is no ‘common principle.”’ Some leave the matter open. Adam Cureton’s (2025: 144) “sovereignty conception” sees practical reason as based in the Categorical Imperative but remains “agnostic” as to its relations with theoretical reason.There are also unifying proposals. Karl Schafer shares Zinkin’s emphasis on “reason as the faculty for comprehension,” oriented by “a demand for systematic unity in (theoretical and practical) cognition.” He encapsulates this in a modest version of the Principle of Sufficient Reason: Roughly, there is always a sufficient reason for everything that we experience (Schafer 2023: 206). Onora O’Neill argues that the central idea of the Categorical Imperative also extends to theoretical reasoning. Like our practical activities, thinking and knowing must respect the principle of universalizability. They only count as reasoned if they can be followed by others (O’Neill 2015, chap. 1; Williams 2023).My sympathies remain with O’Neill’s proposal: I think it goes deeper than Zinkin allows (250–53). But that issue is too large for a short review. Instead, let me bring out Zinkin’s case, alongside two friendly reservations as to how she develops it.For paid-up Kantians, here is a first piece of evidence. “Systematic unity” is key to Kant’s account of theoretical cognition, especially in the first Critique (Appendix to the Transcendental Dialectic; 41, 56). “Systematic union” appears at a key point in Kant’s practical thought (222). The famous “kingdom of ends” posits such union of all “rational beings as ends in themselves” (4:433). I will suggest Zinkin might have emphasized this more.For those more skeptical of Kant, systematicity might still sound like an abstract preoccupation, even a philosophical deformation. Zinkin shows otherwise. Helpfully, she notes the connection between “concept” and “comprehension”: in German, Begriff and Begreifen (98). A well-formed concept enables us to grasp something; comprehension is a deeper grasping or “taking into the mind” (13). A superficial grasp of a concept might enable you to identify particulars. (At least, if the concept is simple and instances are familiar.) But the purpose of cognition is not mere classification (90–96): That is only recognition (32). To go deeper, to really comprehend, cognition must be systematic; it must take a practical form, too.Practical cognition means knowing what to do. Concepts such as fairness or gratitude only make sense if a thinker/doer can judge their apt instantiations. In this case, “systematicity” is another way of highlighting the basic task of practical judgment (O’Neill 2018, chaps. 5–8). This is only possible if we appreciate connections between principles, relations between persons, interrelations between our ends (190). The proper place of a principle or relationship, a person, or an end always depends on a larger whole. So too, what to do in any given circumstance.Both practically and theoretically, systematicity has another importance. It is not just that cognition depends on concepts. Those concepts also ramify: they involve distinctions within a broader conceptual class. These are Kant’s principles of homogeneity, specification, and continuity (A658/B686; 42, 102, 170): contrasts with within a larger set of . Again, this can sound like an abstract preoccupation, an intellectual urge to botanize the world. But recall Kant’s point that comprehension is relative to “our purpose.” In Zinkin’s pithy formula, comprehension grasps the “Why?” as part of the “What?” (30, 56, 248): hence relevant distinctions, the broader class, the purposes at stake.2 One way to see this is to consider our mistakes. Some are trivial. is a for botany, a for eating; pedants lose sight of the “why?” Some mistakes betray humanity at the root. places under for purposes of domination.Zinkin often frames conceptual comprehension as a matter of explicit articulation or reasoning: “thinking something through systematically” (87) or “reflectively” (161). To “understand [= comprehend] something is to be able to explain to myself why I understand it” (65) or why I am performing some action (127). She dismisses habit as automaticity (81, 84, 95) or passivity (235n9), hence the opposite of depth.But Zinkin also claims that comprehension may be felt or enacted. In the stock example: Huck Finn finds himself unable to act on his explicit belief that Jim, a fleeing slave, should be returned to his “owner.” Huck’s belief is superficial; his feelings and actions reveal his “deep comprehension of Jim’s humanity” (149).These competing strains betray, I think, some (Kantian?) inattention to rationality and humanity as embodied. Zinkin emphasizes the intellectual; the inhabited and the enacted remain on the book’s surface.Of course, intellectual purposes often require explicit reflection and explanation. (Below, I emphasize their collective dimensions.) But for many purposes, depth is a matter of engaged experience.
