Concepts (and their contrasts and classifications) sometimes strengthen our practical grasp: “Oppression” clarifies what was puzzling or unseen, for example (217). But concepts can also weaken our grasp. Trivially, a botanical concept becomes pedantry. Fatally, a legal concept betrays morality: the Huck vignette is only bearable because it concerns his good-natured confusions, utterly trivial beside Jim’s plight.In daily life, “systematic” means a grasp on the broader point of one’s activity that carries through to perceptual sensitivity, apt feelings, intelligent habits (6:407), and nuanced responses. This may be more obvious for practical cognition: comprehension is engaged, committed practice. But theoretical cognition can also be tacit and habitual. The skilled cook’s know-how is “theoretical,” for Kant, because it concerns what is the case and how the world works. Regardless of whether the cook can articulate their knowledge, there is nothing shallow about their grasp; it is perfectly sufficient for their purpose.This criticism does not detract from Zinkin’s claim that systematicity is the overarching principle of reason. Indeed, it can support her larger view. Intellectual beliefs may prove superficial. Systematicity means integrating reason into our ways of inhabiting the world and interacting with others; to enact reason is to embody it.As well as emphasizing the intellectual, Zinkin tends to emphasize the individual. Again, I think, this does not fully serve her intent.Zinkin discusses Kant’s formulations of the Categorical Imperative in several chapters: The different formulae reveal the depth of Kant’s ethics. But she places greatest weight on the “most deep” (210) formula of autonomy: “Act according to that maxim through which you can simultaneously will that it become a universal law” (4:421; 163, 208). She gives least attention to the kingdom of ends—even though this explicitly refers to people’s “systematic union” (as noted; 4:433; 222). Zinkin’s examples betray a similar focus. She stresses our duties to others (132, 210, 206, 224, 229) rather than our duties to act with them. Reciprocity, solidarity (198), and cooperation do not get their due.Similarly, Zinkin stresses “cognitive independence and autonomy” (10) throughout the book; autonomy appears as an individual matter (pace O’Neill 2015, chap. 6). For example, “Thinking something through systematically … and even [!] by taking into account what others think, enables me to learn about some object thoroughly and to have my own grasp of [it]…. Such mastery makes me in charge of my own judgment … makes my own judgment authoritative for me” (87). “Taking into account what others think” is an expedient, not a principle of depth or reason. The aim is to become “my own” authority—a framing that surely courts the charge of self-conceit (206).Every student of Kantian autonomy knows how difficult these issues are. Certainly, Kant emphasizes the “courage to use one’s own reason” (8:35; 89, 246). But Zinkin does not cite his “maxim of the power of judgment.” This tells us “to think in the position of everyone else” (5:294), or “to think in communication with them” (7:200, 7:228). Zinkin shares Kant’s distaste for imitation and examples (15, 87, 95). However, she ignores his appreciation of emulation and exemplars (5:232–39, 5:283, 5:318). More broadly, when is trust well placed, testimony well taken? When does self-respect shade into self-conceit?Perhaps, then, we might we think of “depth” or rational comprehension as something we participate in. Of course, meaningful participation demands individual engagement and commitment. But it also rests on a fundamental trust in others’ capacity to participate; it demands attention to what we can do with others; it involves a division of labor that does not make intellectual depth the universal concern Zinkin so often implies (cf. 24:717; quoted at 12).Zinkin’s case for systematicity would be stronger, I suggest, if it placed more weight on reciprocity and intersubjectivity, as central to Kant’s account of reason. This would make better sense of her closing appeal to the humanities (254), where depth and systematicity must count as shared achievements. It might also—although this is an argument for another day—bring Zinkin’s systematicity into closer contact with the idea that universalisability is the underlying principle of Kantian reason.

articles.t: The Darkened Light of Faith: Race, Democracy, and Freedom in African American Political Thought
The Moral Universe
articles.ab: The Moral Universe (TMU) is a state-of-the-art development of nonnaturalistic moral realism by three of its leading contemporary proponents. Despite the literature being by now voluminous, TMU is a genuinely original and sometimes revolutionary addition. Nonnaturalism stands accused of amounting to dogmatic table-thumping, its stance toward morality’s various contested features—reality, objectivity, authority, knowability—characteristically being to insist they obtain while rejecting every demand for explanation. Strategically, nonnaturalists have tended to bet on winning by default after disqualifying rivals. TMU purports to upend the dialectic, demonstrating that a nonnaturalist approach can not only vindicate morality’s key features and integrate them into a broader picture of the world but also satisfactorily explain them. (TMU’s scope is restricted to methodology, metaphysics, and authority, with another volume subsequently to tackle semantics, epistemology, and psychology.) A related, refreshing departure from standard practice is the representation to be focused almost exclusively on positive theory construction, forgoing negative criticism of rivals. It’s impossible to do justice to the book’s range and nuance here, so I’ll focus on issues that most engaged me—acknowledging an ideological predisposition to being an unsympathetic reader.Part 1 can be described as metametaethics (46), which may be too much meta for casual readers’ taste. The authors are unusually self-reflective about what they are doing, greeting readers in chapter 1 with a lengthy discussion of methodology. I understand them to advocate roughly the following process (reminding me of the Build-A-Bear Workshop): Step 1: Gather data. Step 2: Build your theory, defending, explaining, and integrating. Step 3: Critically compare competing theories for their virtues—but only if needed to break ties. (Note that these steps don’t map neatly onto the levels of the “Tri-Level Method,” to which they refer scrupulously throughout the book). This order of activities seems to me like constructing your house prior to conducting a site survey to ensure you’ve selected the best location. One may also be suspicious of the claimed neutrality of a dataset (“starting points”) characterized as “pre-theoretical claims about that domain which inquirers considered collectively have good reason to believe” (20), if gathered without considering what rival theories claim—especially when the authors then suggest that their theory respects this data better than some rivals’ (e.g., 21, 63–64).At key junctures, TMU’s theory-building seems more reliant on negativity than advertised, with the inadequacy of rival theories featuring as a crucial premise in important arguments (e.g., naturalists’ alleged failures to accommodate constraints is one of the four premises in the “overarching argument” for nonnaturalism on page 337), and there are scattered forays into critical commentary that as a proponent of a rival theory I found reminiscent of drive-by shootings. On the basis of brief discussions, the authors offer remarks such as “It’s reasonable to be pessimistic about whether a satisfactory naturalistic view is so much as possible” (336), and they claim that rivals’ prospects “seem dim.” Disavowals of intertheoretic comparison sit uncomfortably with the assertion that nonnaturalism is the upshot of fully discharging moral realism’s burdens (66), for example, and with the closing pronouncement that “a book of the world written in wholly nonnormative terms is fated to leave something out” (346). An excessively cynical reader might suspect TMU’s claimed positivity of being a new gambit for winning by default—not by disqualifying opponents but by selectively ignoring them.Part 1 is significantly occupied with taxonomical issues, addressing the definitions (and burdens) of realism (chapter 2) and nonnaturalism (chapter 3). Whereas the criteria suggested for realism are unremarkable though demanding, I found the definition of nonnaturalism quite a different matter. Nonnaturalism’s “animating idea” is identified as the idea that moral reality is “autonomous.” How? By being “discontinuous with stretches of the natural world” (65). What is the natural world, why only stretches of it, and discontinuous how?The authors are (justifiably) wary of independent attempts at characterizing the natural, and delaying edification, moral naturalism is introduced derivatively, in effect as non-nonnaturalism. The claimed discontinuity turns out to concern normativity—a familiar thought, but I found the way it is developed both obscure and unorthodox. The authors don’t suggest that normativity itself is nonnatural, asserting rather that the normativity of moral properties is recognized by “all parties” (73) and allowing that some parts of “normative reality” like law, etiquette, and games—which nonnaturalists have more typically denied to be genuinely normative at all—may be natural (65). Instead, nonnaturalism is identified as the view that some(!) moral facts are “deeply normative.” This pivotal notion is explicated in terms of having an “ineliminably” normative essence: one that cannot be specified without including a normative fact.To be a metaethical naturalist is therefore to think that morality is non-deeply normative—that is, either (1) inessentially normative or (2) essentially normative, but only eliminably so. Now it is naturalism I struggle to find intelligible. Regarding (1), if everyone agrees that some things are normative, what would motivate denial that some things (such as morality) are essentially so? Regarding (2), something’s essence is “eliminably” normative in case it has a specification that involves only nonnormative facts, as well as having another specification involving a normative fact. (Another “surrogate,” which differs metaphysically and not merely linguistically.) If what it is to be A is to be B, can we make sense of the possibility that also, what it is to be A is to be C, nonidentical to B? I’m skeptical; the authors don’t themselves commit to it, observing only that some philosophers maintain that two facts can be distinct despite one being “nothing over and above” the other (69).TMU’s definition of nonnaturalism seems potentially to encompass theorists normally considered quintessential naturalists, such as some Aristotelians and Humean subjectivists (335–36). I’m particularly interested in the fate of metanormative reductionism. Suppose a philosopher identifies a normative property, like rightness, with a property like maximizing pleasure. Any property involving pleasure-maximization in every specification of its essence would then qualify as “deeply normative” and thus nonnatural! (If what it is to be A is to be A, this may include pleasure-maximization itself.) It would be quite surprising to find self-styled nonnaturalists admitting such possibilities, and indeed the authors deny it, on the grounds that rightness then wouldn’t be a normative property (76; see also 71). I can only surmise they are assuming without argument the falsity of metanormative reductionism. Wouldn’t many parties then want to deny that anything is normative?Morality’s claimed autonomy becomes still more elusive with the suggestion that swathes of nonnormative reality are also deeply normative, or “enchanted.” What is it, then, to be normative, if having a normative essence isn’t sufficient? Readers might expect TMU to have something substantive to say, but we are given a disjunction: something is normative iff it is evaluative, deontic, favoring, fitting, or aretaic. Do these have anything (else) in common? TMU tentatively suggests a unifying appeal to standards: the evaluative involves a “standard of value,” the deontic involves a “standard of permission, requirement, or prohibition,” and so on. But does this really distinguish the normative from the nonnormative, or might being a cloud similarly involve meeting standards of cloudness?In service of realism, chapters 4 and 5 make a case for the existence of moral facts. TMU’s approach loosely resembles G. E. Moore’s case for an external world: “Here’s a hand!,” differentiated by TMU’s focus on essences (111). For some act-types, like recreational slaughter of persons, it is an essential and conceptual truth that they have particular moral properties: recreational slaughter is defeasibly wrong. These are “moral fixed points.” Since these act-types are indisputably instantiated, so are moral properties. (Which moral platitudes are the “fixed points”? Agreeing it is also defeasibly wrong to leave knives within reach of small children, the authors deny this is a conceptual truth. Despite TMU’s discussion [96–98], I fail to see a difference beyond how outlandish the defeaters are. Defeasibility rather suggests nonessentiality.) This strategy strikingly renounces what has forever been nonnaturalism’s central dialectical device, “open question” arguments denying analytic connections between the moral and the nonmoral on the grounds that conceptual truths aren’t substantive. TMU boldly rejects this ground but doesn’t, to my mind, do enough to distinguish substantiveness from nonobviousness (123).This new strategy opens a can of worms. To secure the existence of moral facts, the source of conceptual truth must be attributed to the essences of the (uncontroversially instantiated) nonnormative act concepts/properties. The argument rests on the premise that what it is to be the concept (and property) recreational slaughter essentially involves the concept defeasibly wrong. Anyone doubting recreational slaughter is defeasibly wrong therefore fails to be fully competent with (or is misapplying) the concept recreational slaughter: this would apparently include those who consider it necessarily wrong and anyone lacking moral concepts altogether. Fixed points being necessary, this will be a conceptual truth even in distant worlds where recreational slaughter is always right (e.g., life is universally dreadful, and omissions of recreational slaughter prompt torture of the innocent).Why would the concept of recreational slaughter contain anything more than the conjunction of recreational and slaughter? This surprising claim is defended on the grounds that our reactions to doubts about “fixed points” meet some standard tests for conceptual deficiency, like eliciting bewilderment and raising doubt about a subject’s ability to classify other cases. Passing over nuances (128–29), I worry this too quickly disregards other, more plausible diagnoses such as (recognition of) perversity—or incompetence with moral concepts, a possibility that would seemingly demolish TMU’s argument for moral facts. I might similarly be bewildered and lose trust in your judgment if I learn you like to eat vomit, stab yourself with knives—or think it’s okay to leave them within children’s reach (a nonconceptual truth, recall), but I wouldn’t thereby suspect you of failing to understand what it is to be such an act. Considering the “incredulous stares” (= bewilderment?) the authors anticipate their claim eliciting, indiscriminate application of such a test might impugn their own competence with the concept of a conceptual truth.Fixed points as essential truths illustrate one of TMU’s major explanatory strategies. Moral facts exist because some instantiated act-types essentially involve moral properties. Is this any better an explanation than “dormitive virtues”? The authors respond (145) that appeals to essences potentially provide satisfactory explanations when explanans and explanandum are sufficiently distinct. I suspect a difference between the motivating cases, with the form “That’s just what it is to be K,” and what TMU arguably needs, which is “That’s just because of what it is to be K.” Q: “Why are sisters female siblings?” A: “That’s just what it is to be a sister.” Okay. Q: “Why are tigers usually orange?” A: “That’s just because of what it is to be a tiger.” Although not empty, this seems shallow, prompting further questioning of what it is in tigers’ nature that explains their usual (= defeasible?) orangeness.TMU’s next task is to substantiate and explain the “objectivity” of morality (chap. 6), factored into Stance-Independence (roughly, moral facts don’t depend on anyone’s attitudes) and Constraints (roughly, morality has a particular shape). What most intrigues me here is that TMU’s formulation of objectivity seems entirely compatible with forms of expressivism and perspectivism that treat moral thought as projecting, rather than being about, the thinker’s stances—although these include paradigmatically anti-realist theories that seem unfriendly to TMU’s contention that morality “flows from the nature of things” (1). In brief criticism (app. 2) the authors observe that certain forms of these theories deny moral reality an explanatory role. But not all perspectivist approaches are metaphysically lightweight. Strikingly, TMU allows that some forms of expressivism and constructivism might do no less well with their data than nonnaturalism.Nonnaturalism’s commitment to morality’s elusive autonomy makes particularly pressing the burden of defending and explaining the supervenience of moral reality on the nonnormative facts (“tethering,” chap. 7). TMU’s answer is, in part (omitting significant nuance), that “it is essential to moral properties that their instantiations are fully grounded in instantiations of nonnormative properties” (181). The authors declare themselves comfortable with essences thus functioning as an “unexplained explainer” (187); such appeals are often where the buck stops for TMU’s vindication of nonnaturalism as an explanatory account. While I’m not satisfied, other readers’ mileage may vary.Potentially defusing familiar worries about nonnaturalism’s metaphysical extravagance, TMU allows (without endorsing) that there may be no normativity at reality’s “fundamental layer.” Normative properties may be fully constituted by nonnormative properties (app. 7A). The authors deny this would make moral properties “nothing over and above” their nonnormative grounds, because constitution isn’t identity—for example, Michelangelo’s David is something over and above the marble block that fully constitutes it. While their illustrations are all of concrete particulars being something over what physically constitutes them, it may be significant that metaethics is concerned rather with properties and relations, which (unlike their instantiations) arguably are abstract universals that aren’t physically constituted at all. Sisterhood factors into (1) being a child of the same parents and (2) being female, and it’s puzzling to contemplate it being anything over and above the conjunction of these parts. Neither is the property of being David fully constituted by (being) that block of marble. So I am skeptical about this path to securing respectability for nonnatural properties.Turning to the case for morality’s objective authority, chapter 8 seeks to substantiate/explain why moral reasons are categorical and weighty (“excellent”). To oversimplify a nuanced discussion, moral reasons are inescapable because they aren’t grounded in agents’ commitments, and they sometimes enjoy priority over other reasons because they sometimes defeat them and aren’t invariably defeated. The central argument proceeds familiarly from the claim that morally wrong actions are sometimes blameworthy. I doubt the dialectical force of this argument: anybody questioning whether moral demands are ever categorical and weighty might be expected equally to question this premise.Humean subjectivists object that categorical reasons would be alienating to agents, in a way incompatible with their being normative. Chapter 9 formulates alienation in terms that appear sufficient to dissolve the problem, but despite here driving on the fairway, TMU seems nonetheless to place a pillar in a sand trap. It’s argued that if something is a reason for S to φ because φ-ing promotes satisfaction of S’s desires (the “Desire Promotion View”), then any agent acting on a consideration F that she believes is a reason (“wittingly”) is thereby acting on the “sole basis” that the action promotes her desires—which is “unduly self-regarding.” TMU’s formulation neglects to specify what relationship to S’s desires a consideration F must stand in to be S’s reason, but a primary target (Mark Schroeder) maintains F is such a reason iff it explains why φ-ing promotes S’s desires. Since the fact that φ-ing promotes S’s desires doesn’t explain itself, if S’s basis for acting is her reason F then her basis cannot be that φ-ing promotes her desires. TMU’s charge would stick only if DPV were committed to saying that a witting agent’s sole basis for acting is always the fact that she has a reason (or its grounds) and never the reason itself.Chapters 10 and 11 combine to tackle the age-old question, Why be moral? One task is to rebut the common accusation that mere insistence on the existence of objective moral facts fails to explain why morality matters, more than etiquette, gangster codes, religious devotion, and sometimes self-interest. TMU’s strategy exploits the rich internal structure of the moral domain. The authors profess neutrality on “X-first” debates over which normative notions are ultimately more fundamental (264), but they offer a nonetheless controversial picture. Strong reasons (favoring[?]) are explained/grounded by requirements (deontic), which are explained by what is befitting (fit), explained by what has worth (evaluative). It would seem problematic to make a pro tanto, gradable notion like the strength of reasons derivative from an all-or-nothing notion like requirement. While TMU distinguishes “strong reasons” from reasons’ strength, the stability of this move is questionable.TMU’s case that we should be moral ultimately turns on the claim that as decent people we can’t seriously doubt that the morally right thing is sometimes the (befitting) thing to do. Unfortunately for vindication of the moral cause, this seems question-begging. Looking around the world it’s clear that enormous numbers of our fellow humans today are unpersuaded of such normative opinions, and TMU’s insider explanations seem unfit to persuade anybody who isn’t already a committed morality also anybody who the question to the of While the authors deny their arguments at moral even morally decent people who with their may ultimately be no reason to suspect these either have or the metaphysical of a nonnatural moral on this by the of

articles.t: Why Coherence Matters
articles.ab: Explicating the concept of coherence and establishing a measure for assessing the coherence of an information set are two of the most important tasks of coherentist epistemology. To this end, several principles have been proposed to guide the specification of a measure of coherence. We depart from this prevailing path by challenging two well-established and prima facie plausible principles: Agreement and Dependence. Instead, we propose a new probabilistic measure of coherence that combines basic intuitions of both principles, but without strictly satisfying either of them. It is then shown that the new measure outperforms alternative measures in terms of its truth-tracking properties. We consider this feature to be central and argue that coherence matters because it is likely to be our best available guide to truth, at least when more direct evidence is unavailable.

articles.t: Unknowable Truths
articles.ab: In an anonymous referee report written in 1945, Church suggested a sweeping argument against verificationism, the thesis that every truth is knowable. The argument, which was published with due acknowledgment by Fitch almost two decades later, has generated significant attention as well as some interesting successor arguments. In this paper, we present the most important episodes in this intellectual history using the logic that Church himself favored, and we give reasons for thinking that the arguments are less than decisive. However, we present some new arguments against verificationism that we believe to be dialectically effective.

articles.t: Volume CXXIII Front Matter
Neo-logicism and Conservativeness
articles.ab: Neo-logicists have claimed that Hume's Principle (HP) may be taken as a stipulative definition of cardinal number. However, this claim is threatened by the fact that HP is not conservative over pure second-order logic. I argue that the dominant neo-logicist response to the conservativeness objection is not satisfactory. Then I propose a novel version of neo-logicism, based on Heck's Two-sorted Hume's Principle (2HP), which does meet the conservativeness objection—provided that conservativeness is understood semantically and not deductively. I also argue that on my proposal, the Bad Company problem is solved by conservativeness.

articles.t: What Is It to Be a Solution to Cantor's Continuum Problem?
articles.ab: Cantor’s Continuum Hypothesis (CH) asks what the cardinality of the real line is. It is a mathematically precise problem. Yet, because it cannot be solved using the standard axiomatic framework for mathematics, it is seen by many as a philosophical problem. I want to show what philosophy can contribute to solving the problem by returning it to mathematics, and I will do that by elucidating what it is to be a solution to a mathematical problem. I will argue that CH is an ordinary mathematical problem like the Riemann Hypothesis. I will do this in the course of countering two objections to an alleged solution to CH. This alleged solution, I argue, embodies the general form any solution to CH must take. From this we will see what a solution to CH must be like. It is just like what a solution to the Riemann Hypothesis must be like.

articles.t: The Past as Prologue in advance
New Work for an Old Theory of Action
articles.ab: In this paper I defend the ancient thesis that agents always act under the guise of the good. I do so by arguing that the role that goodness plays in action is isomorphic to the role that truth plays in belief. In particular, I argue that the guise of the good thesis allows us to: (i) fix the topic of ethical and metaethical disagreement just as the aim of belief allows us to fix the topic of alethiological disagreements, (ii) explain the thinness of thin moral concepts in parallel to the thinness of concepts like truth, (iii) develop an account of moral testimony that parallels the best non-reductive accounts of theoretical testimony, and (iv) explains why we are open to our values changing over time in much the same way that we are open to our theoretical premises changing over time.

articles.t: Matthew Boyle: Transparency and Reflection: A Study of Self-Knowledge and the Nature of the Mind
On the Value of Irreplaceable Objects
articles.ab: Bradford (2023) calls attention to the fact that the strength of our reasons to preserve distinctively valuable objects increases as the number of such objects decreases. Bradford develops an account of this phenomenon in terms of ‘irreplaceable value’, and in particular in terms of a notion of the degree of such value, which is distinct from its amount. We present an alternative explanation of this pattern in our reasons, which appeals to the value of diversity: the world is better, other things equal, insofar as it contains more kinds of value. We develop this view in two connected ways: one appeals to evidential probability under conditions of uncertainty, and the other appeals to the value of diversity. We conclude by discussing some explanatory advantages of our view over Bradford’s.

articles.t: Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Patchwork Principles
articles.ab: Benardete paradoxes involve infinite collections of Grim Reapers, assassins, demons, deafening peals, or even sentences. These paradoxes have recently been used in arguments for finitist metaphysical theses such as temporal finitism, causal finitism, and discrete views of time. Here we develop a new finite Benardete-like paradox. We then use this paradox to defend a companions in guilt argument that challenges recent applications of patchwork principles on behalf of the aforementioned finitist arguments. Finally, we develop another problem for those applications by examining the notion of exact duplication.

articles.t: The Ground of Truth
articles.ab: Suppose that p is true. What is the relationship between this fact—p’s being true—and the fact p itself? There is an answer to this question that goes back at least to Aristotle, and that is a mainstay of contemporary work on metaphysical explanation (or grounding). According to this: p is true is grounded by p. For example, snow is white is true because snow is white. The initial aim of this paper is to challenge this answer. Our strategy is to take the best formal work on truth as a guide to its metaphysics. This yields a natural account of the grounds of facts involving truth, and one that satisfyingly resolves the puzzles of ground (due to Fine and others). But this account fundamentally reconsiders the relationship between truth ascriptions and their subjects. Under the proposal, p fails to ground p's being true in every case in which p is itself about truth.

articles.t: Mathematical Access Worries and Accounting for Knowledge of Logical Coherence
articles.ab: A range of current truth-value realist philosophies of mathematics allow one to reduce the access problem for mathematics to a problem concerning mathematicians’ ability to recognize which conceptions of pure mathematical structures are coherent—in a sense that can be cashed out in terms of logical possibility. In this paper, I will clarify what it takes to solve this ‘residual’ access problem and then present a framework for solving it.

articles.t: Ex Ante Pareto and the Opaque-Identity Puzzle
articles.ab: Anna Mahtani describes a puzzle meant to show that the Ex Ante Pareto Principle is incomplete as it stands and, since it cannot be completed in a satisfactory manner, decades of debate in welfare economics and ethics are undermined. In this paper, we provide a better solution to the puzzle which saves the Ex Ante Pareto Principle from this challenge. We also explain how the plausibility of our solution is reinforced by its similarity to a standard solution to an analogous puzzle in quantified epistemic logic. We also show that even if the puzzle were to remain unsolved, its impact on welfare economics and ethics would be limited.

articles.t: Belief About Probability
articles.ab: Credences are beliefs about evidential probabilities. We give the view an assessment-sensitive formulation, show how it evades the standard objections, and give several arguments in support.

articles.t: "Just a Little Gay": How Sexual Orientation Comes in Degrees
articles.ab: You can be a little gay or a lot gay. You can be mostly heterosexual. You can be somewhat lesbian. What I am saying is: sexual orientation comes in degrees. This point is well established in sexuality studies but largely neglected by philosophers. The on-off (or binary) model of sexual orientation, which is implicit in most philosophical theories of sexual orientation, misrepresents social reality. I aim to correct this state of affairs. I propose a theory of sexual orientation that is fundamentally scalar and multidimensional: scalar, because sexual orientation comes in degrees; multidimensional, because there are various dimensions of sexual orientation—desire, disposition, duration, and so on.

articles.t: VII—Are Philosophers Absurd? Progress, Testimony and Division of Labour
articles.inst: London School of Economics and Political Science
articles.ab: Abstract Philosophy now resembles, in many ways, a mature scientific discipline. There is extensive division of increasingly specialised cognitive labour. Big philosophical questions are broken down into ever smaller research questions and addressed in growing thousands of publication units. But to what purpose? Philosophers are notoriously sceptical about deferring to each other’s published findings. Most publications seem to increase, rather than reduce, philosophical disagreement. There is a looming worry about absurdity in this activity. Great intellectual effort—and countless careers—are spent on things that seemingly do not settle core questions of the field. I explore a somewhat more optimistic perspective. Rather than viewing progress as something made by the philosophical community writ large, I suggest we might instead locate progress in the small research communities that populate it. This new perspective allows us to do several things. Firstly, it allows us to reject extreme pessimism about deference to philosophical testimony. Secondly, it provides some rationale for the division of labour found in contemporary philosophy. And thirdly, it suggests that there may be a sense in which many big philosophical questions have already been answered.

articles.t: Peter Momtchiloff on Thirty Years at Oxford University Press
articles.ab: Abstract For most readers of the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Peter Momtchiloff needs little introduction. From 1993 to 2023 he was Commissioning Editor for Philosophy at Oxford University Press (OUP). It was big news in the philosophy community when we heard that Peter was leaving his post in December 2023. In July 2024 we invited Peter along to talk to us at the Aristotelian Society to find out a bit about what he's seen and what he's learned. The discussion between Peter, Jessica Leech and Ellie Robson was shared as a podcast. What follows is an edited version of that discussion for our readers.

articles.t: Correction to: VII—Nietzschean Genealogy and Philosophical Methodology
III—What’s Wrong with the Master? A Critical Analysis of Hegel’s Master–Slave Dialectic
articles.ab: Abstract In his influential master–slave dialectic, Hegel looks to demonstrate that being a master is self-defeating. The master seeks absolute independence and genuine recognition from another. However, they depend upon their slave for their mastery, and the recognition their slave provides is ‘one-sided and unequal’. Thus, Hegel claims that mastery fails to achieve what it seeks. In this paper, I put some pressure on this dialectic. Amongst other things, I argue that what is primarily wrong with the master is the fact that they dominate a slave, not that they somehow fail on their own terms.

articles.t: Duddington and Our Awareness of Others’ Minds
articles.ab: Abstract What enables me to know that others exist? Nathalie Duddington offers two distinctive, and underexplored, insights into the question. She focuses on our capacity to perceive minds in perceiving animate beings, and on the ways in which we stand to be affected by others in knowing them. I will suggest a way of understanding what it is to see minds in action. I will also argue that ways we stand to be affected by others offers a resource for knowing others that takes us beyond perception, and is one that constitutes an antidote to the solipsist.

articles.t: IV—Kumārila Bhaṭṭa on the First-Person Pronoun
articles.ab: Abstract In metaphysical debates about the self, realist philosophers like Kumārila Bhaṭṭa must account for uses of the first-person pronoun that seem to predicate properties inconsistent with the supposedly enduring, immaterial self. Responding to Buddhists like Vasubandhu, in his ‘Position on the Self’ chapter of the Commentary in Verse, Kumārila argues for an invariantist position, despite his well-known contextualist strategies for explaining the meaning of nouns like ‘self’. I show how this strategy accounts for the problem sentences and resolves a further potential problem that might arise with the possessive pronoun ‘my’ when its complement is the word ‘self’.

articles.t: V—Saving Logic from a Metaphysical Limbo: Susanne Langer on Logical Assertion
articles.ab: Abstract Can a logic free from psychological considerations be free from metaphysical ones? The topic of this paper is Susanne Langer’s discussions of the notion of logical assertion, which aim at addressing this question. We will see both that Langer’s remarks are of historical interest and that they can help us understand better what logic should be taken to be concerned with, and what logical assertion should be taken to be.

articles.t: II—Plans, Learning, and Deferring
articles.ab: Abstract Recent work in formal epistemology has attempted to justify synchronic versions of conditionalization. But what is synchronic conditionalization, and how can it be justified? I will argue that we cannot justify it if we understand it as a plan to conditionalize, but may have better luck if we understand it as a disposition to conditionalize. I then draw some connections to rational deference.

articles.t: Response to ‘The Epistemic Harms of National Humiliation’ by Raamy Majeed
articles.ab: Abstract Raamy Majeed (2025) wants to draw our attention away from humiliation as an emotion in international politics, to look at the narratives around humiliation. Such narratives, he argues, generate previously unexamined forms of epistemic injustice, which apply both to out-groups and in-groups. Exploring the role that epistemic injustice might play in national humiliation narratives is an important contribution to our understanding of the harms of these narratives, but I argue that Majeed has not shown that there is epistemic injustice in several of the cases he examines. I also suggest that more could be done to explain how to address narratives of national humiliation, but this will require revising his commitment to only analysing narratives and not the truth of those narratives.

articles.t: Paper from the 2024–25 Session What (If Anything) Is Moral Experience?
articles.ab: Abstract What, if anything, is moral experience? I will argue that moral experience is a distinctive type of perceptual experience—affectively assisted perceptual experience—that, in a way to be explained, provides privileged access to moral reality. I will go on to suggest some ways in which moral experience, so understood, may prove theoretically useful.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: VIII—After the Fall: Malebranche on the Law of the Body
articles.ab: Abstract Malebranche holds that the Fall changes the mind’s relationship to the body from union to dependence. I argue that this change transforms the mind’s normative relationship with its body. The mind depends on the body in that the mind feels subjected to the body’s authority and obligated to satisfy its needs. In addition to reconstructing Malebranche’s phenomenological account of the body’s felt authority, I argue that for Malebranche the obligations springing from our bodily nature are genuine.

articles.t: X—On Time-Slice Democracy and Getting Stuff Done
articles.ab: Abstract This paper explores a puzzle about democracies’ ability to effectively shape our collective lives over time. There are compelling reasons to adopt what I will call ‘time-slice democracy’: only the current demos with its current attitudes should have democratic voice. This might seem to condemn democracies to extreme short-termism and ineffectiveness. I argue that this is not so: democracies can get stuff done if they treat past policy commitments and plans as a strong default, and doing so can be justified on grounds compatible with time-slice democracy.

articles.t: IX—Working Out How Blame Works
articles.ab: Abstract When philosophers talk about the function of blame, they are sometimes giving a functional explanation of blame, and sometimes an instrumentalist moral justification based on blame’s effects. How are these two types of project related? I argue that, in principle, the two projects are compatible, and instrumentalist justifications could draw on a functionalist explanation of blame to show that blame has morally desirable effects. However, there is currently no well-developed functionalist account of blame that can serve that purpose. Furthermore, functionalist explanations need not paint blame in a morally favourable light.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: XI—Artspeak (Or: What Dorothea Learned in Rome)
articles.ab: A familiar experience when engaging with art is that of being in the presence of profundity but finding oneself unable to articulate that profundity to one’s own satisfaction. To make sense of this, I propose a novel kind of deep content in art, ostensive content, which consists in that to which our non-perceptual attention non-accidentally falls through the use of the art object as an ostensive device. Deep content in art is not encoded by representation vehicles on the surface of the art object; it is that to which our attentional gaze falls when we engage well with the artwork.

articles.t: Bertrand Russell’s Transition to the Higher-Order Theory of Existence
articles.ab: I argue that, in the period 1910–15, Bertrand Russell’s theory of existence is inconsistent with his theory of acquaintance. This inconsistency not only highlights that Russell’s thinking about existence is bound up with his epistemology, but also shows that it is only in 1918–19 that he finally comes to his influential higher-order theory of existence. Finally, I briefly argue that Russell’s eventual rejection of the distinction between being and existence goes hand-in-hand with his acceptance of a theory of universals according to which they are essentially predicative.

articles.t: Musical Education and the Rational Part of the Soul in Plato’s Republic
articles.ab: What is the value of educating children in music? Perhaps a childhood musical education can have certain emotional benefits, but can it have any cognitive effects on children’s beliefs and values? For Plato in the Republic, the answer to this question is clearly yes; however, the details of his views about which part of soul musical education develops and exactly what effects it has are more difficult to determine. Answers to this question in the literature fall into two camps. The first camp, where the majority of commentators on this topic fall, argue that musical education targets only the spirited part of the soul, while a select few who make up the second camp argue that musical education also targets the rational part to instil in it opinions that serve as a foundation for the knowledge that it will gain in later education. In this paper, I will agree with the second camp that musical education does target the rational part; however, I will argue that their view falls short in explaining how targeting the rational part in this way helps to achieve the explicit goal of early education of harmonizing the rational and spirited parts. I will then offer a new interpretation of a well-known passage in Book iii to argue that musical education instils in the rational part an ability to perceive and accurately discriminate between fine and shameful items, which prepares the rational part to rule and guide the spirited part.

articles.t: XIII—On Pensiveness: A Defence of Aesthetic Cognitivism
articles.ab: Arguments aim to reach conclusions, but artworks tend to leave us in a state of rumination, perplexity or musing. I describe this state—pensiveness—as a dynamic mode of grappling with some proposition. I then defend the claim that pensiveness is epistemically valuable, in so far as it allows subjects to entertain propositions which they are not yet in a position to know. Pensive artworks, therefore, do not teach us anything; they allow us a glimpse of important things, which as flawed beings we cannot yet grasp.

articles.t: Two Pre-theoretic Counterexamples to Justification Holism in the Epistemology of Logic
articles.ab: An abductivist approach to the epistemology of logic has recently gained traction. A necessary component of logical abductivism is justification holism, asserting that claims of logical entailment can be justified only in the context of an entire logical theory, for example, classical, intuitionistic, and so on. One view that is incompatible with abductivism is an atomistic view on which individual entailment claims can be justified pointwise rather than in the context of a whole theory. This paper provides two atomistic counterexamples to justification holism in the epistemology of logic. Both examples appeal to pre-theoretic commitments of deductive validity. The main aim is to show that there are some foundational entailment claims for which we can have propositional justification independently of theory choice and outside the context of a whole logical theory. If one were to give up on these foundational claims, all semantic and syntactic accounts of deductive validity would be non-starters.

articles.t: Oiling the Wheels of the Philosophy Machine
articles.ab: ‘Philosophy’, like ‘art’, denotes both an activity and the product of the activity, each of which has value in its own right. I start with the idea that the main role of professional philosophers, qua researchers, is to contribute to the production of the product—philosophical works that are in the public domain—and argue that neither our own doxastic states nor their justificatory status is important when it comes to our ability to fulfil that role. In particular, assertion in philosophical contexts is not governed by a norm that requires us to be in any particular doxastic state with respect to the asserted content.

articles.t: XII—Socrates and Dialogue as the Greatest Good
articles.ab: This paper argues that Socratic dialogue is not a value-neutral practice, with ethical value entering the frame only via its content (discussion of the virtues); nor is it solely an instrumental tool to secure a valuable end-product (a definition). I argue in favour of three positive claims. Claim 1 is that dialogue is a value-laden practice. What we tend to suppose are value-neutral norms, such as cooperation, a mutually accepted direction, checking whether a position has been understood before drawing conclusions, and so on, involve ethical values. This explains the prevalence of language familiar from the ethical domain to describe the practice of dialogue in Plato’s works. Claim 2 is that because dialogue involves values in its activity, adhering to norms of dialogue can foster virtuous behaviours simply in so far as participants adhere (well and repeatedly) to the rules of the game. Taken together, these claims loosen the grip of the results-driven focus on an elusive end-product, which supposedly contains all the ethical value. Though dialogue aims at definitions, or virtue, the activity itself also has value and, according to Socrates in the Apology, it has the greatest value for human beings (it is the ‘greatest good’, megiston agathon). I defend this claim by arguing that dialogue is the greatest good because it is thinking aloud, and the virtues are excellences of dialogue/thinking (Claim 3).

articles.t: Kant’s Conclusions in the Transcendental Aesthetic
articles.ab: abstract: In the Transcendental Aesthetic (TA), Kant is typically held to make negative assertions about things in themselves, namely that they are not spatial or temporal. These negative assertions stand behind the neglected alternative problem for Kant’s transcendental idealism. In this paper, I show in a new way how Kant’s view is not subject to this objection, by showing that Kant’s claim that things ‘in themselves’ are not in space means that space is not a necessary constraint on things as a kind . This claim does not involve the denial about mind-independent reality that inspires the neglected alternative objection.

articles.t: "The Poison in the Snake's Fang": Schopenhauer on Malice
articles.ab: abstract: Schopenhauer is one of the few philosophers in the history of Western ethics to dedicate sustained critical attention to the nature, extent, and phenomenology of malice. This paper seeks to elucidate the nuances of Schopenhauer's account of malice. It is argued that part of its significance lies in how Schopenhauer's idiosyncratic conceptual framework allows him to philosophically capture many widespread beliefs about malicious persons—particularly the view that malice is best explained in terms of the agent's own inner suffering. Nevertheless, Schopenhauer's views about malice raise a number of interpretive puzzles, which the paper subsequently aims to elucidate and solve.

articles.t: Wisdom for the Living: Sophia in Plato's Republic
articles.ab: abstract: In proposing an account of wisdom ( sophia ), Plato was intervening in a longstanding debate about the nature of the highest intellectual virtue for a human being. Despite its historical and philosophical significance, wisdom has received limited scholarly attention. This paper offers an account of wisdom in Plato's Republic . I reject the interpretation that wisdom is identical to knowledge of Forms. Rather, wisdom of the city (or soul) is the ability to make good judgments, by the standard of the Forms, about how the whole city (soul) would best fare. This account has implications for Plato's disagreement with Protagoras, the Two Worlds Debate about epistēmē , and the limitations of human wisdom.

articles.t: Look Ma, No Hands!: A New Direction in Kant's Metaphysics of Space Before Directions ' Incongruent Counterparts
articles.ab: abstract: According to a common narrative, Kant held a kind of relationalist view of space from the time of his earliest publication, Living Forces , until 1768, when he published Concerning the Ultimate Ground of the Differentiation of Directions in Space . The narrative holds further that considerations about incongruent counterparts prompted an abrupt volte-face—concerns about right and left hands were supposedly the decisive factor in causing a sudden shift to the metaphysical view expressed in Directions . I argue that the common narrative is wrong, offering a new account of the timeline of, and reasons behind, Kant's rejection of relationalism.

articles.t: Adam of Bockenfield and His Circle on Aristotle's "De memoria et reminiscentia." ed. by Julie Brumberg-Chaumont and Dominique Poirel (review)
JHP Announcements
Mary Shepherd: A Guide by Deborah Boyle (review)
Peirce on Inference: Validity, Strength, and the Community of Inquirers by Richard Kenneth Atkins (review)
Books of Interest
What's in a Name? The Logic of 'God,' Existence, and The Five Ways: "Respondeo dicendum quod Deum esse quinque viis probari potest."
articles.ab: abstract: After discussing the Goal Objection—a twofold objection to Aquinas's Five Ways—the paper disambiguates the use of the Latin deus (god) in Aquinas's discussion. Then, analyzing the semantics of the disambiguated deus , it argues that the Five Ways are not intended to be a demonstration of there being only one god, as one form of the objection has it. Further, the ways do not lead to idolatry or atheism, as another form of the objection has it. They do not intend to demonstrate the existence of God at all, although their conclusions, if true, are made true by the existence of God.

articles.t: Ennead II.4: On Matter by Plotinus (review)
Property and Its Forms in Classical German Philosophy by David James (review)
Editorial Consultants
Spinoza: Life and Legacy by Jonathan I. Israel (review)
The Culmination: Heidegger, German Idealism, and the Fate of Philosophy by Robert E. Pippin (review)
Leibniz's Definitions of an Individual Substance: "Complete Concept" and/or "Law of the Series." Replacement, Development, or Complementarity?
articles.ab: abstract: Throughout his career, Leibniz defines individual substances in different ways. In the 1680s, especially in the Discourse on Metaphysics , Leibniz develops an original definition of substance through the complete concept of an individual (CCI). Most commentators hold that the CCI fades out in Leibniz's later philosophy. Others argue that the "law of the series" (LoS) replaces the definition of an individual substance through the CCI. We argue that these definitions are complementary. Early versions of the LoS inform the development of the CCI in the 1680s and are clearly pronounced in Leibniz's later texts. We discuss several often-neglected texts that show that the CCI is still present in Leibniz's late writings. We support the complementarity thesis by suggesting that the CCI primarily characterizes possible individuals, whereas the LoS characterizes actual individuals. As such, the LoS is especially apt to highlight the dynamic traits that Leibniz ascribes to individual substances from the 1690s.

articles.t: Contents for Volume LXIII (2025)
Pedro da Fonseca: Humanism and Metaphysics ed. by Simone Guidi and Mário de Carvalho (review)
At the Roots of Causality: Ontology and Aetiology from Avicenna to Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī by Francesco Omar Zamboni (review)
Skepticism and the Idea of Body in Hume
articles.ab: abstract: In section 1.4.4 of the Treatise , "Of the modern philosophy," Hume offers a skeptical argument concerning the distinction between primary and secondary qualities. The argument in that section is often understood to aim to undermine the modern philosophy's account of body, according to which bodies lack paradigmatic secondary qualities, by showing that it has "extravagant" skeptical consequences. I argue that Hume does not reject the core commitments of the modern philosophy. His aim in T 1.4.4 is not to undermine any particular account of body but rather to establish the deeply rooted inadequacy of our cognition of external bodies.

articles.t: Indian Philosophy and Yoga in Germany by Owen Ware (review)
Plato's "Phaedo": Forms, Death, and the Philosophical Life by David Ebrey (review)
German Philosophy and the First World War by Nicolas de Warren (review)
The Volitional Theory of Causation: Berkeley to the Twentieth Century by William J. Mander (review)
articles.ab: b o o k r e v i e w sFinally, it must be said that the themes woven throughout the work, whether considered from the angles of Lebensphilosophie, existentialism, phenomenology, dialogical philosophy, or critical theory, are of enduring interest.Each chapter begins with the outbreak of war, regardless of whether the philosopher under consideration was a well-established elder like Cohen or a young up-and-comer like Rosenzweig.De Warren then narrates the thinker's reflections on the era he (i.e.De Warren) considers to have come to a close with the war, in whatever respect he conceives it, and his imagining whether and how a total transformation, for good or ill, is imminent.In some cases, this leads the philosopher to produce his defining work during or immediately after the war; in others, it drives the story forward into the late twenties or even the thirties, as the aftermath of the Great War shades into the beginnings of World War Two.De Warren is juggling a tremendous amount of material as he judges when and how to introduce personal and familial events, which texts and ideas to narrate, and which secondary literature to cite.The degree to which he succeeds at making each portrait feel as though it stands on its own is therefore quite impressive.This is not a salvage or recovery project-if you did not find Scheler compelling before, De Warren is not attempting here to persuade you that Scheler is "relevant" today.He is rather presenting each figure as a microcosm, demonstrating the impact of the war upon philosophy by revealing it in instance after instance.

articles.t: The Cambridge Companion to the Sophists ed. by Joshua Billings and Christopher Moore (review)
Romantic Empiricism: Nature, Art, and Ecology from Herder to Humboldt by Dalia Nassar (review)
topics: History of Science and Natural History

Descartes’s Moral Perfectionism by Frans Svensson (review)
Signs and Demonstrations from Aristotle to Radulphus Brito by Costantino Marmo and Francesco Bellucci (review)

articles.t: De Bayle à Hume. Tolérance, Hypothèses, Systèmes by Gianni Paganini (review)
The Guise of the Good: A Philosophical History by Francesco Orsi (review)
The Inclusive Nature of Being: Sophist 248e–249b
articles.ab: abstract: This paper considers the contentious passage (248e–249d) of the Sophist where the Stranger criticizes the Giants, who associate being with bodies, and the Gods, who identify it with the forms, ultimately providing a third position. There are two prevailing interpretations of this section : “Reading A” has the Stranger argue that being encompasses not only the forms but also other entities, while “Reading B” has the Stranger contend that being, namely, the forms, moves. My strategy is to accept aspects of both interpretations and present a fresh reading by closely examining a passage often underemphasized in the debate (249a4–b3).

articles.t: Adam Smith’s Impartial Spectator Is Also Well-informed
articles.ab: abstract: When we use the shorthand ‘impartial spectator,’ we should not forget that the Smithian authoritative moral perspective is also well-informed. But is there anything more to say about the import and nature of this qualification? In this paper, I argue that the only way for Smith to explain how we can correct two kinds of problematic moral judgments is by invoking well-informedness, understood in a way that involves information about the psychology of moral judgment. I also argue that this interpretation reveals a crucial way in which The Theory of Moral Sentiments functions as a morally educational text.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: Women Philosophers in Nineteenth-Century Britain by Alison Stone (review)
topics: History of Science and Natural History

articles.t: Laws and Nature in Spinoza’s Ethics
articles.ab: abstract: A tradition associated with Aristotle, essentialism , emphasizes the effort to show how effects follow from laws distinctive of the thing in which they occur. A different tradition, associated with the scientific revolution, unificationism , emphasizes the effort to show that nature conforms to laws because it is in some ways uniform. In his accounts of laws and nature in the Ethics , Spinoza defends exceptionless, detailed versions of essentialism and unificationism.

articles.t: Causality and Causal Explanation in Aristotle by Nathanael Stein (review)
How Plato Writes: Perspectives and Problems by Malcolm Schofield (review)
Idealism in Modern Philosophy ed. by Paul Guyer and Rolf-Peter Horstmann (review)
Moore’s Fourth Condition
articles.ab: abstract: G. E. Moore’s “Proof of an External World” has long vexed readers. That Moore could regard the proof as cogent, despite its apparent circularity, has often been read as a failure to register the worry, underwriting the charge of philosophical naivete. This paper offers a new interpretation. Drawing on newly discovered archival material, I argue that “Proof” is best read as the culmination of Moore’s efforts to come to grips with a “fourth condition” on proof—beyond premise–conclusion distinctness, known premises, and validity—namely, a proof’s capacity to extend knowledge. On this interpretation, Moore’s proof embodies a more complex account than commentators have recognized, clarifying both its seemingly paradoxical character and the unease it provokes in readers.

articles.t: Kant’s “Critique of Pure Reason” and the Method of Metaphysics by Gabriele Gava (review)
Averroes and the Problem of the Eternal Intelligibles
articles.ab: abstract: Averroes argues for a single, eternal intellect that all humans share. But if that intellect contains all the intelligibles eternally in act, how can it receive from human images what it already has ? How can temporal acts of abstraction generate supposedly eternal intelligibles? I sketch two solutions : (i) a new reading, which holds that intelligibles are generated and corrupted in the separate intellect ; and (ii) another reading that holds (more traditionally) that the intelligibles exist eternally, yet depend perpetually on abstraction. Though I argue for (i), both interpretations resolve the problems and are clarified by Averroes’s notion of intermediate eternality, revealing an important connection between his psychology and cosmology.

articles.t: Transcendental Idealism and Metaphysics: Husserl's Critique of Heidegger. Vol I by Daniele De Santis; and: Transcendental Idealism and Metaphysics: Husserl's Critique of Heidegger. Vol 2 by Daniele De Santis (review)
Determinism and Enlightenment: The Collaboration of Diderot and d'Holbach by Ruggero Sciuto (review)
The Unity of Reason, Reconsidered: On the "Autonomy of Ideas" in the Later Kant
articles.ab: abstract: In the Groundwork and all three Critiques , Kant expresses the hope of unifying theoretical and practical reason in one system governed by a common principle—but does not clarify how he aims to achieve this unity. Here, I show that Kant refers to the "autonomy of ideas of reason" in his final decade, enabling a new approach to the unity of reason. This concept of autonomy, however, is not the moral autonomy of the self-legislating will, nor the spontaneity of theoretical reason. Instead, it corresponds to the autonomy ascribed to reflective judgment in representing both theoretical and practical ideas of reason in accordance with the principle of purposiveness, which I propose as the unifying principle Kant had been seeking.

articles.t: Soul and Body in Aristotle's Theory of Perception
articles.ab: abstract: A widespread view has it that, for Aristotle, perception's psychological and physiological aspects are phenomenal consciousness and its underlying material basis. I argue on the contrary that they are judgment/discrimination and receptivity: in virtue of our sense organs, we are receptive to objects of perception; in virtue of our souls, we judge or discriminate these objects. In effect, Aristotle divides perception's active and passive aspects between soul and body. I defend this view with special attention to Aristotle's claim that our senses receive form without matter in perception.

articles.t: La notion de volonté dans les écrits de saint Augustin entre 388 et 404 by Evgenia Moiseeva (review)
Berkeley's Theory of Vision: A New Look
articles.ab: abstract: I defend a new interpretation of Berkeley's theory of vision designed to solve a pair of interrelated interpretive problems: the first has to do with visual perception of three-dimensionality and the second with the psychological flexibility of the visual process. Though the first problem has been discussed extensively, previous solutions are unsatisfying; the second problem has not been discussed before. My interpretation breaks new ground and locates the resources to solve both problems by contextualizing Berkeley's theory of vision among underexplored aspects of his metaphysics and his views of human psychology.

articles.t: Consciousness, Time, and Scepticism in Hume's Thought by Lorne Falkenstein (review)
The "Critique of Judgment" and the Unity of Kant's Critical System by Lara Ostaric (review)
Bagehot on Belief
articles.ab: abstract: Anatomizing the nature of belief, Walter Bagehot (1826–77) distinguishes between an emotional state of conviction and an intellectual act of assent . According to Bagehot, the various causes of our nonrational convictions can all be traced back to the vestiges of an undiscriminating childhood impulse to acquiesce before all states of consciousness. I argue that he also regards the intellectual activity of assent as emerging from that same original credulity once it has been chastened by the corrective shocks of experience. I further show that Bagehot's picture of conviction, assent, and our omnivorous original credulity shapes various of his social and political doctrines.

articles.t: Science of the Soul in Ibn Sīnā's "Pointers and Reminders": A Philological Study by Michael A. Rapoport (review)
On the Divine Things and Their Revelation by Friedrich Henrich Jacobi (review)
Spinoza: Scholarship Since 2000
articles.ab: abstract: In this essay, I highlight some of the most auspicious and impressive developments in Spinoza research since 2000. This is at best a partial survey, in both senses of the term. First, it is fairly subjective, reflecting my own interests and preferences. Second, given how much has been published on Spinoza in the past quarter century, there are many items that warrant mention that have not been included. Moreover, I limit my discussion to the literature in languages with which I feel safe in assuming most readers of this journal are familiar. I also offer a new, more accurate translation of the herem (ban) issued against Spinoza, to replace the variety of translations that have circulated for years.

articles.t: Fractured Goodness: Aristotle's Response to Plato's Form of the Good by Christopher Shields (review)
Neoplatonic Pedagogy and the Alcibiades I: Crafting the Contemplative by James M. Ambury (review)
Rousseau's God: Theology, Religion, and the Natural Goodness of Man by John T. Scott (review)
Maimonides's Skeptical Critique of a Divine Intellect, or the Curious Case of Guide I.68
articles.ab: abstract: The philosophers' dictum in Maimonides's Guide of the Perplexed I.68 has been classically read as Maimonides's own opinion that God's intellect in act is identical to the intellecting subject in act and intellectum in act, no different from a human intellect in act. This reading of the chapter generates multiple puzzles and contradicts Maimonides's views elsewhere. I argue instead that the chapter is Maimonides's skeptical critique of the philosophers' (not his own) conception of God's intellect, that careful analysis shows that Maimonides presents four differences between the human and divine intellects, and that the divine intellect, unlike the human, is entirely unknowable.

articles.t: The Politics of German Idealism: Law and Social Change at the Turn of the 19th Century by Christopher Yeomans (review)
Books of Interest
P. F. Strawson and His Philosophical Legacy ed. by Sybren Heyndels, Audun Bengtson, and Benjamin De Mesel (review)
Vice in Ancient Philosophy: Plato and Aristotle on Moral Ignorance and Corruption of Character by Karen Margrethe Nielsen (review)
Seeing More: Kant’s Theory of Imagination by Samantha Matherne (review)
Denken in Zwecken: Bedeutung und Status der Teleologie in der theoretischen Philosophie Kants und Hegels by Karen Koch (review)
Response to Tad Schmaltz, “Lamy, Malebranche, and the Force of Rest: Reply to Nadler ”
The Voice of Virtue: Moral Song and the Practice of French Stoicism, 1574–1652 by Melinda Latour (review)
The Good Cartesian: Louis de la Forge and the Rise of a Philosophical Paradigm by Steven Nadler (review)
June Downey’s Thesis on Berkeley on the Will
articles.ab: abstract: This paper introduces readers to a master ’s thesis defended by June Downey to the Philosophy Department of the University of Chicago in 1898. I have two goals. The first and major goal is to show that an unknown and unpublished piece of work from the end of the nineteenth century is, in fact, well worth reading. Downey ’s paper makes useful contributions to the field by foregrounding the importance of activity in Berkeley ’s metaphysics and in making a novel use of his Philosophical Commentaries . Finally, taking on board the usefulness of Downey ’s unknown work adds insights about the project of adding women to accounts of the history of philosophy.

articles.t: Richard Rufus of Cornwall. Scriptum in Metaphysicam Aristotelis II. Zeta to Lambda ed. by Neil Lewis, Jennifer Ottman, and Rega Wood (review)
Lamy, Malebranche, and the Force of Rest: Reply to Nadler
articles.ab: abstract: In a recent issue of the Journal of the History of Philosophy , Steven Nadler draws attention to the neglected argument of François Lamy that Malebranche ’s doctrine of occasionalism conflicts with his own criticism of Descartes ’s appeal to a “force of rest ” in physics. Nadler claims that this argument is well worth considering insofar as its conclusion seems to be “absolutely correct. ” In this discussion note, I offer reasons to doubt that Lamy is in fact correct in charging that there is an internal tension on this point in Malebranche ’s system. I also briefly consider the significance of Malebranche ’s critique of Descartes for early modern Cartesian physics.

articles.t: Kant and the Interpretation of Religious Scriptures
articles.ab: abstract: This paper shows how interpreting religious scriptures contributes to applied Kantian ethics. It addresses concerns in recent literature with introducing principles of practical reason in the historical and institutional spheres. Just as the formal principles of the moral law apply under all conditions, the pure religion of reason is critically applicable to diverse historically formed religions. Interpreting traditions through pure moral religion responds to the problem of actualizing principles of practical reason in the world. For Kant, the final purpose in the interpretation of holy books is the moral improvement of human beings and the actualization of the highest good in the world.

articles.t: Powers and Abilities in Early Modern Philosophy ed. by Sebastian Bender and Dominik Perler (review)
Mandeville’s Fable: Pride, Hypocrisy, and Sociability by Robin Douglass (review)
The Role of Intention in Anton Wilhelm Amo’s Philosophical Project
articles.ab: abstract: We provide the first in-depth analysis of Anton Wilhelm Amo ’s 1734 Tractatus de Arte Sobrie et Accurate Philosophandi by examining the fundamental role that intention plays in this work. Specifically, we argue that the “Intentional Principle, ” which states that everything that exists (except for God) is the effect of an intentional action, is key to understanding his account of the operations of human and divine spirits and his account of what exists (and why). In doing so, we demonstrate that Amo was a systematic thinker who grounded his philosophy in intention. Furthermore, we show that intentions are key to understanding Amo ’s views on what the ends of philosophy are and how philosophical inquiry ought to be pursued.

articles.t: Leibniz’s Metaphysics of Elasticity: From the System to the Individual
articles.ab: abstract: This paper explores the metaphysical significance of Leibniz ’s conception of elasticity and its development during the 1680s. The first part is devoted to the discussion of elasticity as a system property in the Hypothesis physica nova of 1671. A second section shows the transition, in the second half of the 1670s, from such a conception to an understanding of elasticity as a condition for the spontaneity and individuality of bodies. Finally, through an examination of writings from the 1680s about the transmission of sound and the elastic properties of materials, I will reconstruct the underlying metaphysical framework characterizing Leibniz ’s conception of elastic matter, namely the idea of a “mechanical mirroring ” which is proper to individual bodies.

articles.t: Aristotle’s Nondialectical Inquiry into Friendship in the Eudemian Ethics
articles.ab: abstract: The discussion of friendship in Eudemian Ethics VII is often taken as evidence that Aristotle relies on dialectic in this treatise. I argue that, although he uses some dialectical resources, these are insufficient for fully developing his account of friendship. His approach has four features: the arguments are philosophical, aiming at the nature and truth of friendship; he appeals to phainomena , including both endoxic and non-endoxic claims; resolving aporiai requires substantive philosophical knowledge; and, guided by epistemic optimism, he seeks to preserve what is true in existing beliefs. This contrasts with dialectical argument, which reasons from endoxic premises without aiming at endoxic conclusions.

articles.t: Spinoza in Germany: Political and Religious Thought Across the Long Nineteenth Century ed. by Jason Maurice Yonover and Kristin Gjesdal (review)
Return of the Gods: Mythology in Romantic Philosophy and Literature by Owen Ware (review)
Aristotle’s Practical Epistemology by Dhananjay Jagannathan (review)
Albert the Great on the Soul and Its Powers
articles.ab: abstract: Many scholars hold that Albert the Great favors a distinction theory of the soul and its powers. According to this theory, the soul is a substance, while its powers are qualities. In this paper, I challenge this interpretation. I argue that Albert takes the soul itself to be the power to vivify the body. I also show that, for Albert, such powers as sight, which are qualities distinct from the soul, depend on this basic vivifying power. To this end, I expound Albert ’s claim that the power to vivify is “determined and specified ” by such powers as sight.

articles.t: Bayesianism and the Inferential Solution to Hume's Problem
articles.ab: I examine Howson’s alluring suggestion that Bayesianism, by supplying a logic of inductive inference—conditionalisation—solves the problem of induction. I draw on his historical heritage, especially Hume, Peirce, and Ramsey, to reconstruct the interpretation of the problem of induction that his remarks intimates. Roughly, it is that of how to amend the system with which one meets the world, in the light of new particulars. Unfortunately, his claim that conditionalisation constitutes a solution to this problem, I argue, fails by his own lights, because it turns on the widely endorsed but nonetheless erroneous contention that a justification of conditionalisation qua rule of inference can be given independently from a justification of the priors.

articles.t: Three Ontological Options for the Laws of the Best System
articles.ab: What, ontologically speaking, are best system laws? Should the laws of the best system account be identified with sentences, or propositions, or perhaps something else? These questions differ from more familiar questions about which criteria we should use to pick out the best system laws: regardless of whether laws are picked out using simplicity, informativeness, tractability, predictability, perfect naturalness, or whatever, there remains the question of what, ontologically, the best system laws are. But very little has been written on this issue; and what has been written is often ambiguous. So in this paper, we present and evaluate three ontological options for best system laws: taking them to be sentences, unstructured propositions, and structured propositions. Surprisingly, the two most cited options—sentences and unstructured propositions—face significant problems. Defenders of the best system account might want to take seriously the idea that best system laws are structured propositions.

articles.t: Speaking for Haecceitists
articles.ab: Haecceitism is the thesis that some truths are not necessitated by the qualitative truths. In this paper I explore a general argument that purports to establish that haecceitism leads to objectionably 'cheap' violations of determinism. In response to this argument, I develop a novel position that combines considerations from metaphysics and the philosophy of language to secure the compatibility of haecceitism and determinism. This position has important parallels to the way haecceitism has been developed within counterpart theory, but, crucially, it makes no use of counterpart theory itself.

articles.t: Between the Particular and the Universal: an Ishrāqī theory of imagination
articles.ab: In this paper, I offer a modern adaptation of a theory of imagination that we can find in the writings of Shihāb al-Dīn Suhrawardī (1154–1191) and his followers in the Ishrāqī tradition (‘illuminationism’). I turn to this philosophical tradition because it offers a rare historical example of a type of theory that treats imagination as a primary source of knowledge. That is, on the Ishrāqī account, even an ideal human knower must know certain things via imagination. What I offer is a ‘modern adaptation’ of the theory in that I try to extract the theory of imagination from the cosmological and theological framework of the Ishrāqī thought. The resulting theory is still Ishrāqī in that it relies on a unique form of Platonism about knowledge that, I suggest, we can find in Suhrawardī's writings. Finally, I discuss how the reconstructed Ishrāqī conception of imaginative knowledge is especially appealing as a theory of moral knowledge.

articles.t: Fear and Loathing in Silicon Valley:Does AI Threaten our Valuing Practices?
articles.ab: We often have a visceral negative reaction to the prospect of AI taking over our creative activities or being used to demonstrate care and concern. What justifies this reaction? In this paper, I argue that AI raises two existential threats to our valuing practices. The first existential threat is forward-looking—when we offload our labor onto AI, we risk flattening our valuing landscape, turning activities and products that could have once been valued for the meaningful processes that resulted in their creation into things that can only be valued for their functionality. The second threat is backward-looking—AI forces us to reckon with the valuing discord that already exists in our lives. When we see that other people don’t care about whether the art or writing they’re consuming is AI-produced, we must reckon with the fact that they never shared in our valuing practices.

articles.t: Colonial Injustice and Self-Respect
articles.ab: What explains the necessary wrong of colonialism? I argue that colonial institutions unfairly treat the colonized as if they are moral inferiors, which consequently diminishes colonized peoples' social bases of self-respect. Because colonizers politically subjugate colonized peoples, colonial institutions permeate colonized peoples' basic structures of society. But colonial institutions degradingly treat the colonized as moral inferiors. So, these institutions unjustly diminish colonized individuals' social bases of self-respect. This result shows that, contra some recent philosophical discussion, colonialism is necessarily wrong for substantive—as opposed to merely procedural—reasons. After replying to several objections, I argue that my self-respect approach is superior to Stilz's (2019), Ypi's (2013), and Ferguson and Veneziani's (2021) accounts of colonialism's necessary wrong. Finally, I describe my view's implications for future work on just war theory, self-determination, and social oppression.

articles.t: The Agentic Value of Intrusive Thoughts
articles.ab: This paper investigates the relationship between the content of one's intrusive thoughts—such as intentionally swerving into oncoming traffic—and one's values. I first consider two approaches that are already on the table within empirical and philosophical literature – either one's intrusive thoughts indicate a moral failure of the person who has them, or they are to be seen as noise and to be disregarded.
