Differently put, I propose that negligence has a positive counterpart, which I dub “posigence.” To motivate this proposal, I introduce cases in which an agent has sufficient reason to act in a way that promotes her own well-being but sets back (or at least, fails to promote) the interests of another, but inadvertently omits to do so, manifesting therein good quality of will.

articles.t: Book review
“Bullshit, broadly construed”
articles.ab: Abstract Frankfurt’s well-known analysis is useful for understanding bullshit assertions in spoken and written language. But the term “bullshit” is routinely applied to a wider range of phenomena. Paper work is bullshit. Textbook prices are bullshit. Airport security lines are bullshit. Even within the realm of language, Frankfurt’s analysis applies straightforwardly only to utterances that purport to aim at the truth. Yet, bullshit is possible not only in speech acts other than assertion, but also in conversational contexts where truth—even for assertions—is not the goal. I argue that Frankfurt’s essay contains the resources for a generalized theory of bullshit that encompasses the full range of phenomena, and of which the classic Frankfurtian analysis is a special instance. I contrast the account with other adaptations of Frankfurt’s approach. I conclude by exploring the important role that the concept of bullshit can play in debating and evaluating our practices more generally.

articles.t: Book review
Artificial power, domination and control of humanity’s future
articles.ab: Abstract In the face of rapidly improving AI capabilities, AI theorists have warned about the risks of ceding power to autonomous artificial agents. In particular, going sufficiently far down this path might mean ‘losing control of our future’: an outcome some have ranked as a worst-case catastrophe nearly on par with human extinction. A natural way to motivate this judgment is via the thought that losing human control might lead to our domination by future AI systems. Republican political philosophers such as Pettit have held that domination characteristically involves important kinds of harms, even when the dominating party is benevolent and non-interfering. Is this thought correct? After developing an account of what it means to control humanity’s future, I show that AI systems possessing such control would indeed be likely to dominate humans on our best theories of arbitrary power. However, contrary to republican orthodoxy, I argue that this need not lead to two of the three primary harms traditionally associated with domination: the psychological and social costs of subordination, and the burden of obligatory strategic behavior. Meanwhile, the third harm—pervasive uncertainty about interference—remains a serious concern even in otherwise human-friendly AI power scenarios. These results should be of interest to theoretical political philosophy, as they suggest that artificial power has unique features which are as yet underrepresented in discussions of domination.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

articles.t: Consciousness as Representing One’s Mind: The Higher-Order Approach to Consciousness Explained
Synergy and disagreement
articles.ab: Abstract Synergy effects are taken to occur if equally well-informed and competent people agree, or nearly agree, that a certain proposition is true (or that it is false); these people should then take their agreement as confirmation that their reasoning has been correct and adopt an even greater (or lower) credence towards the issue under debate. Thus understood, synergy effects appear to occur quite frequently. The paper argues that a necessary condition for synergy effects to occur is that we cannot take our evidence at face value. This might happen either because we should be epistemically cautious in cases of presumed asymmetrical proneness to error (cases in which the relevant evidence supports either credence 1 or credence 0 towards the proposition at issue are the prime examples hereof); or because background information rules out the option supported by our remaining evidence. This result preserves the intuitive appeal of considerations on synergy but significantly restricts their scope. It thereby also reconciles considerations on synergy with a natural interpretation of conciliatory views on peer disagreement.

articles.t: The Social Contract: Political Equality from Putney to Rawls
Epistemic charity examined
articles.ab: Abstract Epistemic charity says that we should (or may) interpret others in the most favourable way consistent with the evidence. Though this could be refined in several ways, this paper develops an argument against all of them, insofar as they endorse a certain ‘signature’ of charity, where the favourable interpretation is combined with an acknowledgement of, and uncertainty over, countervailing evidence. Though initially plausible, the signature is susceptible to a version of triviality arguments prominent in the literature on conditionals. The second half of the paper evaluates responses to the argument and generalizations of it to other default epistemic rules. Ultimately, a resolution is suggested, requiring that the friend of epistemic charity combine their optimism with realism in a different way, via fragmented states of mind.

articles.t: How precaution should track uncertainty in animal sentience judgements
articles.ab: Abstract Debates about animal sentience often appeal to precaution: where the evidence of sentience is strong enough, taxa should be treated as sentient in law and policy. I argue that what is called ‘evidence of sentience’ in fact has two dimensions—robustness of indicators and credibility of the indicator–sentience link—and that standard, threshold-based formulations of precaution ignore this structure. Using a simple model, I show that conjunctive high-threshold rules are over-conservative and excessively fragile, and I sketch an inverse-threshold-with-floors principle better suited to sentience policy.

articles.t: The Mind that Matters
articles.ab: Abstract What kind of mind is necessary and sufficient for moral status—for having interests that matter morally in and of themselves? This paper defends Affective Sentientism, the view that moral status requires the capacity for affective experiences such as pleasure, pain, and emotion. I argue that affective consciousness is what makes an entity a welfare subject, and that all and only welfare subjects have moral status. The connection between affect and welfare is systematic: I show that every major candidate welfare good has an affective component, often because such goods require the capacity to care. I also argue that even if the properties of being phenomenally conscious, being autonomous, or having a neutral level of welfare could come apart from affective consciousness, none of them could ground moral status in its absence. I conclude by exploring the implications for the moral status of animals and artificial intelligence systems.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: Epistemic communities
articles.ab: Abstract This paper investigates the concept of epistemic community. Despite its frequent usage, the term lacks a clear and unified characterization. I argue that epistemic communities are essential to understanding how individuals form justified beliefs in contexts of epistemic dependence. Through an extensive review of prominent theorists, I demonstrate that epistemic communities are often used to ground trust, justify testimony, and structure the distribution of epistemic resources and norms. I propose a functional definition: an epistemic community is a group that shares epistemic norms and resources through networks of epistemic dependence. These communities range from local, tight-knit groups to diffuse, societal structures, and can confer either epistemic value or distortion. I show that epistemic communities are not just descriptive units but normative forces in belief formation.

articles.t: The Heart and its Attitudes
The Ubiquity of Humor
articles.ab: Abstract I defend the Ubiquity of Humor thesis (UH), according to which every situation admits of a perspective from which its humorous features become visible. I argue that humor, on any plausible theory, attaches to relational features present in every actual situation, and that the perspectives required to perceive them are always available. Accepting this explains why we speak of humor as something one has a “sense” for, why a good sense of humor is an aesthetic accomplishment, why funniness connects unstably to truth, and why the capacity we admire in those who find adversity funny is the one we condemn in those amused when they shouldn’t. Alternatives to UH either fail to account for these things or are otherwise flawed. I also address the most pressing objections, including that UH implausibly classifies horrific or mundane cases as funny and that its reasoning overgeneralizes to all aesthetic value.

articles.t: The Joy of Chinese Philosophy
articles.ab: Michael Beaney (畢明安) is best known for his work in the history of analytic philosophy. In recent years, Beaney has extended his research focus to ancient Chinese logic and philosophy, seeking to establish a profound dialogue between Western and Chinese philosophies. He contends that rich analytic traditions exist within ancient Chinese philosophy, which concern themselves with paradoxes, the meaning of language, and the validity of inference. The Joy of Chinese Philosophy focuses on the ‘Dialogue on the Joy of Fish’ (濠梁之辯) at the end of the ‘Autumn Waters’ chapter of the Zhuangzi—a conversation of barely over a hundred characters that has sparked two millennia of debate. The book comprises nine chapters with a highly ingenious structural design. Beaney suggests that readers begin with the two ‘inner’ chapters (Chapters 4 and 5) and then gradually expand outwards. Chapter 4 provides a meticulous conceptual analysis of eight keywords in the dialogue: yóu (遊 – roaming), lè (樂 – joy), chū (出 –coming out), zhī (知 – knowing), běn (本 – root/original), gù (固 – certainly/firmly), ān (安 – how/where), and yú (魚 – fish). It demonstrates the multiple connotations of each Chinese character in classical Chinese and their subtle applications within the dialogue. Chapter 5 systematically examines eight representative interpretations: playful, literary, mystical, contextualist, phenomenological, Western logical, Mohist logical, and species-relativist, before proposing his own ‘connective conceptual analysis’, concerned with the movement not from something to its parts, premises, or paraphrasings but to its connections to appropriate things in the wider whole or system.
topics: Environmental and Cultural Studies in Latin America and Beyond

articles.t: Emotional outsourcing
articles.ab: Abstract Prompting a chatbot to write an apology or a love letter on your behalf is a form of emotional outsourcing—an act in which a person gives over a process paradigmatically expressive of emotions or interpersonal commitments to another entity or person to complete on their behalf. This paper explores the features of emotional outsourcing in the context of interpersonal communication. We argue that troubling, or dissonant, cases of outsourcing involve the absence of relevant parties from the emotional work of that relationship (‘the missing person problem’). This omission prevents certain relational goods from obtaining, including those necessary for the social formation of one’s personal identity. Far from allowing one to achieve a quality product, outsourcing one’s interpersonal writing can thus prevent important aims of that writing from coming about. We end by contrasting dissonant outsourcing with avenues for resonant outsourcing through shared participation in communal linguistic practices.

articles.t: Evidentialism and the epistemic condition on evidence possession
articles.ab: Abstract An important question for evidentialism is: what does it take to have evidence? Feldman (2004) and McGrath (2018) argue that evidence possession requires more than psychological access—it must also satisfy an epistemic condition, such as being justified. In this paper, I argue that the epistemic condition either results in a problematic regress or denies internalism unless one distinguishes between two senses of evidence possession. Developing this distinction helps to clarify the structure and nature of our evidence. In particular, it shows that one’s evidence, at a fundamental level, is self-supporting and consists of one’s mental states rather than their propositional contents.

articles.t: Against individualistic accounts of group belief
articles.ab: Abstract We often ascribe beliefs to groups, institutions, companies, and similar social entities, and many philosophers inquire into the nature of such beliefs. While different accounts have been proposed, many agree that group belief should be analysed in terms of the behaviour and the attitudes of the group’s members. In this paper, I raise a principled worry against such individualistic accounts of group belief. The basic concern is that individualistic accounts of group belief cannot be squared with existing accounts of the nature of belief from the philosophy of mind, such as dispositionalism and functionalism. My focus will be on group belief, but parallel concerns can be raised for individualistic accounts of group justified belief, group knowledge, and group assertion.

articles.t: Racism : Word, concept, and the pairing-dependence question
articles.ab: Abstract The debate over the inflation of racism should be understood not as a disagreement about first-order facts, but as a set of competing answers to the Pairing-Dependence Question (PDQ): why should a particular concept of racism be expressed by ‘racism’? Once PDQ is made explicit, prominent defences of inflation that appeal to explanatory power prove unsuccessful. Explanatory considerations may justify representing structural injustice with a concept, yet they underdetermine which word should express that concept. I conclude that inflation was presumptively unjustified because it exposed a term with entrenched moral-pragmatic significance to avoidable evaluative risk, given that the wider concept which it expresses could have been expressed by another term instead.

articles.t: Affective uncertainty
articles.ab: Abstract Uncertainty shapes what we believe, how we act, and how we live—and it also affects our emotions, with important implications for private and public life. This paper develops an account of affective uncertainty, which arises when competing appropriate emotions leave us unsure how to feel overall—what I call affective dilemmas. Despite its significance, affective uncertainty has been largely overlooked by philosophers of uncertainty, who focus on epistemic and moral uncertainty, and by philosophers of emotion, who often adopt a narrower view of affective normativity. I argue that affective uncertainty is irreducible to epistemic or moral uncertainty, as it stems from affective incommensurability—the incommensurability of the values that justify different emotions. I suggest that existing uncertainty frameworks—including those for normative uncertainty—fail to address it, and that in some cases affective ambivalence may be the appropriate response.

articles.t: Non-moral blame
articles.ab: Abstract A lot of blame is very obviously moral. But what about the cases that aren’t so obvious? I might appear to blame you for your bad art, your prudentially bad actions, or your bad cooking. Some take the view that even though there are genuine non-moral values in the world, there’s no genuine non-moral blame. According to them, the instances above are either cases of moral blame (carefully disguised) or they’re not actually blame at all. This paper argues against that view. Real cases of non-moral blame are common. I make this argument in a number of ways, including by making the case for why moral and non-moral blame are often intertwined, and why that shouldn’t put off our intuitions, and by showing that non-moral blame is structurally similar in every way to moral blame except for the value in question.

articles.t: Shame and Being Looked Down Upon
articles.ab: Abstract People sometimes experience shame in response to being looked down upon, despite rejecting the negative attitudes taken towards them by others. I aim to explain why—while also holding onto the idea that shame is a response to an apparent flaw in oneself. At the heart of my proposal is the idea that many people treat being well-regarded by specific communities of others as a personal ideal. I defend this account against an objection from Calhoun, namely that it conflicts with the claim that shame in response to oppression is generally rational. On the contrary, I argue that we can only fully make sense of what is bad about such shame by abandoning this claim. Finally, I contrast my view with an alternative based on the ideal of ‘self-presentation’. I object that this fails to emphasize the importance of the negative valence of being looked down upon.

articles.t: Computing machinery and causal intelligence
articles.ab: Abstract This paper develops an argument inspired by Judea Pearl for the view that deep learning models are incapable of causal reasoning. The argument embraces Pearl’s conclusion but rejects his approach, which focuses on a mini-Turing test restricted to causal questions. The argument presented draws on the traditional debate between empiricism and nativism, presenting a challenge for the sort of empiricism that has been associated with deep learning. The paper then considers an objection based on the fact that large language models perform fairly well on various causal benchmarks. In response to this point, a diagnosis is offered of how such models’ performance might be explained without attributing to them genuine causal reasoning abilities. The paper concludes by connecting the discussion to the limitations of the original Turing test and familiar critiques of behaviorism.

articles.t: On aesthetics and stereotypes
articles.ab: Abstract Murdoch (1970), Nussbaum (1990), and Simoniti (2023) say our capacity to apprehend aesthetic properties is morally helpful: they think it helps us resist stereotypes and other obstacles to seeing other people as they really are, and as individual subjects. I argue that this is not the full story: aesthetic properties can actually encourage us to use stereotypes, and irrationally influence which features we stereotypically associate with a group. The mere inclusion of aesthetic properties within stereotypes, alongside everyday aesthetic perception in the background of our interaction with others, can: 1. Make stereotypes come to mind more easily; 2. Make them appear more plausible; 3. Irrationally influence which features a stereotype most prominently associates with a group; 4. Make it easier to infer from someone having one feature ascribed in a stereotype to their having other characteristics the stereotype ascribes; 5. Make the influence of stereotypes on our thoughts relatively incorrigible.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: Age-weighted democracy
articles.ab: Abstract The slogan “one person, one vote” is held to be essential to democracy. I argue, against its standard interpretation, that the power of one’s vote should decline with age. The idea of relational equality it expresses is ambiguous, in ways currently unappreciated, between synchronic and diachronic conceptions. The standard interpretation is that voters must relate as equals synchronically in each election. I argue that they can do so diachronically, across elections. From the original position, rational people would prefer a voting procedure giving more weight to their younger selves. The argument turns on the asymmetrical structure of political authority between cohorts: older cohorts influence the formative conditions of younger ones in ways the young can never reciprocate. Age-weighted voting addresses this asymmetry, concentrating more of our overall political influence on the parts of our lives that we live to experience. The strongest counterargument is committed to a form of epistocracy.

articles.t: Personal Identity and the Self
articles.ab: IThis excellent, substantive and original book (building on Madden 2016) has four sections.In section 1, Madden argues that the best formulation of the topic of the book is not given by its title (!) but by the irredeemably perspectival question, 'What are we?'.Section 2 considers a 'no-bearer' theory of experience, which answers the question 'What are we?' with 'Nothing'.This is rejected, and section 2 ends by introducing the view Madden endorses, 'hybrid animalism'.This is a version of the popular animalist theory that we are animals, presented as a theory of our persistence with a 'best candidate' structure.Madden then defends hybrid animalism in section 3.In the final section 4, Madden confronts the popular 'multiplicity' challenges to animalism: thinking animal parts, dicephalus cases and split-brain cases, endorsing a version of functionalism -teleological functionalism (Madden 2024: 58) -as a way of responding.His treatment of dicephalus cases and split-brain cases is particularly interesting.He argues that it is consistent with animalism that the Hensel twins are two animals.This is because of their distinct, neurologically based, psychology, which, in accord with his hybrid view of personal persistence, matters.On the other hand, split-brain patients are one animal since the lack of psychological unity they display is not enough to disqualify them (just as a football team remains one team when its players are divided in the middle of a match into two non-communicating groups by the descent of a thick fog (Madden 2024: 69)).I will focus on the core section 3, where Madden defends his own version of animalism.I explain why I am unconvinced.

articles.t: Belief-that, belief-in, and the unity of belief
articles.ab: Abstract The English ‘believe,’ like equivalents in many languages, gets used in several ways: ‘believe in me,’ ‘believe me,’ ‘believe my claim,’ ‘believe that p.’ It might seem that all the attitudes in question reduce to belief-that. I argue for a very different view. Linguistic data suggests that ‘believe’ in all its uses refers to an attitude which is closest to belief-in, although belief-in is just one particularly strong variety of it. This general attitude is one of reliant commitment, which I call by its Ancient Greek name, pistis. The use of ‘believe’ for belief-that thus reveals a folk conception of belief-that as pistis: pistis in a representation or its content, qua guide to or part of reality. I argue that this conception is promising: it yields an account of belief that explains its relation to knowledge, truth, and action, and can help resolve debates about its nature and its norms.

articles.t: What is the format of pre-attentive vision?
articles.ab: Abstract A current debate in the philosophy of cognitive science centers around the representational format of visual processing prior to the deployment of focused visual attention. Recent work has argued that pre-attentive vision’s properties imply it represents in a map-like format. This argument is based on the empirical phenomena of conjunctive illusions and conjunction searches. In this paper, I argue instead that we should adopt an iconic view of pre-attentive vision, where it represents in a picture-like format. I’ll first argue that the map-like view cannot accommodate a certain type of phenomenon in the pre-attentive vision literature: gist perception. I argue that gist perception implies a holistically bound format and that this favors the iconic view. Second, I’ll argue that conjunctive illusions and conjunction search can be explained by means other than positing map-like representations in early vision.

articles.t: Book Review
Book Review
Book Review
Instrumentalism and higher-order defeat
articles.inst: The University of Texas at Austin
articles.ab: Abstract Standard accounts of higher-order defeat run into well-known Bayesian hurdles. In this paper, I explore the prospects of overcoming those hurdles by applying a thoroughgoing instrumentalist approach: treating our reasoning capacities as we’d treat any other instrument. I argue that instrumentalism cannot coherently accommodate the defeatist’s position when that position involves genuine higher-order uncertainty—that is, rational uncertainty about what rationality requires. At the end of the paper I gesture at an approach to modeling our responses to defeaters that is both instrumentalist and Bayesian, but that abandons the thought that the cases typically described as cases of higher-order defeat involve genuinely higher-order uncertainty.

articles.t: A Humean account of temporal preferences
articles.ab: Abstract Two central questions regarding future bias are (a) why we are future-biased, and (b) whether future bias is justified. With respect to (a), I propose a Humean explanation of future bias in terms of the workings of the imagination, which makes our imaginings of future events more vivid than our imaginings of past events. However, in order to defend this explanation, a potential tension within Humean psychology needs to be resolved: since, per Hume, memory is more vivid than imagination, we ought to be past-biased. My proposed resolution makes use of Hume’s mechanism of sympathy (when applied to one’s own future self). With respect to (b), I argue that, rather than focusing on the question of rationality, we should focus on whether future bias is a virtue, by considering, in a Humean spirit, how agents’ temporal preferences affect others, when assessed from ‘the general point of view’.

articles.t: A note on mereological extensionality principles
articles.ab: Abstract This paper is a small contribution to the study of extensionality principles in mereology. We argue that the extensionality of composition logically implies the extensionality of parthood, and that this entailment persists in the presence of weak supplementation even if we restrict the former principle to cases of proper composition.

articles.t: Introduction to the Special Issue of The Philosophical Quarterly on Uncertainty
articles.ab: Abstract

articles.t: Principles across distant worlds? A reply to Yoshimura
articles.ab: Abstract This discussion note challenges Yoshiki Yoshimura’s recent attempt to defend Scanlonian contractualism against the distant world objection. While Yoshimura’s amended contractualism initially appears capable of avoiding the objection, I argue that his proposal ultimately falls short in certain relevant cases. Moreover, I suggest that attempts to revise the view reveal a deeper problem for Yoshimura’s overall strategy that has important implications for principle-based views more generally.

articles.t: Philosophy of Education in Dialogue between East and West: Japanese Insights and Perspectives
Book review
Pragmatist Quietism: A Meta-Ethical System
Hermeneutic decentering
articles.ab: This paper identifies a phenomenon called hermeneutic dismissiveness, which it positions in relation to willful hermeneutical ignorance (Pohlhaus 2012), hermeneutical clashes (Falbo 2022), and ameliorative conceptual engineering (e.g. Haslanger 2000). It then develops a generalized version of Iris Murdoch's (1970) notion of unselfing, for which I use the term decentering: this involves decentering not just one's (individual) self but also the (collective) “we”s with which one identifies. Hermeneutic decentering is then discussed as a kind of work that might serve to counteract hermeneutic dismissiveness, through an application of what Murdoch calls “attention to reality inspired by, consisting of, love” (Murdoch 1969: 65). The paper concludes with a brief discussion of some of the obstacles to hermeneutic decentering, and reflections on how these might be addressed.

articles.t: Reason in tranquility: Hume's critique of superstition
articles.ab: This paper examines a tension in Hume's philosophy between his epistemic critique of superstition and his naturalistic epistemology. While Hume faults superstition for its epistemic flaws, naturalistic interpretations often claim that he evaluates reasoning by its psychological force, such as liveliness or irresistibility. This raises a challenge: if superstitious reasoning stems from standard psychological processes and exhibits psychological strength, how can it be epistemically discredited? I argue that Hume's notion of good reasoning involves more than psychological force. He appeals to calm passions as an additional normative standard. Calm passions arise in response to epistemic factors, particularly certainty, whereas superstitious reasoning provokes violent passions through its uncertainty. Importantly, however, calmness does not require absolute certainty, and it marks a moderate and attainable level of epistemic commitment—one that enables inquiry while resisting the violent agitation characteristic of both superstition and radical skepticism.

articles.t: Book review
Question-centred consequentialism
articles.ab: Objective consequentialism provides a deceptively simple standard for choosing between alternatives: you should perform the best alternative. But sometimes there are different sets of alternatives, and the best alternative in one set is incompatible with the best alternative in another set. So, what should you do? This is the classic problem of act versions. In this paper, I argue against the extant candidate solutions to this problem, and I provide a new solution. According to my proposed solution, there is one set of alternatives that is relevant for determining right and wrong. An act is obligatory just in case it is the best relevant alternative, and an act is right just in case it entails the best alternative. This consequentialism resolves the problem of act versions and motivates a weak logic of obligation.

articles.t: Cognitive noise generates higher-order uncertainty
articles.ab: Some of our judgments under uncertainty are clear and reliable—how likely do you think this fair coin is to land heads? Others are ambiguous and noisy—how likely do you think I am to own a dozen spoons? I propose that ambiguity is higher-order uncertainty: subjective probabilistic uncertainty about our own subjective probabilities. I show that such higher-order uncertainty is mathematically coherent and would be behaviorally significant—predicting forms of bias (violations of “Reflection’’ principles) disallowed by virtually all Bayesian models in cognitive science. But if we do have higher-order uncertainty, why can’t we resolve it simply by acting? Because cognitive noise makes the link between subjective probabilities and behavior stochastic. I summarize the empirical evidence for this, describe a popular model of it, argue that reasonable agents should be expected to exhibit cognitive noise when and only when they have higher-order uncertainty, and report on a new experiment showing that higher-order uncertainty predicts cognitive noise.

articles.t: Satisficing, maximizing, and bounded rationality
articles.ab: It is often argued that maximizing normative theories are inappropriate for bounded agents. I argue that leading motivations for theories of bounded rationality are substantially compatible with some traditional maximizing normative theories. This finding expands the audience for theories of bounded rationality by making room for advocates of maximizing normative theories, and has implications for knowledge-action principles, the relationship between descriptive and normative theorizing, and the definitions of central tenets of bounded rationality.

articles.t: What Is Time?
articles.ab: Abstract Augustine says that he knows what time is as long as no one asks him to say what time is. Many of us are in the same boat. Nevertheless, M. Oreste Fiocco, in his Time and the World: Every Thing and Then Some, attempts to answer the question What is time?. I argue that his answer falls short of actually saying what time is. Then I consider the standard way to answer this question, according to which time is one of four more or less similar dimensions that make up a unified manifold appropriately called spacetime. I offer several arguments against this view. I also consider several other proposals, including the claim that there is no such thing as time, and the claim that time is a logical construction out of maximal, consistent propositions. But in the end I defend an answer to our question according to which time is best understood as a complicated and multifaceted dimension of reality (akin to the modal and moral dimensions) that is concerned with the ways reality has been, is, or will be.

articles.t: Another Failed Modal Collapse Argument
articles.ab: Abstract The doctrine of divine simplicity says that God is not composed of parts (physical or metaphysical). Modal collapse arguments aim to show that the necessary co-existence of God and creation follows from the doctrine. As noted by Christopher Tomaszewski, R. T. Mullins’s version of this argument assumes that a crucial term occurring within its premises is rigid, leaving the argument invalid or question begging. I examine a recent attempt by Mullins to repair his argument and defend the rigidity of this term. Mullins assumes a test for discerning rigidity on which he and Tomaszewski agree. I argue that this test is false and then provide a new test. My test bodes ill for modal collapse arguments in general.

articles.t: Inquiry and deception
articles.ab: Abstract We all have been deceived, whether by politicians, pundits or peers. Likely more often than we would wish to admit. But what is it to be deceived? As we argue, victims of deception settle on a false answer to a question. This settling proposal not only makes good on the intuitive idea that sceptical agents are harder to deceive than their non-sceptical peers, but also finds support in the infelicity of reporting an agent as both inquiring and deceived. Want to avoid being duped? Our proposal provides an answer: inquire further, don’t settle.

articles.t: A Mereological Slingshot
articles.ab: Abstract I examine a package of views about facts: (1) the mereological sum of two facts is their conjunction, (2) the sum of facts obeys the laws of classical mereology, (3) facts are closed under disjunction and (4) facts are identical when they necessarily co-obtain. I show that this package of principles collapses: they jointly entail that there is at most one fact. I discuss four possible solutions, each consisting in the rejection of one of the principles.

articles.t: Partial truth and subject-matter: a difficult marriage
articles.ab: Abstract The idea that partial truth is just truth of a part cannot be defended unless a theory of propositional parthood is put forward. Since it is known that truth-conditional implication cannot play that role, subject-matters have been used to fuel a two-component theory of propositional parthood. Can this yield a satisfactory theory of partial truth? We show that such an ambition conflicts with natural logical constraints for partial truth.

articles.t: Abilities as Modal Ties?
articles.ab: Abstract The idea that abilities should be understood as a modal tie between one's motivational states and one's actions is at the core of the most prominent views of abilities. I develop a novel challenge against such views of ability arguing that all these accounts cannot properly account for inabilities and compulsions.

articles.t: Risk attitudes when choosing for others
articles.ab: Abstract This paper provides a defense of the principle ‘avoid risk for others:’ when a person’s risk-attitudes are unknown, it is wrong to take, on their behalf, some of the risks that they could rationally choose to take.

articles.t: Against the standard semantics for ‘all’ and ‘every’
articles.ab: Abstract This paper presents a new problem for the standard semantics for ‘all’ and ‘every’ on which ‘every F is G’ and ‘all Fs are Gs’ are true just in case the set of things that satisfy ‘F’ is a subset of the set of things that satisfy ‘G’. I argue that the standard semantics makes highly counterintuitive predictions about what credences it is rational to adopt in a generalisation ‘every F is G’ when we are confident but not certain that nothing is F. I show how, unlike the better known counterintuitive result that if nothing is F, ‘every F is G’ is true, this problem cannot be avoided by appealing to pragmatic principles, nor by rejecting some orthodox principles about the relationship between credences and propositions.

articles.t: Individual Intentions in Shared Intention
articles.ab: Abstract There is disagreement among philosophers about the following claim: when we share an intention to perform some action, we each have an intention towards that action. That disagreement turns on the interpretation of thought experiments, specifically whether reports of a shared intention are accurate in cases in which one of the participants lacks a participatory intention. We subject the standard interpretations of thought experiments to empirical testing. Our results suggest that attributions of shared intentions are appropriate only when each individual has a participatory intention, supporting accounts of shared intention that include participatory intentions as a necessary component.

articles.t: The Polar Conception of Vagueness
articles.ab: Abstract In his 1990 lecture ‘Concepts without boundaries’, Mark Sainsbury presents a system that he calls the polar conception of vague concepts. In this paper, it is demonstrated that the polar conception naturally gives rise to a weaker than classical logic -- namely, a quantum logic characterised by the failure of the law of distribution -- based on the relation of proximity to polar cases. After the quantum account is presented, it is suggested that the rejection of the law of distribution is well motivated in the context of vagueness.

articles.t: Please Mind the Gap: Two Problems for the Constitutive Theory of Inference
articles.ab: Christopher Blake-Turner; Please Mind the Gap: Two Problems for the Constitutive Theory of Inference, Analysis, , anaf069, https://doi.org/10.1093/analys/a

articles.t: The Lottery Problem for Ranking Theory
articles.ab: Abstract Ranking Theory has been developed as an alternative to subjec- tive probability for modelling partial belief. It goes further than probability in that it jointly models both full and partial belief. One selling feature is that the Lottery Paradox does not arise in Ranking Theory. However, all is not well when it comes to modelling lottery beliefs with ranks. In this paper, I show how lotteries create problems for Ranking Theory.

articles.t: Values as Evidence in the Sciences
articles.ab: Abstract Ethical statements can sometimes serve as legitimate evidence for purely descriptive hypotheses. This role for ethical statements need involve neither wishful thinking, nor dogmatism. This is first shown using a simple example that employs thick moral concepts. A far more significant example with a similar structure is then given from within the sciences. It draws on two different committees’ deliberations about the impact of the hormonal pregnancy test Primodos.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: Constitutivism and Ideal Agency
articles.ab: Abstract According to Michael Smith’s constitutivist account, moral norms are grounded in rational requirements. These requirements, he argues, can be derived from constitutive features of ideal agency. We target a key component of Smith’s account, namely the thesis that a rationally ideal agent has intrinsic desires to help and not interfere with other agents’ rational capacities. We cast doubt on two arguments for this thesis put forward by Smith (2015, 2020).

articles.t: The Permissible Play Principle: How to ensure you are playing videogames permissibly
articles.ab: Abstract Sometimes actions that are (morally) impermissible in the actual world also seem impermissible in virtual worlds. For example, rape is impermissible in the actual world, and it also seems impermissible to direct a videogame character to rape another in a virtual world. But sometimes actions that are impermissible in the actual world seem permissible in virtual worlds. For example, stealing is impermissible in the actual world, but it may seem permissible to direct your video game character to steal another character’s possessions in a virtual world. This asymmetry has complicated the task of finding the line between permissible and impermissible gameplay. So, how should we play video games while this line remains unclear? Is there a way of playing games that ensures our actions are permissible? In this paper we consider a promising moral principle that might guarantee permissible gameplay.

articles.t: Fantasy, Pleasure, Desire, and Morality
articles.ab: Abstract It is natural to suppose that to fantasize about something is just to pleasantly imagine it, and thus that investigating the natures of imagination and pleasure is all we need to do to investigate the nature of fantasy. I argue that this picture is too simple. Even if fantasizing about something is pleasantly imagining it, it is unclear what the nature and object of the relevant pleasure are. I distinguish two natural views about this, the Activity View and the Object View, and I argue that the latter makes it easier than the former to justify two claims: that one cannot fantasize about something without desiring it, and that it can be inherently morally objectionable to fantasize about certain things. Although I suggest that we should therefore accept the Object View, my larger aim is to encourage inquiry into the nature of fantasy by illustrating how interesting it can be.

articles.t: Success Correlation and Peer Disagreement
articles.ab: Abstract You learn that you disagree about P with someone who—according to your evidence—should be your equal in discerning whether P. Some argue that rationality requires weighing your judgment and your Peer’s judgment equally. I show that this ‘equal weight view’ requires the undefended stipulation that your evidence suggests zero correlation between your success in initially determining whether P and your success in reevaluating P in the face of Peer Disagreement. I describe a Peer Disagreement in which self-trust is rationally mandated, given that this further stipulation fails. Finally, I suggest that default, asymmetric self-trust in the face of Peer Disagreement is justified, given a reasonable expectation of a baseline correlation between success in initial determinations whether P and success in reevaluations of P in the face of Peer Disagreement.

articles.t: On Two Explanatory Identity Criteria: One for Individuals, the Other for Properties
articles.ab: Abstract Many philosophers believe that identity facts are non-fundamental facts, facts grounded in other facts. In this paper, we discuss what might ground the identity facts for individuals and properties by examining two explanatory identity criteria. One criterion, which we call the Explanatory Leibniz’s Law, is for individuals. The other, which we call the Explanatory Intensional Criterion, is for properties. We argue that, when combined with the widely accepted claim that grounding chains do not contain loops, these two criteria give rise to a contradiction.

articles.t: Are all truths maximally risky?
articles.ab: Abstract According to the modal account, risk is a function of modal closeness. A puzzling consequence of this account is that all truths are maximally risky. I defend this puzzling claim against several objections found in the literature, by drawing connections between axiom T for safety and risk and between counterfactual reasoning and risk. I conclude by briefly explaining why we find the conclusion puzzling and by advocating for a pluralist notion of risk where modal risk is a legitimate notion alongside the probabilistic one.

articles.t: Kratzerian ‘want’, decision theory, and upward entailment
articles.ab: Abstract Kyle Blumberg has recently argued that (i) the ideal worlds account of desire — according to which for S to want p is for all of S's top-ranked worlds to be p-worlds — has difficulties accounting for certain cases involving the ascribee's ignorance. He takes these cases to be (ii) a reason to disprefer the Kratzerian account of `want' to its rivals, and (iii) to doubt that desire ascriptions are upward entailing. I challenge all three claims. Along the way, I motivate and develop a Kratzer-style account, according to which what a subject wants depends not just on their information and preferences, but also on the decision rule they embrace and the salient decision problem.

articles.t: What’s Wrong with Teaching Controversial Issues Directively?
articles.ab: Abstract How should controversial issues be taught in schools? In the philosophy of education, this question is often answered along the following lines: if a topic is controversial, it should be taught non-directively. A common justification for this idea is that other ways of teaching controversial issues would simply amount to indoctrination. In this paper, I would like to critically discuss this idea in more detail. More specifically, I will argue that a general categorization of directive approaches to teaching controversial issues as indoctrinatory is not as convincing as one might initially think. Against this background, I will then develop an alternative explanation for the pedagogical illegitimacy of directive approaches to teaching controversial issues. The basic idea behind this explanation is that such approaches undermine an important educational goal of teaching controversial issues by depriving students of the opportunity to arrive at well-formed judgments on these issues.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

articles.t: Belief Inertia and Awareness-Evidence Commutativity
articles.inst: London School of Economics and Political Science
articles.ab: Abstract It is alleged that imprecise probabilism can render one unable to update one’s credence in light of new evidence. While such belief inertia by itself is already quite worrying, I argue that it has other worrying epistemic implications that were previously unnoticed. It opens the possibility that one’s doxastic state depends not only on the evidence one has but also on the temporal order between awareness growth and evidence acquisition. I find this implication difficult to accept.

articles.t: Plural Expression and Converse Relations
articles.ab: Abstract Since the work of George Boolos in the 1980s, philosophers have become more comfortable making use of plural reference and plural quantification in their theorizing. Plausibly, part of the reason is that it sometimes has a philosophical payoff. Mereological nihilists, for example, can do justice to the apparent truth of everyday claims involving singular reference or singular quantification over composite objects by paraphrasing them as claims involving plural reference or plural quantification over only mereological simples. But the analogous question of whether predicates can plurally express multiple relations has not received attention. I show that answering affirmatively can have philosophical payoffs of its own, illustrating this by explaining how it allows the directionalist about relations to articulate their position in such a way that it avoids Timothy Williamson's (1985) challenge. The result is an expanded range of formal tools which the philosopher can make use of in their theorizing.

articles.t: Correction to: Distribution can be dropped: Reply to Rumfitt
Correction to: Following all the rules: Intuitionistic completeness for generalized proof-theoretic validity
What Self?
articles.ab: Maximilian Tegtmeyer; What Self?, Analysis, , anaf093, https://doi.org/10.1093/analys/anaf093

articles.t: ‘Oh Slur, Where Is Thy Sting?’
articles.ab: Gary Ostertag; ‘Oh Slur, Where is Thy Sting?’ Critical Notice of Una Stojnić and Ernie Lepore, Inflammatory Language: Its Linguistics and Philosophy, Analy

articles.t: The heuristic use of conditionalisation
articles.ab: Abstract I provide an example in which Bayesian conditionalisation fails to validate plausible claims about rational permissibility. The example suggests that conditionalisation should be treated as a heuristic principle: useful in many situations, but not all. This raises the question of how to characterise the cases in which it is appropriate to use conditionalisation. I show that one can answer this question by appealing to the framework of objective Bayesian inductive logic to provide sufficient conditions for the applicability of conditionalisation.

articles.t: Expertise and Social Epistemic Warrant
articles.ab: Abstract John Stuart Mill claims in On Liberty that the robust ability for individuals to question and dispute claims is a necessary condition for us to be justified in believing those claims. But it is not obvious why even bad objections must be allowed to be voiced. On a recent interpretation of Mill’s view, censorship of bad objections does not threaten experts’ justification, but it does threaten laypeople’s justification. Laypeople must be assured that experts are in the business of responding to objections, rather than unfairly dismissing them. But laypeople cannot tell which objections are bad, so even these must be allowed to be voiced. Here, I argue that there is no way to cordon off experts from the epistemically deleterious effects of censorship, regarding many questions of interest. If Mill’s argument is right, then, the epistemic impacts of censorship are more radical than it might seem at first glance.

articles.t: Narrow and Wide Necessity
articles.ab: Abstract There are two distinct perspectives one can take when considering the necessity constraint on defensive force: (1) which defensive option among those averting a threat would minimize harm to attackers (specifically, those potentially liable to defensive harm); and (2) which of these options would minimize harm to bystanders (specifically, those not liable to defensive harm)? This article introduces the concepts of narrow necessity for perspective (1) and wide necessity for perspective (2), following similar terminology for proportionality analysis. Currently, the ethics of defensive force literature lacks these concepts. Adopting them establishes a parallel structure for the proportionality and necessity constraints, so that both have narrow and wide perspectives. This proposal has the advantage of clarifying the scope of the necessity constraint, while also explaining paradigm violations of necessity that raise problems for competing proposals.

articles.t: Not So Simple! Primitive Concepts and the Threat of Spinozism in the Pre-Critical Kant
articles.ab: Abstract Kant’s precritical possibility proof for the existence of God is often thought to have Spinozistic implications. One important reason for this is that Kant’s reasoning in the Beweisgrund appears to entail that God is extended or spatial. Kant argues that God exemplifies all primitive predicates. Since he also treats extension as such a primitive predicate, it seems to straightforwardly follow that God is extended. This paper argues that Kant’s argument in the Beweisgrund does not, in fact, lead to this Spinozistic conclusion. Importantly, Kant distinguishes between concepts that are primitive for us and concepts that are primitive in themselves. This distinction equips Kant with the resources to block the Spinozistic conclusion that God is extended: he can accept that extension is a primitive concept for us and at the same time reject that extension is a concept primitive in itself, and thus exemplified by God.

articles.t: Making Up for What? Slavny on Corrections and Compensation
articles.ab: Giulio Fornaroli; Making Up for What? Slavny on Corrections and Compensation, Analysis, , anaf097, https://doi.org/10.1093/analys/anaf097

articles.t: Past Achievements and Future Bias
articles.ab: Abstract According to the Permissive View, it is rationally permissible for a person’s preferences to be both future-biased about pleasant experiences and temporally neutral about achievements. Some philosophers argue that, intuitive though it may be, the Permissive View can’t be right because it runs afoul of a plausible requirement for rationality: namely, that it is rationally impermissible to form one’s preferences by moving back and forth between different evaluative perspectives. Samuel Scheffler has recently attempted to show that this requirement is in fact compatible with the Permissive View. This paper casts doubt on Scheffler’s attempt. I argue that Scheffler either fails to reconcile the Permissive View with the requirement for evaluative consistency or commits himself to unacceptably counterintuitive claims.

articles.t: Could Factual Awareness Be Anything But Knowledge?
articles.ab: Henry knows there is much he can doubt even if he is aware of a tomato. A tomato in disguise might look like a tamarillo. A sneaky persimmon might be mistaken for a tomato. We can hide tomatoes in shadows or the fog where Henry might see them without being able to identify them. Confront Henry with tomatoes while he’s on ayahuasca, and he might doubt their reality. Awareness of things is not a form of knowledge. Now that that’s settled, let’s focus on awareness of facts. How is factual awareness related to factual knowledge? According to one proposal, a thinker is aware that p if she knows that p (‘A = K’ hereafter) (Unger 1975; Williamson 2000; Littlejohn 2015). This view is appealing to those who think that the mind only makes facts available to us via knowledge. People who find this view attractive typically think that reports that suggest that there are modes of awareness like visual perception that involve awareness of facts (e.g. Henry saw that the tomato was red and bulgy) are misleading if taken to be about (mere) perceptual relations and not knowledge (Gisborne 2010; French 2013; Travis 2013). In his recent book, Awareness and the Substructure of Knowledge, Silva (2023) argues that factual awareness is distinct from knowledge.

articles.t: Rational Persuasion, Effort and ‘Easy Resistibility’
articles.ab: Abstract It is standardly assumed that for it to be morally permissible to use an influence to change someone’s mental state or behaviour, that influence must be fully or substantially non-controlling. Or, as it has also been put, if an influence is not ‘easily resistible’, then we have a pro tanto reason against employing the said influence. Currently, the most dominant account of easily resistibility is effort-based, i.e. for an influence to qualify as easily resistible it must not require too much effort to resist. This paper argues that the effort-based account faces considerable challenges in that it implies that paradigmatic cases of rational persuasion are not easily resistible. Two objections to this contention are considered and ultimately rejected, and three directions for future research are suggested.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

articles.t: Awareness and Knowledge
articles.inst: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
articles.ab: You crave a gin and tonic, and you have just been served a glass containing what very clearly appears to you to be a gin and tonic. As it happens, appearances in this case are misleading: the liquid in the glass is gasoline, but there’s nothing to suggest this to you, and so you don’t suspect it at all. In such a case, we may say, there is a reason for you to refrain from drinking the contents of the glass – namely, whatever reason there is for you to refrain from drinking gasoline.1 Nonetheless, the fact that the glass contains gasoline is not a fact that, in these circumstances, can motivate you to refrain from drinking the contents of the glass, or make it rational for you to refrain from drinking the contents of the glass. Thus, even though there is a reason for you to refrain from drinking the contents of the glass, this is not a reason that you have. In the situation described, you may not have any reason to refrain from drinking the contents of the glass.

articles.t: Defending Awareness and the Substructure of Knowledge : Replies to Aronowitz, Littlejohn and Neta
articles.ab: It is difficult to convey my gratitude for the time and effort that Sara, Clayton and Ram spent on developing probing and insightful questions about Awareness and the Substructure of Knowledge. I, strangely, know more now about my own project than I did when I wrote it. Despite our disagreements about how some of the questions below are to be answered, I was exceedingly pleased to learn of their varying degrees of openness to and, in some cases, agreement with the central idea that there are factive states that fall short of knowledge. Perhaps these replies will increase our degree of agreement. Belief Fundamentalism, i.e., the thesis that belief is a constituent part of knowledge, is crucial for drawing a psychological line between the genus factual awareness (whose species can be obtained without belief) and knowledge (which is a species of factual awareness that constitutively requires belief). But Aronowitz develops a counterargument. We both hit our targets. But our targets are not the same.

articles.t: Awareness and the Substructure of Knowledge, By Paul Silva Jr
articles.ab: Paul Silva Jr Knowledge exists, and it’s normatively significant. There also exist knowledge-like states that fall short of knowledge, and these can also be normatively significant. We can call these normatively significant knowledge-like states whatever we like. In Awareness and the Substructure of Knowledge (Silva 2023) I call them states of factual awareness for semantic reasons. But those wanting to emphasize the connection of these states to knowledge itself could use another expression. Pick your term. It doesn’t matter. These states exist, and oversights concerning them are at the root of some persistent problems in epistemology. To start, what evidence is there that states of factual awareness can exist while falling short of knowledge? There are two approaches. Chapters 2 and 5 develop the first line of evidence by developing a ‘conceptually engineered’ concept that refers to these real factive relations. This approach starts with a view of knowledge as a high-grade state that requires a subset of the following: a true belief condition, a reliability condition on belief, an anti-luck condition on belief (e.g. safety) and an undefeated justification condition for believing (believing for sufficient reasons). Virtually all views of knowledge involve some subset of these conditions. The next step draws on evidence that believing that p is but one kind of state an agent can be in that represents p as true. This more general class of states includes, but need not be limited to, seeming states as well as constellations of belief and seeming states (plus inferential abilities) by which thinkers inferentially represent p as true. Generalizing away from safe representations to reliable representations (as safety is a kind of reliability), we can isolate a state of reliably formed true representation that is logically weaker than knowledge. It is a kind of state that exists and is entailed by, but does not itself entail, knowledge. When augmented with an adequate account of ‘reliable formation’, this kind of state seems to imply that one is aware of a fact in a sense of ‘aware’ that fits the semantic data that appear in Chapters 3 and 4.

articles.t: Awareness in the Context of the Mind
articles.ab: In these comments, I focus on three questions raised by Silva’s theory of awareness and propose an amendment to his original account. Silva’s (2023) book aims to put a new category on the table in epistemology: awareness. To be aware of a fact is to have a representation of it that is true and brought about in the right way. On some versions of awareness, ‘brought about in the right way’ means ‘brought about in a way that makes the representation non-accidentally true’. At the end of the book, Silva also puts forward a version of awareness which does not make explicit reference to luck. On this view, ‘brought about in the right way’ means ‘brought about by cognitive abilities to form true representations’. For instance, imagine I glance at a piece of paper and see that the letter is from my sister. I do this so quickly and subliminally that I can’t be said to believe the letter is from my sister. Moreover, I might hold misleading evidence that suggests the letter cannot be from my sister: she told me that she hates writing letters now and only sends emails. But in any case, I register that the letter is from my sister without believing it through my cognitive abilities, in this case attention and perception, which function to produce and maintain true representations. Thus I am aware that the letter is from my sister.

articles.t: A new argument for compatibilism
articles.ab: Abstract I offer a new argument for the compatibility of free will and determinism. The argument rests on three premisses, which are plausible and intuitive, or so I argue. Given that acceptance of the premisses commits one to a metaphysics that combines a causal powers ontology with a Humean conception of the laws of nature, I propose calling the resulting account of free will ‘semi-Humean compatibilism’.

articles.t: One Language, but Maybe Still Many True Logics?—A Review of One True Logic : A Monist Manifesto
articles.ab: Owen Griffiths and A.C. Paseau’s One True Logic: A Monist Manifesto is the first serious book-length defence of logical monism (and hence rejection of logical pluralism).1 As such, it will no doubt have an immense impact on debates about nihilist, monist and pluralist stances regarding logic for some time to come. But this influence will not be of the sort one might guess at based on the title alone. Debates regarding logical monism, pluralism and nihilism typically revolve around two inter-related questions: (The Counting Question) How many correct or acceptable logics are there? (The Identification Question) Which logic, or logics, are correct or acceptable? The first part of Griffiths and Paseau’s book, unsurprisingly given the title, argues that the correct answer to the Counting Question is ‘one’. Other works addressing the Counting Question, however, typically proceed by attempting to show that the author’s preferred algebraic codification (or codifications) of logical consequence is (or are) correct, or at least are better than the algebraic codifications of their opponents. In short, such arguments provide a direct answer to the Identification Question, and the Counting Question is settled as a corollary. Griffiths and Paseau, however, take a different track. They do not ‘officially’ endorse any one particular logical consequence relation (e.g. classical, intuitionistic, many-valued etc.) as the one true logic. Instead, their defence of logical monism takes a different approach, arguing for logical monism indirectly by way of an attempted refutation of logical pluralism. As a result, they do not (again, at least ‘officially’) answer the Identification Question at all.

Replies to Critics

articles.t: Why Classification May Not Matter in Category-Dependent Aesthetic Judgments
articles.ab: Abstract It is widely acknowledged that aesthetic judgments of works of art are (often, if not always) category-dependent. In this paper, I argue that the categories in which a work is correctly perceived, judged and appreciated are not necessarily the categories to which it actually belongs. The principle that the adequate appreciation of a work must be made in a category to which it belongs should be rejected because it cannot accommodate the strangeness of some innovative works of art. An innovative work might be correctly judged in an old category to which it does not belong, which supports my conclusion that classification may not really matter in category-dependent aesthetic judgments.

articles.t: Puzzlement as a Guide to Understanding
articles.ab: Abstract In this paper, I draw attention to a familiar yet overlooked epistemic state: puzzlement. We experience that by which we are puzzled as being in some way incomprehensible to us. Puzzlement is thus distinct from the mere absence of understanding. It is a polar rather than privative opposite of understanding. The distinction between puzzlement and the mere absence of understanding, I go on to argue, raises a novel problem for reductive analyses of understanding in terms of knowledge.

articles.t: Causalism and the Grounds of Agency
Whence Original Inquiry?
articles.ab: Can inquiry begin with a standpoint that is maximally non-committal or without presupposition? And if it can, what value might there be in such presupposition-free inquiry? I answer negatively on both fronts: such presupposition-free inquiry is neither possible for us, nor the only way available to us for knowing what our world is really like. I begin by defending these two claims. I then discuss how Fiocco’s (2024) recent book Time and the World: Every Thing and Then Some poses a direct challenge to my position, and how that challenge might be overcome.

articles.t: Essence and Emancipation: On Jenkins’ Ontology and Oppression
Time and the World: Every Thing and Then Some
Getting Lost Along the Way: Lenman’s Holism, Expressivism and Communitarian Constructivism
Is Global Error Theory (Sort Of) Defensible?
articles.ab: According to the global error theory, normative judgements are beliefs that ascribe normative properties, but as such properties do not exist, all normative judgements are false (Streumer 2017). Global error theory is not an intuitively plausible view. In his book The Possibility of Moral Community, Jimmy Lenman (2024: 9) makes the point effectively: For intelligent animals like (on a good day) us who care about what happens to them some things are smart and some things are dumb and we should do the smart things and not do the dumb things. This is not a puzzling fact. It is a bad idea to add large amounts of sulphuric acid to your bathwater before you get in the bath. There is no good reason to believe Socrates was in fact a rhinoceros. Other things being equal you ought not to plot the murders of all and only people who go out of their way to treat you kindly. These are not convictions it would be easy to give up or dismiss as nonsensical. That we might be wrong about stuff as basic as this … is hard to believe. A global normative error theory tells us that we are wrong. If it is true, it really does not matter what you do next. You could finish reading this book. Or you could eat it. Or you could hide in the cupboard, convinced that it is going to eat you. To echo John McEnroe, this cannot be serious. Can it?

articles.t: Against Modus Ponens for Might
articles.ab: Abstract Suppose that you and I are at the mint and see a new coin. We have no way of knowing whether the coin will ever be flipped. Still, we know something: We know that if the coin were flipped, it might land heads. We know that if the coin were flipped, it might land tails. Surprisingly, this simple case is flatly inconsistent with theories of counterfactuals from (1971, 1973) and (1968, 1980). In this short paper I explain why, and consider how the problem might be solved.

articles.t: Could the World Be Flat?
articles.ab: Flatworldism denies that there are hierarchical relationships of ontological priority between things: a coffee cup is no less fundamental than the particles that make it up, and a corporation is no less fundamental than its employees. In this discussion of Marc Fiocco's Time and World, I entertain several versions of flatworldism, including Fiocco's own version. After drawing connections between flatworldism and ontological pluralism, I suggest that some versions of flatworldism, including ontological pluralism and ontological nihilism, fare better with respect to explanatory power than Fiocco's formulation.

articles.t: The Educated Eye
Is Schouten’s Liberalism Radical Enough?
Oil and Water: Why Schouten’s Political Liberal Anatomy Cannot Accommodate Luck Egalitarianism
articles.ab: The Anatomy of Justice outlines a novel framework within liberal egalitarian political philosophy.One of her book's chief ambitions is to explain how two accounts of egalitarianism -'luck egalitarianism' and 'relational egalitarianism' -can be combined into a single coherent schema for thinking about justice.Schouten claims that this unification can be accomplished within a 'political liberal' framework.My main objection to Anatomy is that insofar as it purports to formulate a version of political liberalism, it cannot include a luck egalitarian component in its account of basic justice.My discussion proceeds in four parts.First, I provide some general background to the debate between luck and relational egalitarians.Second, I explain why luck egalitarianism is fundamentally incompatible with political liberalism.Third, I briefly note a concern with Anatomy's rejection of 'ideal theory'.Part four concludes.

articles.t: Response to Critics
A Risky Problem for Permutation Invariance
articles.ab: Abstract According to the principle of Permutation Invariance, the ethical comparison of welfare distributions should be unchanged by permutations on the set of individuals—including infinitary permutations, if the population is infinite. This paper highlights a problem for Permutation Invariance involving risky prospects, improving upon a related result due to Jonsson and Peterson (2020). It is shown that, given plausible auxiliary assumptions, proponents of Permutation Invariance must reject either a weak ex ante Pareto principle or the decision-theoretic axiom of negative dominance (introduced by Lederman, forthcoming).

articles.t: On Carolina Sartorio’s Causalism: Unifying Action and Free Action
The Anatomy of Justice

articles.t: Can eliminativism save evolutionary naturalism from defeat?
articles.ab: Abstract This paper evaluates whether eliminativism – the thesis that the posits of folk psychology do not refer to anything real – can be employed by the naturalist to deflect Alvin Plantinga’s evolutionary argument against naturalism (EAAN). I start by trotting out Plantinga’s argument. After that, I present the conditionalization problem and propose to treat eliminativism as a defeater-deflector against EAAN. I then argue that eliminativism does not fall prey to Plantinga’s response against other potential defeater-deflectors from philosophy of mind. The next part consists of showing why the probability that our cognitive faculties are reliable on evolutionary naturalism combined with eliminativism is high. The last part of the article is aimed at arguing that despite the initial appeal, eliminativism is not a solution most naturalists would be happy to adopt – that is because eliminativism forces the naturalist to interpret naturalism as a methodological postulate.

articles.t: Relational Egalitarianism and Reciprocity
Radical Ontology and the Limits of Inquiry
Why metaphysics is not like mathematics
articles.inst: Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico
articles.ab: Abstract In the recent literature, moderate naturalistic metaphysicians have been attempting to justify the existence of ‘free range’ analytic metaphysics by employing an analogy with pure mathematics: just as pure mathematics is justified by its potential applications to science, so too, they argue, is analytic metaphysics justified by its potential applications in philosophy of science. Employing standard textbook logical tools to evaluate analogies, we argue that the analogy doesn’t hold: there are relevant dissimilarities between the two disciplines. The grounds and domain of application of metaphysics and mathematics to science are ultimately different, and arguments intended to justify the epistemic value of metaphysics for science often presuppose its value rather than demonstrate it. This is why metaphysics is not like mathematics.

articles.t: Nonuniform Substitutions Can’t Get you From Classical Logic to any Traditional Relevant or Quasi-Relevant Logic
articles.ab: Abstract The paper demonstrates that you cannot land anywhere at all between the basic relevant logic B and the strongest traditional relevant logic R by restricting classical logic to the largest of its subsets that is invariant under any plausible class of nonuniform substitutions. Nor does it help to extend the upper limit to one of the quasi-relevant logics like RM3 or KR. This is a serious but not-quite-fatal blow to a tantalizing possibility raised by a body of recent work in the area.

articles.t: Voting as a Socially Constructed Duty
articles.ab: Abstract The “particularity problem” challenges arguments for a duty to vote by showing that the reasons usually offered—promoting the common good, avoiding free-riding, doing one’s part—can be satisfied by many alternative actions. We argue that this response does not always dissolve duties. Some actions remain obligatory even when substitutable, because cultural practices single them out as canonical expressions of underlying reasons. Celebrating birthdays is one example. Our culture fixes birthdays as the focal way of showing love and recognition, and parents who ignore them fail in their role, even if they meet the same ends in other ways. We argue that voting functions similarly.

articles.t: Teleosemantics and Metasemantics
articles.ab: Abstract What do you get if you cross the hypothesis that words are tools with the standard theory of how tools get their function determined? The Kripkean theory of reference. This note contextualizes this simple result as a bridge between teleosemantics and metasemantics.

articles.t: Global validity and the formality of logic
articles.ab: Abstract In a paper published in this journal, Golan argues for the thesis that there is no tenable notion of global metainferential validity. The conclusion rests on the premise that metainferential validity for propositional languages should be closed under uniform substitution of arbitrary formulas for atoms. This paper looks into Golan's justification for this premise in terms of the formality of logic. It is argued that neither formality as schematicity nor formality as topic-neutrality implies closure under uniform substitution of arbitrary formulas for atoms as requirement. It is also argued that the justification of such a requirement in terms of the formality of logic makes Golan's conclusion irrelevant for logical research.

articles.t: Domination, Freedom and Relational Egalitarianism
articles.ab: Abstract The republican critique of domination often rests on both a particular account of unfreedom – what will here be called ‘the any-option account’ – and an account of the badness of domination that appeals to the value of relational equality. This paper argues that these two accounts are incompatible: if what makes domination objectionable is that it undermines egalitarian social relations, then some alternative account of freedom must be adopted.

articles.t: Artificial Speech Acts
articles.ab: Abstract Can Large Language Models (LLMs) perform speech acts? I show how a norm-based argument against LLM-assertion can be generalized so as to support a negative answer to this question. I then investigate how the resulting no-speech-act-view interacts with several other debates about how to conceptualize the linguistic outputs of LLMs. I argue that it conflicts with the popular conception of LLMs as bullshitters and that it helps decide between two competing externalist accounts of how artificially generated expressions refer. I close by discussing a challenge to the no-speech-act-view and by suggesting a novel strategy for addressing it. A general lesson from this discussion is that our understanding of LLMs' linguistic outputs will profit from complementing extant meta-semantic theorizing with more detailed meta-pragmatic theorizing about discourse between humans and LLMs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

articles.t: Questioning the Grounds for Buddhist Physicalism
articles.ab: The Buddha puts forward a dualist metaphysics in the early Buddhist discourses (Nikayās). The first centuries after the Buddha’s death led to the emergence of multiple schools and traditions that attempted to organize, interpret and systematize the Buddha’s teachings. Though the philosophers in these traditions regarded the Nikayās as authoritative, that did not deter them from interpreting the Buddha’s teachings in ways that were conducive to their theoretical and practical concerns. For example, the Abhidharma philosophers reduced the five psychophysical aggregates (skandhas) into constituent, discrete psychophysical events (dharmas) and reinterpreted impermanence as momentariness. The Yogācāra school rejected the psychophysical dualism of the Nikayās in favour of consciousness-only idealism. It is in this spirit that Siderits (2025: 5) raises a closely related question: might there be room in the Buddhist tradition for a newly developed physicalism? Siderits presents considerations to suggest that a Buddhist physicalism is possible and indeed plausible. Siderits’ book is a masterful consideration of a live issue in contemporary philosophy: the place of consciousness in a physicalist world. We applaud the spirit of the book and Siderits’ motivation to consider Buddhist physicalism as a live option in contemporary philosophy, a contender for having the correct metaphysical view of phenomenal consciousness. In this critical notice, we will, of course, take a critical perspective on Siderits’ important book. Buddhist Physicalism? is wide-ranging; we will focus on one important set of themes regarding the ontology of composites and the invocation of persons.

articles.t: How Far Can We Take Frege at His Word?
articles.ab: [No abstract]

articles.t: Is divine aseity extrinsic?
articles.ab: Abstract Largely assumed to be intrinsic, recent work in analytic theology suggests aseity might be an extrinsic property. This has most vividly been discussed in the literature on the Christian trinitarian doctrine of divine processions, which requires aseity to be extrinsic so as to avoid the ontological subordination worry. This paper argues that the existing literature ignores a crucial point, which is that divine aseity is distinct from mere aseity. Consequently, I point out that while mere aseity may be extrinsic, divine aseity is still probably intrinsic.

articles.t: On what is said: Logic and Lies
articles.ab: Abstract While ordinary usage of saying allows both extensional and intensional interpreta-tions, only the extensional interpretation of Grice’s what is said is useful to a theory of lying. Yet what is said cannot be reduced to conventional meaning, for it obeys a Closure Principle: if one says something, one also says everything entailed by it.

articles.t: Normativity and the Indefinite Singular in Morality
articles.ab: Abstract Indefinite singular (IS) noun phrases—such as “A virtuous person prioritizes self-improvement”—are a familiar but under-theorized feature of moral discourse.
